yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight that he must speak with me, and I knew at once what such a message meant, as such messages generally do.

We met the next day at a coffee house in the town, where he was already seated, and so busy over the instrument in his hand that he did not at first perceive me. He looked nervous, and in the same breath professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his own.

I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded and said that it was all right, and then walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

My friend was of opinion that I made too much of the business; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me notwithstanding.

rows.text: Ryan sent me word at midnight that he must speak with me, and I knew at once what such a message meant, as such messages generally do.

notes.after: and I knew at once what such a message meant, as such messages generally do

notes.text: a framing generalization the matter invites, laying the narrator's dry judgement over her own case, in her usual way of irony
notes.after: as such messages generally do

rows.text: We met the next day at a coffee house in the town, where he was already seated, and so busy over the instrument in his hand that he did not at first perceive me. He looked nervous, and in the same breath professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his own.
I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded and said that it was all right, and then walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

notes.after: I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded and said that it was all right

rows.text: My friend was of opinion that I made too much of the business; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me notwithstanding.

lessons: Their passage tells the matter in bare, unjoined sentences, where Austen gathers the event, its meaning, and the narrator's judgement into one balanced period. I joined the three opening sentences into a single period ending on the general truth "as such messages generally do," which lets the narrator's dry irony land without adding any new feeling. His speech is reported rather than quoted ("he professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment"), and her composure is shown by conduct ("I only nodded") rather than named; practise joining your clauses with "and" and "but" so that the main point arrives late, and let feeling show in what people do.

the meeting at the coffee shop and what he said
walking home in the rain, ice cream, the narrator's composure
her roommate's verdict, her own doubt, and the hurt

plan.gist: the midnight message and its immediate meaning
plan.why: open with the event and let the narrator's knowledge of its meaning land in a period that ends hard

plan.gist: the meeting, his manner and his speech
plan.why: give feeling by conduct and countenance, and report his speech in the narrator's syntax

plan.gist: the walk home in the rain and the pint of ice cream
plan.why: her composure is shown by what she does, not named

plan.gist: the roommate's judgement, her own doubt, and the hurt that remains
plan.why: close on the turn of the matter: the verdict and the lingering hurt

faults.quote: My friend was of opinion
faults.why: The writer's 'roommate' became 'friend'. The relationship is changed and a detail dropped.

faults.quote: so busy over the instrument in his hand that he did not at first perceive me
faults.why: The writer only says he was scrolling on his phone. The rewrite adds that he did not notice her, which is a new incident beyond the source.

faults.quote: and in the same breath professed that he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his own
faults.why: 'In the same breath' ties his nervousness to the speech, which the source does not say. 'Attachment' also shifts 'serious' from the relationship to the feeling.

faults.quote: as such messages generally do
faults.why: This adds a sardonic general judgement and a slightly arch tone that the writer's plain, hurt narrator does not have. The note admits it is added commentary, but it tips the feeling toward irony and away from the sincere hurt.

faults.quote: as such messages generally do
faults.why: The phrase is awkward and nearly tautological ('such a message meant, as such messages do'). It reads as a clumsy pastiche, not a real Austen irony.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me word at midnight that he must speak with me
faults.why: 'Sent me word' is period-appropriate. But the rewrite keeps the modern first name 'Ryan', 'ice-cream' and 'the business' in a thin costume. The narration lacks Austen's balanced periods and free indirect judgement, and the passage is mostly flat transposition.

faults.quote: I only nodded and said that it was all right
faults.why: Reported speech is correct, but 'all right' is a modern idiom Austen would hardly use. 'Walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream' is likewise anachronistic and comic in this register.

faults.quote: ate a whole pint of ice-cream
faults.why: The modern image sits uneasily in the period diction. The rewrite does nothing to bridge it, so the effect is unintentionally comic.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 33, ¶ 38
faults.why: The citation is precise-looking but unconvincing as support for this move. Ch. 18, ¶ 9 for 'feeling shown by conduct' is similarly doubtful. The notes also skip the changes to 'coffee house', 'instrument', 'my friend' and the added 'did not perceive me'. Paragraphs 2 and 4 get no notes even though they hold the largest liberties.

faults.quote: I joined the three opening sentences into a single period
faults.why: The lesson claims a joined period, but it is only a loosely conjoined sentence with a tag. The advice about 'main point arrives late' is not borne out by the actual sentence, and nothing explains the invented 'instrument' detail.

faults.quote: but it hurt me notwithstanding
faults.why: This slightly softens the writer's flat 'it still hurt'. 'Notwithstanding' is stiff, and 'perhaps I did' follows the 'overreacting' doubt in a looser way than the original.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the events and their order but adds an invented detail (he did not notice her), changes 'roommate' to 'friend', and leans on a strained 'as such messages generally do'. The Austen voice is partial and the notes are thin and unreliable.

yours:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
My dear Papa and Mamma,

Camp is tolerable upon the whole, and I have no very great complaint to make of it. The food is, I am sorry to say, very indifferent; and the companion of my room snores so violently as to keep me from my rest. Yesterday we went upon the water in a little boat, and, in turning it, I was overturned into the lake, at which the whole party laughed without mercy. It was mortification enough for one day, as you may guess.

But there is one girl here, a Kayla, whom I like very much indeed, for she is from the country of Ohio, and knows more of horses than anybody I ever met with. We sit together by the lake after dinner and talk of everything in the world; and I am half of opinion that she likes me, though I cannot be quite sure of it.

Will you be so good as to send me a little more in the way of eating, and the cord for my little instrument of talking at a distance, which I foolishly left behind me. The people who have the care of us are rather strict, but upon the whole they are kind enough, and we are all very well.

Your affectionate son, Jake.

P.S. Pray do not let Max make use of my room while I am away.

rows.text: My dear Papa and Mamma,

Camp is tolerable upon the whole, and I have no very great complaint to make of it. The food is, I am sorry to say, very indifferent; and the companion of my room snores so violently as to keep me from my rest. Yesterday we went upon the water in a little boat, and, in turning it, I was overturned into the lake, at which the whole party laughed without mercy. It was mortification enough for one day, as you may guess.

But there is one girl here, a Kayla, whom I like very much indeed, for she is from the country of Ohio, and knows more of horses than anybody I ever met with. We sit together by the lake after dinner and talk of everything in the world; and I am half of opinion that she likes me, though I cannot be quite sure of it.

Will you be so good as to send me a little more in the way of eating, and the cord for my little instrument of talking at a distance, which I foolishly left behind me. The people who have the care of us are rather strict, but upon the whole they are kind enough, and we are all very well.

notes.after: the cord for my little instrument of talking at a distance

rows.text: Your affectionate son, Jake.
P.S. Pray do not let Max make use of my room while I am away.

lessons: Your letter names its feelings in one short slang word each ("okay", "gross", "so embarrassing"), where Austen names feeling and character in abstract nouns of judgement and lets the verdict land late. Try building each sentence as one balanced period with the point at the end, as in "at which the whole party laughed without mercy," and leaning on her nouns, as in "mortification enough for one day," which does the work of "so embarrassing" while suggesting the narrator is already beginning to laugh at himself.

plan.gist: Dear Mamma and Papa
plan.why: The letter keeps its salutation; her young letter-writers address parents warmly and simply.

plan.gist: Camp is tolerable, on the whole
plan.why: The deflating 'I guess' becomes a hedged verdict in her abstract nouns, setting the letter's dry tone.

plan.gist: the food is disagreeable and my companion snores
plan.why: Complaints are named in words of judgement and joined in one period, not listed in slang.

plan.gist: the canoe overturning and the laughter
plan.why: The incident is told in one balanced period with the point (the laughter) arriving last.

plan.gist: mortification
plan.why: The feeling is named by her noun of judgement, as the writer's 'so embarrassing' renders; a short verdict closes the paragraph.

plan.gist: Kayla described
plan.why: The remark is turned by 'but there is', and Kayla is introduced as the letter's pleasing object.

plan.gist: Ohio, horses, talk at the lake, uncertainty
plan.why: Her good qualities and their talks are joined in periods; the uncertainty keeps the writer's own hedge, in freer syntax.

plan.gist: more provisions, and the charger
plan.why: Requests are made plainly, the second confessing a want in the writer's own voice.

plan.gist: the conduct of the directors
plan.why: The slight strictness is given by litotes and judgement, the direction of feeling kept exact.

plan.gist: Your affectionate son, Jake
plan.why: A letter keeps a letter's close; her young writers sign with affection.

plan.gist: the room and Max
plan.why: The postscript stands apart, a plain request, as letters end.

faults.quote: went upon the water in a little boat, and, in turning it, I was overturned into the lake
faults.why: The canoe becomes 'a little boat', and 'flipped the canoe' becomes 'in turning it', which is not the same event. 'Into the lake' and Jake's own fall are added; the original only says he flipped the canoe.

faults.quote: so violently as to keep me from my rest
faults.why: The writer said only that the bunkmate snores like crazy. Lost sleep is a new consequence.

faults.quote: laughed without mercy
faults.why: 'Without mercy' sharpens the feeling beyond 'everybody laughed'.

faults.quote: whom I like very much indeed, for she is from the country of Ohio, and knows more of horses than anybody I ever met with
faults.why: 'For' makes Ohio and horses the reason he likes her, which the writer did not say. 'Knows a ton' becomes a superlative claim ('more than anybody I ever met').

faults.quote: talk of everything in the world
faults.why: 'Talk about stuff' is casual and vague, and this inflates it.

faults.quote: and we are all very well
faults.why: This is an invented assurance of general health that the writer never gave.

faults.quote: the country of Ohio
faults.why: Ohio is a state, so this reads as a slip or unintended comedy.

faults.quote: a little more in the way of eating
faults.why: This is an awkward, vague circumlocution for 'snacks'.

faults.quote: I have no very great complaint to make of it
faults.why: It sits oddly before an immediate list of complaints, so the sentence reads as slightly self-contradictory.

faults.quote: the cord for my little instrument of talking at a distance
faults.why: The periphrasis is so heavy that it becomes a joke, and it is a modern anachronism put in period dress. 'Cord' also loses 'charger'.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 31, ¶ 25
faults.why: The citation looks fabricated or unverifiable. Nothing in that passage is a periphrasis for a gadget, so the source is not apt.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Real changes go unnamed: 'okay I guess' to 'tolerable upon the whole', the litotes, 'mortification enough', 'a Kayla', the 'at which' construction and the formal signoff. Only one move is noted, and the notes do not match the rewrite's four paragraphs.

faults.quote: Your affectionate son, Jake.
faults.why: The sign-off is plausible, but the whole letter is stiffly formal for a young camper's letter. It leans on stock Regency phrases ('upon the whole', 'Pray', 'very well') more than on Austen's irony, so it reads as costume in places.

judge.verdict: A competent Regency-flavoured rewrite with an apt lesson, but it adds small facts and feelings, garbles the canoe, 'country of Ohio' and the charger periphrasis, and leaves nearly all of its moves unannotated. The one citation looks invented.

yours:
The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
The office was large, and fitted up in all the profusion of the newest taste; and every body in it wore the loose coarse dress of the place and drank coffee of a very superior sort. In my suit I felt myself wholly out of place, and could only hope that my countenance did not betray it.

The manager was a woman named Priya, who was friendly, though of a manner somewhat too eager; and she began directly upon the business for which I came, by asking me what I thought my powers, and what my failings. I said that I was one who could never leave any thing imperfect, which is, as every body who has ever been asked it knows, the confession of one who has nothing better to say; but she smiled, and seemed not disposed to think the worse of me for it.

When the interview was over I called my sister, who said she had no doubt I had performed it to admiration; and I hope she is right, for the rent falls due next week, and I am essentially without money.

I said that I was one who could never leave any thing imperfect, which is, as every body who has ever been asked it knows, the confession of one who has nothing better to say; but she smiled, and seemed not disposed to think the worse of me for it.

notes.after: I said that I was one who could never leave any thing imperfect, which is, as every body who has ever been asked it knows, the confession of one who has nothing better to say

notes.text: a dry generalisation the weak answer invites, letting the narrator's verdict fall on her own answer rather than merely naming it; the voice's one ironic liberty, and the passage's single such framing
notes.after: which is, as every body who has ever been asked it knows, the confession of one who has nothing better to say

rows.text: When the interview was over I called my sister, who said she had no doubt I had performed it to admiration; and I hope she is right, for the rent falls due next week, and I am essentially without money.

notes.after: who said she had no doubt I had performed it to admiration

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer names each thing in one short flat sentence, where the voice joins the matter into periods whose point arrives late, and lets judgement fall through abstract nouns and understatement rather than slang. The rewrite joins the three opening staccato sentences into one balanced period ("fitted up in all the profusion of the newest taste"), turns the lame answer into an ironic generalisation ("the confession of one who has nothing better to say"), and renders the sister's encouragement as reported speech ("she had no doubt I had performed it to admiration"). Practise joining short clauses with ", and" and "; and" so the verdict comes last, and letting the narrator's dryness do the work of the writer's adjectives.

plan.why: the voice sets the scene before the scene, so the out-of-place feeling has something to be out of place in

plan.why: the verdict on the self belongs at the end of the setting, arriving late in the period

faults.quote: and could only hope that my countenance did not betray it
faults.why: Invented content. The writer never says the narrator worried about hiding the discomfort. This is added anxiety, not commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: and I hope she is right, for the rent falls due next week, and I am essentially without money
faults.why: The writer's 'I really need this job' is dropped. That is the emotional point of the passage, and the structure notes themselves call it the point of the whole. The rent and being broke are kept, but the need for the job is gone.

faults.quote: she had no doubt I had performed it to admiration
faults.why: The sister's hedged 'probably nailed it' becomes certainty ('no doubt'), which intensifies the feeling beyond the writer's. 'To admiration' also overstates 'nailed it'.

faults.quote: of a manner somewhat too eager
faults.why: 'Intense' becomes 'eager', which is a different quality. The 'too' also adds a mild criticism the writer did not make.

faults.quote: wore the loose coarse dress of the place
faults.why: 'Hoodies' is rendered as 'coarse', which adds a disparaging judgement. The casual-versus-suit contrast survives only vaguely.

faults.quote: I am essentially without money
faults.why: 'Essentially' is a modern hedge used for 'basically', not in Austen's sense. The phrase reads awkwardly and weakens the stakes.

faults.quote: the loose coarse dress of the place
faults.why: 'Coarse' is odd for a description of casual clothing, and the phrase obscures what is meant.

faults.quote: which is, as every body who has ever been asked it knows, the confession of one who has nothing better to say
faults.why: Heavy and slightly confused. The long insertion before the main predicate makes the dry verdict clumsy.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 43, ¶ 5
faults.why: The citations give precise chapter and paragraph numbers for loose parallels. They look unverifiable and over-precise as support for the moves.

faults.quote: the voice's one ironic liberty, and the passage's single such framing
faults.why: The notes do not report the other additions and shifts: the 'countenance' clause, 'eager' for 'intense', 'no doubt' for 'probably', and the dropped need for the job. They claim fewer liberties than were taken.

faults.quote: I hope she is right, for the rent falls due next week
faults.why: The writer's closing beat, 'I really need this job', is gone. The close turns into a bare financial remark, so the intended emotional close is lost. The tense also drifts into the present.

faults.quote: the need arriving last as the point of the whole
faults.why: The lesson and build notes praise the need as the closing point, but the rewrite omitted it. The teaching does not match the output.

judge.verdict: The rewrite gets Austen's balanced periods and ironic generalisation, and it is mostly readable. But it drops 'I really need this job', adds an invented worry, inflates the sister's 'probably' into 'no doubt', and uses a non-Austen 'essentially'. The notes also under-report these changes.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children. The father seemed an amiable man; his sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast.

My mother, who could never rest till she knew the whole of any new arrival, carried over a plate of biscuits almost before the family had done taking out. She meant to learn where they came from, what the father did for a living, and whether they went to church, and she did not return till she had satisfied herself on every one of these points.

It was soon learnt that the father was a lawyer, and that he was a single man; that is to say, he had been parted from his wife. My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to settle me for years.

rows.text: A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children. The father seemed an amiable man; his sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast.

notes.text: The first paragraph gives the household a mother and father together — 'The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish' — so the 'mom' first reads as the father's wife; the last paragraph then says the dad is 'single. Well, divorced.' I made the standoffish woman the father's sister who shares his house: the household keeps a second adult, the narrator's mother still has someone to receive her, and nothing said of her (her coolness, her place in the house) conflicts with her being a sister, whereas a wife cannot stand beside 'single.'
notes.after: The father seemed an amiable man. His sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast.

rows.text: My mother, who could never rest till she knew the whole of any new arrival, carried over a plate of biscuits almost before the family had done taking out. She meant to learn where they came from, what the father did for a living, and whether they went to church, and she did not return till she had satisfied herself on every one of these points.

It was soon learnt that the father was a lawyer, and that he was a single man; that is to say, he had been parted from his wife. My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to settle me for years.

notes.text: The passage echoes Pride and Prejudice's opening: a new household arrives, and a mother schemes to marry her child to the eligible man in it. The rewrite takes the method of showing the mother's scheme through busy neighbourly conduct (the biscuits standing in for the visit of introduction) and through the child's dry, knowing narration; it also keeps the man's eligibility — lawyer, divorced — established before the mother's look, so the look has its cause, as Mrs Bennet acts only on a confirmed single man of fortune.
notes.after: My mother would not lose a moment in carrying over a plate of biscuits … It was soon learnt that the father was a lawyer, and parted from his wife. My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake.
My mother's countenance, at this intelligence, took a look which I had too often seen to mistake; I knew exactly what she was thinking.

notes.text: The voice lets the narrator, looking back, judge the mother's scheme dryly in a brief closing clause, as Austen's children-narrators report a parent's designs; it adds no new incident, only the knowing frame the passage itself invites by ending on the set-up.
notes.after: which I had too often seen to mistake

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage names each plain fact in a short, unjudging sentence, while Austen builds long periods that let the narrator judge as she tells. Most of my sentences join two of yours with a semicolon, and the judgement comes in her abstract nouns — 'an amiable man', 'a colder cast' — so the reader feels the narrator's dry eye on the mother long before the close. Practise the balanced period ('A new family came to live next door at the end of last week, with a large cart and two little children') and the verdict by understatement ('She has been trying to settle me for years', whose 'settle' keeps the comic distance without a single modern phrase).

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the household a mother and father together — “The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish” — so the “mom” first read as the father's wife; your last paragraph then says the dad is “single. Well, divorced.”
sense.quote: The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the standoffish woman the father's sister, not his wife: “The dad seems nice. His sister, who lives with him, is kind of standoffish.” — the least change, since the household keeps a second adult, the narrator's mother still has someone to be received by, and nothing said of her (coolness, sharing the house) conflicts with her being a sister, whereas wife cannot stand beside “single.”

sense.problem: A true echo: a new household arrives in the neighbourhood and a mother schemes to marry her child to the eligible man in it.
sense.quote: A new family moved in next door last weekend. … My mom got this look on her face. … She has been trying to set me up for years.
sense.resolution: Pride and Prejudice, opening: the arrival of a single man of good fortune and a mother's campaign to secure him. The rewrite may take from it the method of letting the mother's scheme show through busy neighbourly action (the cookies standing in for the visit of introduction), and the habit of reporting the parent's designs through the child's dry, knowing narration — but it must earn the eligibility: Austen's Mrs Bennet acts on a confirmed single man of fortune, so keep “lawyer” and “divorced” before the look, never after it.

faults.quote: his sister, who keeps his house, was of a colder cast
faults.why: The writer said 'the mom'. The rewrite makes her a sister and adds that she keeps his house. The mend was needed, but the housekeeping detail is an invention beyond what the mending required, and it makes her the father's sister rather than leaving her an unspecified woman.

faults.quote: she did not return till she had satisfied herself on every one of these points
faults.why: This invents an incident: the mother's long stay and her satisfaction. The writer only said she wanted to find out everything.

faults.quote: almost before the family had done taking out
faults.why: This adds a detail about timing and unloading. The writer's 'right away' is kept, but the phrase is clumsy and elliptical, with an object missing after 'taking out'.

faults.quote: at the end of last week
faults.why: The writer said 'last weekend'. The phrase shifts the timing slightly.

faults.quote: that is to say, he had been parted from his wife
faults.why: This is a reasonable rendering of 'divorced'. It also reintroduces a wife, which sits oddly beside the sister who now fills the mom's place and is not explained.

faults.quote: a large cart
faults.why: A 'huge truck' becomes a 'large cart'. The substitution is period-flavored but loses the writer's emphasis, and a cart for a lawyer's household is odd.

faults.quote: took a look which I had too often seen to mistake
faults.why: The syntax is slightly strained: 'took a look' is an awkward verb phrase for a countenance, and the sentence leans on an unidiomatic construction.

faults.quote: who keeps his house, was of a colder cast
faults.why: The present tense 'keeps' sits beside the past 'was', and the tenses are mixed.

faults.quote: I knew exactly what she was thinking.
faults.why: This is left in plain modern phrasing. 'Exactly' is not Austen's register and it reads as modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: The voice lets the narrator, looking back, judge the mother's scheme dryly in a brief closing clause, as Austen's children-narrators report a parent's designs
faults.why: Austen has no children-narrators. The claim is inaccurate, and no closing clause was added, so the note describes nothing.

faults.quote: cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 22, ¶ 40
faults.why: The citation is unlikely to support the specific sentence. It is vague and probably not verifiable, and it is attached to a move that is mostly the rewriter's own invention.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The second paragraph made notable changes (invented satisfaction, 'biscuits' for cookies, 'could never rest till') but none are noted.

faults.quote: the biscuits standing in for the visit of introduction
faults.why: This overclaims Austen's practice and mislabels what the rewrite does. The Mrs Bennet comparison is aptly drawn, but the claim that she 'acts only on a confirmed single man' is a loose reading.

faults.quote: the household keeps a second adult, the narrator's mother still has someone to receive her
faults.why: The mending rationale is partly speculative and the 'someone to receive her' point is invented. The mend itself is acceptable, but it is justified with reasoning the text does not support.

faults.quote: Most of my sentences join two of yours with a semicolon
faults.why: This is inaccurate: the rewrite has few semicolon joins. The lesson is partly generic, and 'settle' is not shown to be a transferable move.

judge.verdict: The rewrite correctly catches and mends the mom/divorced contradiction and has a passable Austenian surface. But it invents incidents (the mother's lingering, the sister who keeps house), leaves some modern phrasing, and its notes include inaccurate claims about Austen and a doubtful citation.

yours:
The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:
The party was at Jessica's house; and as her parents were out of town, the whole was conducted very much as the younger people pleased, the music being suffered to be exceedingly loud. We stood in the kitchen, my friend Emma and I, knowing scarcely anybody of the company; when a tall young man, whose name was Chris, came over and began talking to us. He had rather too much of self-importance about him, but was, at the same time, not wanting in humour.

He declared the party to be excessively dull, and the people tiresome; an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility. Emma could not help rolling her eyes; and I thought him very rude. It was afterwards, however, when everybody else had left, that I saw him helping to clear away; and I could no longer feel that I had judged him rightly.

rows.text: The party was at Jessica's house; and as her parents were out of town, the whole was conducted very much as the younger people pleased, the music being suffered to be exceedingly loud. We stood in the kitchen, my friend Emma and I, knowing scarcely anybody of the company; when a tall young man, whose name was Chris, came over and began talking to us. He had rather too much of self-importance about him, but was, at the same time, not wanting in humour.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: The party was at Jessica's house; and as her parents were out of town, the whole was conducted very much as the younger people pleased, the music being suffered to be exceedingly loud.

rows.text: He declared the party to be excessively dull, and the people tiresome; an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility. Emma could not help rolling her eyes; and I thought him very rude. It was afterwards, however, when everybody else had left, that I saw him helping to clear away; and I could no longer feel that I had judged him rightly.

notes.text: None: the passage hangs together, and reaches its point, which is that a hasty judgement is undone by seeing what a man does when unobserved. No mending needed. The nearest scene of Austen's is Darcy at Hunsford (Pride and Prejudice ch. 34), pride judged too soon and the judgement afterwards revisited; the rewrite takes from it the discipline of letting the offence be spoken aloud and the reversal come through a single observed act rather than a stated moral.
notes.after: It was afterwards, however, when the rest of the company had gone, that I saw him helping to clear away; and I could no longer feel that I had judged him rightly.
an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility.
Emma could not help rolling her eyes; and I thought him very rude.

notes.text: A narrator's verdict on the speech the writer reported, in Austen's abstract noun of judgement; the matter already implies the rudeness the next sentence states.
notes.after: an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility

lessons: Your passage tells the same matter in eleven short, bare statements; Austen's manner is to let a scene stand in a few long periods whose clauses balance on semicolons and 'and', the main judgement arriving late. Joining your first three sentences into one period ('The party was at Jessica's house; and as her parents were out of town...') gives the setting a single composed shape; and turning your 'He said the party was lame...' into reported speech with a dry verdict laid on it ('an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility') lets the narrator judge what is there instead of merely recording it. Practise joining your short sentences into balanced periods, and letting your narrator close a sentence with an understated verdict of her own.

outline.gist: Party at Jessica's house, parents away
Everyone from school present; music loud
Narrator and Emma in the kitchen, knowing few people
Tall young man Chris approaches and talks
He is arrogant but amusing
He calls the party dull and the people tiresome; Emma rolls her eyes
Narrator thinks him rude
Later sees him helping clear up after everyone left
Perhaps the narrator was wrong about him

plan.gist: The party and the absence of Jessica's parents, told as one period
plan.why: Austen anchors a scene in a single composed sentence of place and circumstance before anything happens.

plan.gist: The company and the loud music
plan.why: The setting of the crowd comes before the narrower scene, so the kitchen feels like a refuge within it.

plan.gist: Emma and the narrator in the kitchen, knowing few
plan.why: The point of view settles on the two girls and their isolation before the stranger enters.

plan.gist: Chris's approach and his manner
plan.why: The man is named and judged in the same period, so the offence and its agent arrive together.

plan.gist: His reported censure of the party, and Emma's look
plan.why: Reported speech keeps his rudeness in the narrator's own dry voice; Emma's face shews the judgement without stating it.

plan.gist: The narrator thinks him rude
plan.why: A brief verdict sentence stands alone for the turn.

plan.gist: Later, the observed act of clearing up
plan.why: The reversal comes as a single unobserved act, as it does in Persuasion's letter and Darcy's later conduct, not as a moral spelt out.

plan.gist: Perhaps I was wrong about him
plan.why: The last sentence, short, lets the whole point land.

sense.problem: None: no contradiction, unclear person or missing step; the telling reaches its point, which is that a hasty judgement of a person can be undone by seeing what he does when unobserved.
sense.quote: But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
sense.resolution: No mending needed. The nearest scene of Austen's is Darcy at Hunsford (Pride and Prejudice ch. 34): pride judged too soon, and the judgement later revisited. A rewrite may take from it the discipline of letting the offence be spoken aloud and the reversal come through a single observed act rather than a stated moral — but nothing here is at fault.

faults.quote: The party was at Jessica's house; and as her parents were out of town, the whole was conducted very much as the younger people pleased, the music being suffered to be exceedingly loud.
faults.why: The writer's 'Everyone from school was there' is dropped without comment. 'Conducted very much as the younger people pleased' is an inference the writer never made.

faults.quote: and I could no longer feel that I had judged him rightly.
faults.why: The writer's 'Maybe I was wrong about him' is tentative. The rewrite states a firmer conclusion, so the degree of feeling shifts.

faults.quote: Emma could not help rolling her eyes
faults.why: 'Could not help' adds an involuntary quality to Emma's reaction that the writer did not give.

faults.quote: an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility; ... and I thought him very rude.
faults.why: The narrator's added verdict on incivility is followed at once by 'very rude', so the same judgement is said twice. The writer's turn from the speech to 'I thought he was rude' is blunted.

faults.quote: not wanting in humour ... an opinion which, it must be owned, wanted civility
faults.why: 'Wanting/wanted' is used twice in two different senses within a few lines, which sounds repetitive.

faults.quote: the whole was conducted very much as the younger people pleased
faults.why: 'The whole was conducted' is an awkward construction. It also casts a casual house party as a managed event.

faults.quote: The party was at Jessica's house;
faults.why: The opening clause is a flat modern declarative, only stitched to the next clause with a semicolon. Austen would more likely open with a more composed and circumstantial sentence.

faults.quote: We stood in the kitchen, my friend Emma and I, knowing scarcely anybody of the company;
faults.why: First-person recollection with 'my friend Emma and I' is more modern chatty than Austen's detached narration. The narrator never voices the dry irony Austen's narrator would.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 47, ¶ 32
faults.why: The chapter and paragraph citations look invented, and the sentence cited has nothing to do with the cited passage. The same holds for the Mansfield Park ch. 12 ¶ 23 and Pride and Prejudice ch. 59 ¶ 21 citations. Specific numbers give a false precision.

faults.quote: a hasty judgement is undone by seeing what a man does when unobserved.
faults.why: The writer never says Chris was unobserved. The note also compares the passage to Darcy at Hunsford, which does not match a reversal through a small observed act.

faults.quote: Feeling shown by conduct: “Emma could not help rolling her eyes; and I thought him very rude.”
faults.why: The eye-roll was the writer's own detail, so crediting it as an Austen move overstates what changed. The notes do not report the dropped 'Everyone from school' or the strengthened ending.

faults.quote: The last sentence, short, lets the whole point land.
faults.why: The rewrite's ending is a long, hedged-by-nothing sentence, not the short closing line the outline says. The outline also describes a 'brief verdict sentence [that] stands alone' that the rewrite lacks. The lesson's 'first three sentences' joined does not match the rewrite, which lost the third.

faults.quote: It was afterwards, however, when everybody else had left, that I saw him helping to clear away;
faults.why: The order is kept, but the writer's short closing doubt is turned into a settled conclusion, and the outline's promised stand-alone verdict is not delivered.

judge.verdict: A competent Austenian pastiche with some apt diction, but it silently drops 'Everyone from school', hardens the writer's tentative ending, and repeats the rudeness verdict. The notes use dubious precise citations and the outline and lesson describe features (short closing sentence, three joined sentences) the rewrite does not have.

yours:
I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
I wanted milk, and therefore took my keys and drove to the store. The place was exceedingly crowded, and a man in a hooded jacket stood in the passage the whole breadth of the aisle, talking upon his telephone with that particular pretence of occupation which a telephone conversation is so apt to give.

I had no wish to be rude, and therefore begged his pardon and would have passed; but he took not the smallest notice of me, and it was some minutes before he moved and I could get the milk. Then it was that I saw my former suitor at the counter, and was thrown into a confusion I could not well command.

"Hey," said she; "long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," said I; "you too." I paid and left with all the speed I could, and, honestly, the whole had been the work of the most awkward ten minutes of my week.

rows.text: I wanted milk, and therefore took my keys and drove to the store. The place was exceedingly crowded, and a man in a hooded jacket stood in the passage the whole breadth of the aisle, talking upon his telephone with that particular pretence of occupation which a telephone conversation is so apt to give.

notes.text: the voice supplies the judgement that the man's manner of ignoring her was no accident but an affectation of the instrument; this is the narrator's dry verdict on the snub, and it is the one irony the scene invites.
notes.after: with that particular pretence of occupation which a telephone conversation is so apt to give

rows.text: I had no wish to be rude, and therefore begged his pardon and would have passed; but he took not the smallest notice of me, and it was some minutes before he moved and I could get the milk. Then it was that I saw my former suitor at the counter, and was thrown into a confusion I could not well command.
"Hey," said she; "long time no see. You look great."

notes.technique: Speech tagged after its first clause
notes.after: "Hey," said she; "long time no see. You look great."

rows.text: "Thanks," said I; "you too." I paid and left with all the speed I could, and, honestly, the whole had been the work of the most awkward ten minutes of my week.

notes.after: the whole had been the work of the most awkward ten minutes of my week.

notes.text: the voice sums the matter as a piece of business concluded, which lets the last line land as a verdict rather than a mere complaint.
notes.after: the whole had been the work

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences run short and each does one thing, where Austen gathers several matters into one balanced period and lets the point land in the final clause: \"I wanted milk, and therefore took my keys and drove to the store\" joins your three-sentence opening into a single movement. The feeling of your panic is raised into an abstraction the voice can handle — \"thrown into a confusion I could not well command\" — which lets the narrator name the state without losing composure. And the snub is made ironic by litotes, \"took not the smallest notice of me,\" which damns the man more than \"totally ignored\" ever could. Practise joining your short sentences with \", and\" and \"; but\", and naming a feeling by its conduct rather than its force.

outline.gist: errand: milk needed, so drove to the store
store crowded; a hoodied man blocked the aisle, talking on his phone
narrator said excuse me; he ignored her; at last he moved and she got the milk
saw her ex at the checkout and panicked
brief polite exchange with the ex
paid and left fast; most awkward ten minutes of the week

plan.gist: the errand, briefly stated, with its reason
plan.why: Austen opens with the necessity that sets the matter in motion, named plainly.

plan.gist: the crowded store and the man blocking the passage
plan.why: the difficulty of the place is set before the difficulty of the person, so the scene has its ground.

plan.gist: the request, the disregard, the eventual yielding
plan.why: the small trial is told in one balanced period, the snub and its issue together.

plan.gist: the ex at the checkout, felt as mortification
plan.why: the real point of the errand arrives here, and is made to land hardest by being withheld till now.

plan.gist: the brief civilities
plan.why: speech kept short, as it is in life, and reported with the narrator's dry economy.

plan.gist: the retreat and the narrator's judgement on the whole
plan.why: the ironic verdict closes it, as Austen closes a small scene with a summing word.

faults.quote: my former suitor at the counter
faults.why: The ex is a woman ('she said'). 'Suitor' is a man who woos, so it changes the relationship and the sex of the figure, and it says nothing of a past romance between equals. 'Former' is also thin for 'ex'.

faults.quote: with that particular pretence of occupation which a telephone conversation is so apt to give
faults.why: This invents a claim that the man is only pretending to be busy. The writer never said so. It is more than commentary, since it recasts what the man was doing.

faults.quote: it was some minutes before he moved
faults.why: The writer said only 'finally'. A specific duration is an added fact.

faults.quote: stood in the passage the whole breadth of the aisle
faults.why: 'Passage' and 'aisle' name the same thing, so the phrase is clumsy and almost garbled. Austen would not write it this way.

faults.quote: the whole had been the work of the most awkward ten minutes of my week
faults.why: 'The work of' is a malapropism. The ten minutes are the episode itself, not something that did or produced it. The closing verdict, the line meant to land, is muddled.

faults.quote: "Hey," said she; "long time no see. You look great."
faults.why: The modern slang is left untouched in an Austen frame ('Hey', 'long time no see'). The dialogue reads as costume, and the semicolon tag does not fix it.

faults.quote: and, honestly, the whole had been
faults.why: 'Honestly' is a modern filler and sits oddly in an otherwise formal period. 'Telephone' and 'hooded jacket' also sit awkwardly with the diction.

faults.quote: thrown into a confusion I could not well command
faults.why: The writer's 'basically panicked' is casual and self-mocking. This formal rendering softens the comic panic and loses its force.

faults.quote: the voice supplies the judgement that the man's manner of ignoring her was no accident but an affectation of the instrument
faults.why: The note misdescribes the added clause. It sits before any snub, and it is about pretended busyness, not the ignoring. The note also assumes the narrator is female, though the draft never says so.

faults.quote: cites Northanger Abbey, ch. 25, ¶ 1
faults.why: The citation looks inapt or unreliable. That passage gives no model for this phrase, which is itself the garbled one. The Emma ch. 51 citation for speech tags is likewise doubtful.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 2 holds a real change: 'would have passed' is added and the plain sentences are recast with 'begged his pardon'. The lesson praises the litotes there, yet no note records it.

faults.quote: joins your three-sentence opening into a single movement
faults.why: The writer's opening is two sentences, so the lesson is inaccurate. The 'naming a feeling by its conduct' advice is also shaky, since the rewrite names it as 'confusion'.

judge.verdict: The shape is kept and a few Austenian moves are real (the 'therefore' opening, litotes, the speech tags), but the rewrite has a wrong-gender 'suitor', added claims about the man and the delay, and a garbled final sentence. The notes' citations and descriptions are shaky, so the teaching is only partly reliable.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
To all who are concerned in the undertaking,

The setting up, which was to have been on Tuesday, is now fixed for Thursday; for the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices, and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature.

I must beg that each of you will have your several parts of the papers ready by noon on Wednesday; and whoever among you is at a stand, let him tell me of it today, and not tomorrow.

With thanks, Sam.

rows.text: To all who are concerned in the undertaking,

notes.text: The writer's bare 'Hi team' becomes a formal address; the voice names the persons by what they are about rather than by a modern word, which is her way of opening a note of business.
notes.after: To all who are concerned in the undertaking,

rows.text: The setting up, which was to have been on Tuesday, is now fixed for Thursday; for the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices, and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature.

notes.after: for the lawyers have not yet signed the list of prices, and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature.

notes.text: The voice frames the bare change of day as a matter appointed and then altered, giving the news its due weight in one balanced period rather than two staccato clauses.
notes.after: which was to have been on Tuesday, is now fixed for Thursday

rows.text: I must beg that each of you will have your several parts of the papers ready by noon on Wednesday; and whoever among you is at a stand, let him tell me of it today, and not tomorrow.
With thanks, Sam.

lessons: Your note commands and staccatos; the author's manner joins each fact to its cause and its condition in one balanced period, so that the delay and its reason arrive together ("for the lawyers have not yet signed... and I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature"). She turns bare commands into reported entreaties ("I must beg that each of you...") and lets the warning land by understatement ("at a stand... and not tomorrow"), which the reader feels as courtesy rather than office pressure. Practise joining two of your short sentences with "for" or "; and", and putting a request as what you "beg" rather than what you order.

reading.kind: letter (a brief business note of news, reason, request, and close)

outline.gist: Address the team
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed the pricing page; do not ship without it
Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
If blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow
Thanks, Sam

plan.gist: Address the persons concerned in the undertaking
plan.why: A note of business opens on its company, as a letter opens on its reader; the voice names the persons rather than the modern 'team'.

plan.gist: The delay, and the cause of it, in one period
plan.why: Her periods join the fact and its cause with 'for', the news first and the reason following, so the reader takes the whole matter at once.

plan.gist: The readiness of the papers, and the warning against silence
plan.why: The request is put as a reported entreaty rather than a bare command, and the condition attached to it, so the two turn on one point of time.

plan.gist: Thanks, with the name
plan.why: Her letters end on a short courteous line, the thanks and the name standing alone.

faults.quote: The setting up, which was to have been on Tuesday
faults.why: "Launch" becomes "setting up", which does not name a product or service going public. The reader cannot tell what is being moved.

faults.quote: the list of prices
faults.why: The writer's "pricing page" is a specific page of the product or site. A "list of prices" is a different object, and the lawyers' sign-off is now about a list, not the page.

faults.quote: I would not send it abroad while it wanted that signature
faults.why: "It" can refer to the list of prices or to the setting up. The writer's "shipping without it" was unambiguous, and the rewrite introduces a muddle.

faults.quote: send it abroad
faults.why: "Send abroad" suggests dispatching something overseas. It does not mean releasing a product, so the idiom is a stretch and reads as a riddle.

faults.quote: let him tell me of it today, and not tomorrow
faults.why: The "let him" imperative addressed to a mixed team is stiff, and the masculine pronoun shifts away from the "you" the writer used. It also reads like a rule-giver, not Austen's courteous register.

faults.quote: With thanks, Sam.
faults.why: The close is flat and modern in cadence, with the name run onto the same line. Austen's closing courtesies are more formed, so this stays close to the original "Thanks, Sam".

faults.quote: To all who are concerned in the undertaking,
faults.why: The phrasing is a plausible costume, but the whole note is two sentences of bureaucratic periphrasis. It lacks the ironic observation, free indirect colouring, or characteristic Austen vocabulary that would mark it as her.

faults.quote: cites Persuasion, ch. 9, ¶ 29
faults.why: The citation pins a passage in Persuasion to a sentence the rewrite itself composed. The reference looks invented or inapt, and it does not show a real Austen sentence that does the move.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 3:
  (no notes)
Paragraph 4:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The rewrite's request paragraph ("I must beg") and the "let him tell me" warning carry the main moves, yet go unannotated. The structure note's paragraph numbers do not match the rewrite's three paragraphs.

faults.quote: The request is put as a reported entreaty rather than a bare command
faults.why: "I must beg that each of you will" is a direct entreaty, not a reported one. The claim mislabels the move, and the warning is not softened in any such way.

faults.quote: lets the warning land by understatement ("at a stand... and not tomorrow")
faults.why: "Not tomorrow" is the writer's own blunt phrasing carried over, not understatement. The lesson misattributes the effect and may mislead the writer.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and the requests and has a genuine Austen-like "I must beg" and a balanced "for" period. But "setting up", "list of prices" and "send it abroad" blur what is being launched and what is awaited. The notes cite a doubtful source, mislabel a move, and leave key sentences unannotated.

yours:
Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: The Saturday was spent in cleaning the gutters, in mending the sink, which had long wanted it, and in calling upon my grandmother, who talked for a full hour of her neighbour's cat. By the evening I was exhausted, yet felt no little pride in myself; a satisfaction of which I was not ashamed.

rows.text: The Saturday was spent in cleaning the gutters, in mending the sink, which had long wanted it, and in calling upon my grandmother, who talked for a full hour of her neighbour's cat. By the evening I was exhausted, yet felt no little pride in myself; a satisfaction of which I was not ashamed.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: felt no little pride in myself
a satisfaction of which I was not ashamed

notes.text: the writer's 'proud of myself' is rendered as a framed verdict the narrator may own only by understatement, which is her way of making pride agreeable.
notes.after: a satisfaction of which I was not ashamed

lessons: Your passage names its doings and its feeling plainly, one sentence each; Austen lets the day's business stand in a single balanced period and keeps the feeling for a closing verdict, where 'no little pride' (litotes) does the work of 'weirdly proud' more quietly. The pride is owned only through understatement, 'a satisfaction of which I was not ashamed', which makes it agreeable rather than boastful; practise one such balanced period and one litotes close on your own matter.

outline.gist: Saturday's occupations: gutters, sink, grandmother's long call about a neighbour's cat
by evening, exhausted but oddly proud

plan.gist: the day's work and the grandmother's call, in order of doing
plan.why: Austen sets the day's business plainly before any reflection on it, letting the facts speak before the verdict.

plan.gist: the evening's fatigue and pride, in one judging sentence
plan.why: she closes on the narrator's verdict on the whole, the pride qualified by litotes so the irony lands gently.

faults.quote: in mending the sink, which had long wanted it
faults.why: Invents a fact: the sink had long needed mending. It also drops the writer's 'leaky', so the fault being fixed is no longer named.

faults.quote: calling upon my grandmother
faults.why: In Austen's usage 'calling upon' means paying a visit in person. The writer telephoned, so the act is changed, and the period idiom is misapplied.

faults.quote: yet felt no little pride in myself
faults.why: 'Weirdly' is lost. The writer's surprise at being proud, the mild oddness of the feeling, is replaced by plain strong pride.

faults.quote: a satisfaction of which I was not ashamed
faults.why: Adds a new attitude, a defensive denial of shame, that the writer never expressed. It goes beyond commentary on what is there and changes the feeling from puzzled to self-justifying.

faults.quote: The Saturday was spent
faults.why: 'The Saturday' with the article reads oddly. The writer's day is simply 'Saturday', and the opening feels stiff rather than idiomatic.

faults.quote: who talked for a full hour of her neighbour's cat
faults.why: Austen would usually colour this with ironic commentary on the grandmother's talk, or at least a balanced clause. Here it is plain, so the voice is thin and mostly rests on archaic phrasing and one litotes.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 59, ¶ 34
faults.why: The paragraph-level citation is doubtful and unverifiable, and the passage does not clearly illustrate the litotes claimed. It looks like false precision.

faults.quote: cites Mansfield Park, ch. 12, ¶ 23
faults.why: The same doubtful precision. 'Ironic verdict' is also a stretch for a sentence that sincerely says the narrator is not ashamed.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the writer's 'proud of myself' is rendered as a framed verdict
faults.why: The notes do not report the real liberties: the invented 'which had long wanted it', the lost 'leaky' and 'weirdly', and the change of 'call' to 'calling upon'.

faults.quote: practise one such balanced period and one litotes close on your own matter
faults.why: Only two moves are offered, and the lesson is somewhat generic. It does not show how to turn a list into Austen's cadence, or why the closing denial of shame works.

judge.verdict: A compact, readable rewrite with a passable Austen flavour, but it invents a detail about the sink, misuses 'calling upon', loses 'weirdly', and adds a feeling of not being ashamed. The notes use shaky citations, leave these changes unreported, and teach little.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to carriages on the days of rest. To put a carriage anywhere in the town is a thing of no small difficulty, and the pavements are too narrow for the carriages of children; other places have made the trial, and their shopkeepers are doing better than they have ever done before.

Some persons in trade will complain that their customers cannot reach them; but they will grow accustomed to it. Most people walk from the carriage-house already, in truth.

We should make the trial this summer.

a thing of no small difficulty

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage gives bare statements in short sentences, while the author's manner names the difficulty in a period of balanced clauses and lets the narrator's judgement fall understated. I joined your three short middle sentences into balanced periods with "and" and ";" so the particulars arrive before the verdict ("a thing of no small difficulty"), and I rendered "nightmare" and "garage" as "no small difficulty" and "carriage-house" in her words. Practise building one period that holds complaint and answer together, as in "but they will grow accustomed to it," where the turn lands hardest.

plan.why: the proposal named at once, in the narrator's formal, deliberative register

plan.gist: the placing of carriages is a great inconvenience and the pavements too narrow
plan.why: the reasons follow in one period, joined, the particulars before the verdict

plan.gist: other places have tried it and their shopkeepers do better than ever
plan.why: the precedent lends judgment, the improvement made to sound greater than before

plan.why: the objection stated plainly, then its weight taken off at once

faults.quote: the pavements are too narrow for the carriages of children
faults.why: 'Strollers' becomes 'carriages of children', yet 'carriages' is also the word for the vehicles being banned. The sentence now confuses the two senses. Closing the street to carriages would also seem to help the narrow pavements less than it should.

faults.quote: Most people walk from the carriage-house already
faults.why: A carriage-house is a private outbuilding for storing carriages, not a public garage. The transposition is a mistranslation, and walking from one's own carriage-house to Main Street makes little sense for the argument.

faults.quote: Our town should close Main Street to carriages on the days of rest.
faults.why: 'Weekends' becomes 'days of rest', which is Sunday only. This is a shift in meaning, and 'Our town should close' is left in modern phrasing.

faults.quote: To put a carriage anywhere in the town is a thing of no small difficulty
faults.why: The writer said downtown parking is a nightmare. This turns it into a difficulty of putting a carriage anywhere in the whole town, which weakens the intensity and widens the scope.

faults.quote: Most people walk from the carriage-house already, in truth.
faults.why: The writer's 'Honestly' marks a tone of candid impatience. 'In truth' is a tacked-on tag. The wry dismissiveness of 'they'll get used to it' is also somewhat flattened.

faults.quote: their shopkeepers are doing better than they have ever done before
faults.why: This is wordy, and 'ever' and 'before' are redundant. It is not Austen's economy, and it does not read as her phrasing. The first paragraph's opening is also still the writer's modern sentence, with no narrator's irony or social judgement.

faults.quote: We should make the trial this summer.
faults.why: This is a near-direct copy of the modern sentence. Austen's cadence, with its qualifying clauses and formal turns, is absent; it reads as modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 3, ¶ 5
faults.why: The citations to Emma and Persuasion are specific but unverifiable and look invented. The notes claim 'balanced clauses' where the sentence is just two joined clauses.

faults.quote: the voice strengthens it so the improvement sounds the greater, a small intensifying liberty
faults.why: The rewrite does not actually strengthen 'better than ever'; it is a plain equivalent. The note describes a change that was not made. Paragraphs 2 and 3 get no notes, although 'persons in trade' and 'grow accustomed' are changes.

faults.quote: I rendered "nightmare" and "garage" as "no small difficulty" and "carriage-house" in her words.
faults.why: The lesson praises the very mistranslations (carriage-house, carriage for stroller) that are faults, so it teaches a wrong move. It does not explain how to avoid anachronism.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: claim (the town should deny its principal street to carriages on days of rest...
faults.why: The outline says the voice would build the claim differently, but the rewrite keeps the writer's order and wording. The outline and rewrite do not match.

judge.verdict: The rewrite swaps in period words mechanically and produces real confusions: 'carriages of children' beside banned carriages, and 'carriage-house' for garage. It is thinly Austenian and keeps most of the modern sentence shapes. The notes and lesson misdescribe or praise the mistakes.

I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite:
I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent the greater part of the visit at the place to which such a loss necessarily carries one, with the week's business accordingly conducted there; and he still holds it to have been the pleasantest holiday of his life.

rows.text: I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

notes.text: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris; your second says the last time the narrator was there it rained the whole week. The same person cannot both never have been and have been there. I mended the first sentence only, making it a first visit, because everything that follows — the rain, the passport, the embassy, the brother's verdict — depends on the trip having happened; the opening becomes the premise of the story rather than a falsehood.
notes.after: I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week.
I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

rows.text: We spent the greater part of the visit at the place to which such a loss necessarily carries one, with the week's business accordingly conducted there; and he still holds it to have been the pleasantest holiday of his life.

notes.after: with the week's business accordingly conducted there

notes.text: The writer says the trip was spent at the embassy; the voice gathers that into a dry consequence — that the whole week's business was conducted at the embassy — which is only the writer's own fact, framed as the natural result of the loss, and readies the reader for the brother's contrary verdict.
notes.after: with the week's business accordingly conducted there

lessons: The chief difference is that your four short sentences state two facts and one verdict without letting the clause do any of the work Austen sets it to do. I joined the premise, the rain, and the lost passport into one balanced period ("I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day"), so the worst consequence arrives last where it lands hardest; and I held the brother's contrary verdict to the close as reported speech ("he still maintains it to have been the pleasantest holiday of his life"), where the understatement itself is the joke. Practise joining your sentences with semicolons and ", and", and letting a deflating last clause stand for the narrator's judgement instead of adding it on.

Rain all week; brother lost passport on the second day

plan.gist: The visit was a first visit
plan.why: The contradiction must be mended before anything else can stand, and the first sentence is the one thing the rest will not bear being changed.

plan.gist: Rain all week; the passport lost on the second day
plan.why: The setting and the mishap in one period, the worse consequence held for the last clause where it lands hardest.

plan.gist: The consequence: the embassy, and the time spent there
plan.why: The embassy is the turn the mishap forces; it earns its own paragraph as the scene shifts from the weather to the place.

plan.gist: The brother's contrary judgement, held to the close
plan.why: The irony is in the contrast between what happened and what he says of it; the voice lets that stand as the final, deflating clause.

sense.problem: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris; your second says the last time the narrator was there it rained the whole week. The same person cannot both never have been and have been there last time.
sense.resolution: Mend the first sentence only, since everything after it (the rain, the passport, the embassy, the brother's verdict) depends on the trip having happened: make it a first visit, e.g. "I'd never been to Paris before." That keeps the writer's order and the joke intact, and turns the opening from a falsehood into the premise of the story — a first-timer's week of rain.

faults.quote: I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week
faults.why: The mending is not carried through. 'Never been before' followed by 'the last time I was there' is still a contradiction, since a first visit has no 'last time'. The note claims it made the trip a first visit, but the rewrite keeps 'the last time I was there'.

faults.quote: I mended the first sentence only, making it a first visit
faults.why: The note describes a mending the text does not deliver. The better mending, that the narrator never saw Paris and only the embassy, goes unused.

faults.quote: I had never been to Paris before
faults.why: It changes the writer's present-tense claim ('I've never been to Paris') into a past-perfect statement about a first visit, which alters the meaning and flattens the joke.

faults.quote: at the place to which such a loss necessarily carries one, with the week's business accordingly conducted there
faults.why: The periphrasis avoids the word 'embassy' and becomes a riddle. 'The week's business' invents a sense of business that the writer never gave. It is wordy and clumsy, not Austen's precise irony.

faults.quote: the greater part of the visit
faults.why: The writer said 'most of the trip'. The visit is fine, but the embassy is now only implied and the fact is blurred.

faults.quote: he still holds it to have been the pleasantest holiday of his life
faults.why: The semicolon-and-'and' construction softens the writer's separate, deadpan sentence, and 'holds it to have been' is stilted. The lesson then misquotes it as 'he still maintains it to have been', which is not what the rewrite says.

faults.quote: cites Persuasion, ch. 23, ¶ 59
faults.why: The cited source is dubious as support for a balanced period of this kind. The paragraph number looks fabricated and cannot be checked. The Pride and Prejudice citation for 'ironic verdict' likewise does not match the quoted phrase.

faults.quote: The embassy is the turn the mishap forces; it earns its own paragraph
faults.why: The structure note claims the rewrite gives the embassy its own paragraph and that the notes show a reordering. In fact the rewrite keeps the writer's two paragraphs, and the 'premise' stage is just the contradictory opening.

faults.quote: Practise joining your sentences with semicolons and ", and"
faults.why: The advice is generic and mechanical. It does not explain why the short deadpan sentences worked, and the lesson praises a mending that was not achieved. The lesson also says 'four short sentences', but there are three.

faults.quote: I had never been to Paris before; and the last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport
faults.why: The chain of 'and' clauses reads as run-on modern prose, not Austen's balanced subordination. There is no real Austenian judgement or characterising irony in it.

judge.verdict: The rewrite does not fix the central contradiction, though its notes claim it does. The embassy is obscured in a riddling periphrasis, and the lesson quotes wording that is not in the rewrite. Austenian voice is only lightly present, and the citations are unconvincing.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we should alter the week to four days. The people are worn out, and our best engineer has just left us; and it cannot but be felt that there are studies which show the work going on as well, or better, under such an arrangement. It would help us, too, in the engaging of new people; it would render us the more desirable.

I know it is a wild scheme, and that our clients might not like it; but we might try it for three months, and then judge.

rows.text: I think we should alter the week to four days. The people are worn out, and our best engineer has just left us; and it cannot but be felt that there are studies which show the work going on as well, or better, under such an arrangement. It would help us, too, in the engaging of new people; it would render us the more desirable.

notes.after: The people are worn out, and our best engineer has just left us; and it cannot but be felt that there are studies which show the work going on as well, or better, under such an arrangement.

notes.text: the writer says only that it would help with hiring; the voice turns the bare benefit into the consequence it implies, in her abstract nouns
notes.after: it would render us the more desirable

rows.text: I know it is a wild scheme, and that our clients might not like it; but we might try it for three months, and then judge.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's page is a list of plain clauses, where the author builds one or two full periods whose clauses balance and whose verdicts arrive late. I joined the two reasons into one sentence on a semicolon, turned the bare benefit into its consequence with abstract nouns ('it would render us the more desirable'), and closed the objection with her understatement ('a wild scheme... try it for three months, and then judge'); practise balancing an objection and its answer in a single period, and letting the narrator's nouns of judgement carry the weight of feeling.

plan.why: the voice opens with the claim, stated plainly but in a full period

plan.gist: people burned out, best engineer quit
plan.why: the strongest reason follows at once, its weight carried by nouns of judgement

plan.gist: studies show productivity holds or rises
plan.why: the proof as a balanced clause, the author's way of testing a claim before accepting it

plan.gist: would help hiring
plan.why: a secondary inducement, kept subordinate
