faults.quote: it cannot but be felt that there are studies which show the work going on as well, or better
faults.why: Adds a hedge ('cannot but be felt') that weakens the writer's flat claim that studies show productivity holds or rises. It also changes 'productivity stays the same or goes up' into 'the work going on', which is vaguer.

faults.quote: it would render us the more desirable
faults.why: This is an addition. The writer said only that it would help hiring. The 'desirable' clause repeats it and adds a new idea about how appealing the company is.

faults.quote: a wild scheme
faults.why: The writer said 'risky'. 'Wild scheme' is a stronger, more disparaging judgement and shifts the feeling. It also undercuts the writer's own proposal.

faults.quote: and then judge
faults.why: The writer said 'see'. 'Judge' implies a formal evaluation, which is a slight shift.

faults.quote: I think we should alter the week to four days.
faults.why: 'Alter the week to four days' is odd and unAustenian. Austen would not open with a bare modern 'I think we should' either. The opening does not read like her.

faults.quote: The people are worn out
faults.why: This is modern and flat, not Austen's idiom. 'Worn out' is acceptable, but 'The people' is a vague and strange term for staff or colleagues.

faults.quote: our best engineer has just left us; and it cannot but be felt
faults.why: The semicolon followed by 'and' is clumsy. It runs a human loss and a statistical claim together, with no Austenian irony or balance. The result is a mild imitation, not her cadence.

faults.quote: in the engaging of new people
faults.why: This is a stilted nominalisation. Austen would say 'engaging new people' or use another idiom. 'Engaging' for hiring is also ambiguous.

faults.quote: it would render us the more desirable
faults.why: Awkward and unclear. It is not evident whether it means desirable as an employer, and it reads as slightly comic.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 29, ¶ 10
faults.why: The citation is unlikely to be accurate or apt. It gives a specific chapter and paragraph for a sentence that is not a quotation from it and shows no parallel.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The second paragraph has real changes ('wild scheme', 'judge', the 'but' construction) that go unreported. The 'wild scheme' shift in feeling is not flagged.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the writer says only that it would help with hiring
faults.why: This does flag the addition. However, it understates it, since the rewrite also adds the hedge 'cannot but be felt' and the 'wild' intensification, which are not noted.

faults.quote: I joined the two reasons into one sentence on a semicolon
faults.why: The lesson says the rewrite closed the objection with understatement, but 'wild scheme' is stronger than the writer's 'risky'. It also says the objection and answer are balanced in one period, which is true only loosely. The advice is generic and partly inaccurate about what was done.

faults.quote: the voice answers its own objection in the narrator's dry turn
faults.why: The outline claims dry narrator irony, but the rewrite has none. The description overstates what the text does. The order is also kept, so little structural gain is shown.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps all the facts and order but reads as a mild archaic costume, with stilted phrasing ('in the engaging of new people', 'render us the more desirable') and some shifts of feeling ('wild scheme'). The notes cite an implausible source, miss changes in paragraph 2, and give a lesson that overstates what was done.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all put out by it. In truth, my relief was as great as it was unworthy; for I had been dreading the engagement the whole week past, and I am far from proud of that.

I told her it was perfectly fine, and that we should do it another time. But I do not think we shall.

rows.text: When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all put out by it. In truth, my relief was as great as it was unworthy; for I had been dreading the engagement the whole week past, and I am far from proud of that.

notes.after: for I had been dreading the engagement the whole week past, and I am far from proud of that.

notes.text: the narrator looks back and judges her own feeling, as Austen's first-person narrators do; the writer said only that she was relieved and not proud, and the voice frames both in one abstract phrase
notes.after: my relief was as great as it was unworthy

rows.text: I told her it was perfectly fine, and that we should do it another time. But I do not think we shall.

lessons: Your passage names a feeling plainly in short sentences; Austen's manner is to hold several clauses in one period and let the feeling be judged rather than merely stated. "My relief was as great as it was unworthy" joins the relief and the shame in a single balanced phrase, and the closing "But I do not think we shall" works because the short sentence is saved for the deflating turn. Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" or a semicolon, and letting the main point arrive late in the sentence.

plan.why: the fact first, set down plainly, as the voice states what happened before what it felt

plan.why: the feeling named in the voice's abstract nouns, a turn the short sentence may carry

faults.quote: my relief was as great as it was unworthy
faults.why: The writer said only that she was relieved and not proud. The rewrite adds a degree ('as great as') and an explicit judgment ('unworthy') that goes beyond 'not proud' and shifts the intensity of the feeling.

faults.quote: put off our dinner
faults.why: 'Put off' means postponed, but the writer said 'cancelled'. This softens the event, and it sits oddly beside the later 'do it another time' and the narrator's doubt that they will.

faults.quote: I was not at all put out by it
faults.why: 'Put out' is fine for 'not upset', but 'put off' and 'put out' in the same sentence is clumsy and sounds like an unintended echo.

faults.quote: put off our dinner, I was not at all put out by it
faults.why: The repeated 'put' phrasing reads as a jingle. Austen would vary it, or the repetition would be deliberate and pointed, which it is not.

faults.quote: Honestly, I was relieved.
faults.why: The writer's 'Honestly' marks a candid admission. The rewrite replaces it with 'In truth' but folds the relief into a long balanced clause, so the confessional plainness is diluted.

faults.quote: I told her it was perfectly fine, and that we should do it another time. But I do not think we shall.
faults.why: This is close to the original with only light period dress. Austen's reported speech would not usually keep 'perfectly fine'. The Austen-specific syntax and vocabulary are thin, so it reads as modern prose lightly dressed.

faults.quote: the whole week past
faults.why: This is a mild archaism, but the rewrite has little else of Austen's irony or abstract diction, and the whole is only gently costumed.

faults.quote: cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 12, ¶ 29
faults.why: A very specific chapter and paragraph citation that cannot be verified and is probably invented. The sentence cited is also not a known passage.

faults.quote: the narrator looks back and judges her own feeling, as Austen's first-person narrators do
faults.why: Austen's novels are overwhelmingly third-person. The claim about first-person narrators is inaccurate.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 2 has changes ('should', 'shall', 'But', 'perfectly') that go unremarked, and the notes do not mention the 'put off' for 'cancelled' alteration.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" or a semicolon
faults.why: The advice is generic. The writer's short sentences also work well for confession, and the lesson never says when to keep them short. The lesson claims the closing sentence 'works' by saving the short sentence, but the rewrite merely added 'But' and 'shall'.

faults.quote: the voice frames both in one abstract phrase
faults.why: The 'liberty' note describes the addition as judgment, but the real liberty is the added intensity ('as great as', 'unworthy'), which the note does not name accurately.

judge.verdict: A faithful-feeling but thin rewrite: the relief and doubt are preserved, yet 'unworthy' and 'put off' alter the feeling and the event, and the voice is only lightly applied. The notes contain a dubious citation and a false claim about Austen's narrators, so the teaching value is weakened.

yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight that we needed to talk, and I knew at once what that message must mean; for there are few of us who have not learned, by this or that small sign, to read the sentence that follows such a prelude.

The next day we met at a coffee shop in the lower part of the town, where he was already before me, bending over his little instrument with that pretence of occupation by which a man who is not easy seeks to seem so. He looked nervous, and his being so was the second sign, which a reasonable person might have taken for a comfort of sorts, since it showed that what he had to say cost him something; he said he was not ready for anything serious, and then, with the old kindness that made the hurt the worse, that it was not me, it was him.

I wanted to cry, but I did not, for there is in most of us a pride that would sooner keep the face quiet than let the grief be seen where it is no longer wanted; so I only nodded and said it was all right. Then I walked home in the rain, and, like a person who turns to any steady thing for company, ate a whole pint of ice cream before the evening was done.

My friend, with whom I shared my room, thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it still hurt, and a pain does not cease to be a pain because a friend can name it less than it is.

He looked nervous, and his being so was the second sign, which a reasonable person might have taken for a comfort of sorts, since it showed that what he had to say cost him something; he said he was not ready for anything serious, and then, with the old kindness that made the hurt the worse, that it was not me, it was him.

Then I walked home in the rain, and, like a person who turns to any steady thing for company, ate a whole pint of ice cream before the evening was done.
My friend, with whom I shared my room, thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it still hurt, and a pain does not cease to be a pain because a friend can name it less than it is.

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences stand short and bare, one fact apiece, where Eliot gathers a morning's feelings into long sentences that qualify themselves as they go. I joined your first three sentences into one period built on ", and" and "; for," so that the outward fact and its inward meaning arrive together. Notice also how the narrator steps back to our common lot—"there are few of us who have not learned"—and how the small outward acts, nodding and eating ice cream, are made to carry the whole inward ache; practise joining clauses with ", and" and letting an abstract noun (pride, pain) name the feeling instead of stating it outright.

plan.gist: the restraint, the walk in rain, the ice cream
plan.why: the small outer acts carry the inward ache; the narrator steps back once to what is true of us all.

plan.gist: the friend's judgment, the concession, the hurt that remains
plan.why: the turn lands last, short, as a verdict the long sentences earn.

faults.quote: with the old kindness that made the hurt the worse
faults.why: Invents a history and a characterisation (Ryan's 'old kindness') not in the draft, and shifts the feeling; the writer gave no sign he was kind.

faults.quote: and his being so was the second sign, which a reasonable person might have taken for a comfort of sorts, since it showed that what he had to say cost him something
faults.why: Adds a new reflection and a softened view of Ryan that the writer did not hold; the 'second sign' also presupposes a first sign (the midnight text) that is only implied.

faults.quote: where it is no longer wanted
faults.why: Adds a reason for her not crying (grief unwanted) that is not in the draft.

faults.quote: like a person who turns to any steady thing for company
faults.why: Adds a motive for the ice cream that the writer did not give.

faults.quote: My friend, with whom I shared my room
faults.why: The roommate is rendered as 'friend'; this adds an assumption of friendship and is wordy.

faults.quote: a pain does not cease to be a pain because a friend can name it less than it is
faults.why: Adds a new claim about the friend's judgment; stronger than the draft's mild 'But it still hurt', and the phrase is somewhat garbled.

faults.quote: bending over his little instrument
faults.why: A phone as 'little instrument' is a coy periphrasis that reads as a riddle and mildly comic; 'scrolling' is lost.

faults.quote: in the lower part of the town
faults.why: 'Downtown' rendered clumsily; 'before me' with 'where he was already' is awkward.

faults.quote: can name it less than it is
faults.why: Malformed idiom; it is unclear what 'name it less than it is' means.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me word at midnight
faults.why: 'Ryan' and 'ice cream', 'coffee shop', 'pint' stay modern, and the first-person confessional with 'I wanted to cry' is closer to modern prose than Eliot's third-person narration; the voice relies on semicolon chains rather than her ironic, sympathetic narratorial commentary.

faults.quote: for there are few of us who have not learned, by this or that small sign, to read the sentence that follows such a prelude
faults.why: The generalising move is Eliot-like but is a bit generic and abstract; 'sentence that follows such a prelude' is slightly strained.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 82, ¶ 4
faults.why: Specific chapter and paragraph citations are doubtful, and the notes do not explain how the quoted sentence uses the move; a note for 'periphrasis' cites ch. 71, ¶ 57 equally unverifiably.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 1, 3 and 4 have no notes though they contain the main changes (the generalising aside, 'pride' clause, the added closing reflection); the added content is not reported as additions.

faults.quote: practise joining clauses with ", and"
faults.why: The lesson is thin and partly generic; it praises abstract nouns while the rewrite adds content rather than just manner, and it does not warn the writer about the added inventions.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a plausible Eliot cadence and keeps the order of events, but it adds several unsupported feelings and motives (Ryan's 'old kindness', the unwanted grief, the friend's mislabelling) and has a few awkward phrasings ('little instrument', 'name it less than it is'). Notes are sparse and the lesson does not flag these additions.

yours:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is all right, I suppose, though the food is what I can hardly bring myself to eat, and the boy who shares my bed breathes so heavily in his sleep that I lie awake listening to him.

Yesterday we went out in a boat, and I turned the boat over and into the water I went, and everybody laughed; and it was so embarrassing I did not know where to look. We are all of us disposed to think a small misfortune of the body more disgraceful than it appears to the lookers-on, for no one is so ready to laugh at another's topple as the person who was lately in danger of the same.

But there is a girl here named Kayla who is really fine, and I think I like her better than any of the rest. She comes from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about horses, more than I should have thought any girl could know. We sit by the lake after dinner and talk of all sorts of things, and I think she likes me, but I am not sure.

Can you send me some more things to eat between meals, and my charger for the telephone, which I entirely forgot to bring? The counselors are a little strict, but for the most part they are well enough.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please do not let Max use my room.

rows.text: Dear Mom and Dad,

notes.cite: The Mill on the Floss, ch. 8, ¶ 7

notes.text: the narrator's 'we' framing of the boy's embarrassment: a general truth the matter invites, and Eliot's usual way of lifting a particular feeling into common knowledge.
notes.after: We are all of us disposed to think a small misfortune of the body more disgraceful than it appears to the lookers-on

notes.text: a gentle verdict on the laughers, from the same sympathetic understanding, not an added incident or feeling.
notes.after: for no one is so ready to laugh at another's topple as the person who was lately in danger of the same

rows.text: But there is a girl here named Kayla who is really fine, and I think I like her better than any of the rest. She comes from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about horses, more than I should have thought any girl could know. We sit by the lake after dinner and talk of all sorts of things, and I think she likes me, but I am not sure.

Can you send me some more things to eat between meals, and my charger for the telephone, which I entirely forgot to bring? The counselors are a little strict, but for the most part they are well enough.
Love, Jake
P.S. Please do not let Max use my room.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short clipped sentences say each fact alone, while Eliot's manner joins them into long periods that qualify themselves and carry the feeling inside, as in "though the food is what I can hardly bring myself to eat, and the boy who shares my bed breathes so heavily in his sleep that I lie awake listening to him." She also steps back to a general truth about the boy's embarrassment ("for no one is so ready to laugh at another's topple as the person who was lately in danger of the same"), which turns a private mortification into common knowledge; practising one such "we are all of us" per page, and letting one sentence hold two or three facts, will lift any of the writer's own letters into her voice.

outline.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
camp is okay but the food is gross, bunkmate snores
canoe flipped, everyone laughed, embarrassing
girl named Kayla, from Ohio, knows horses, they talk at the lake, unsure she likes him
send snacks and phone charger; counselors strict but fine

plan.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
plan.why: a letter keeps its greeting where it stands; the voice does not touch it

plan.gist: the general account of camp, then the food and the bunkmate, joined as one large qualified period
plan.why: the voice gathers small complaints into one long sentence, the particular inside the general

plan.gist: the canoe upset, the laughter, the embarrassment, told with the inward feeling and a small general truth
plan.why: the turn of the matter lands hardest when the feeling is named and then widened to what we all know of such failures

plan.gist: Kayla, from Ohio, her knowledge of horses, their talk at the lake, his half-hope and uncertainty
plan.why: the better news before the doubt within it, each clause qualifying the last, the inner state given from inside

plan.gist: the snacks and the charger, with the counselors judged mildly
plan.why: requests and the verdict on the counselors are both matter of the letter and go in one paragraph together

plan.gist: Love, Jake
plan.why: the close stands as the writer gave it

plan.gist: the plea about Max and the room
plan.why: the postscript comes last as the writer set it, its own paragraph

faults.quote: I think I like her better than any of the rest.
faults.why: Invented feeling. The writer never says Jake likes Kayla more than the others, and the claim goes beyond a mere comment on what is there.

faults.quote: more than I should have thought any girl could know
faults.why: Adds an attitude of surprise that the writer did not express. The writer says only that she knows a ton about horses.

faults.quote: so embarrassing I did not know where to look
faults.why: The embarrassment is intensified and a new image is added. The original says only 'so embarrassing'.

faults.quote: for no one is so ready to laugh at another's topple as the person who was lately in danger of the same
faults.why: Adds a new claim that the laughers were themselves lately in danger. This is an invented incident and a judgment. The notes call it 'a gentle verdict' and 'not an added incident', which is inaccurate.

faults.quote: I lie awake listening to him
faults.why: The writer says only that the bunkmate snores like crazy. Jake being kept awake is added.

faults.quote: some more things to eat between meals
faults.why: 'Snacks' is rendered clumsily. 'Between meals' adds detail.

faults.quote: the boy who shares my bed
faults.why: Misleading. It suggests a shared bed rather than a bunk, which is unintended comedy and a malapropism for bunkmate.

faults.quote: and into the water I went
faults.why: A jaunty, modern-comic inversion that is not Eliot's idiom. It sits oddly beside the formal diction.

faults.quote: the food is what I can hardly bring myself to eat
faults.why: An awkward cleft construction. 'Gross' is turned into inability to eat, which changes the degree.

faults.quote: a girl here named Kayla who is really fine
faults.why: 'Really' is modern and slangy, and 'fine' is a weak equivalent of 'really cool'. The register is inconsistent.

faults.quote: Love, Jake
faults.why: Nothing in the voice is applied to the letter's other parts. The second half is mostly light archaizing with little Eliot-like qualification or narratorial reflection.

faults.quote: for no one is so ready to laugh at another's topple
faults.why: The generalization does not fit the scene. The 'lookers-on' laughing and the 'danger of the same' idea are muddled, so the aphorism reads as a non-sequitur.

faults.quote: Begins your paragraph 2, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: The notes treat splitting a paragraph as a structural move, yet the split is arbitrary and not explained. Most of the voice's moves in paragraphs 1, 4 and 5 go unnoted, even though the diction was altered there.

faults.quote: cites The Mill on the Floss, ch. 8, ¶ 7
faults.why: The cited source is dubious. It is presented as the origin of a 'we are all of us' move without a verifiable quotation, and the cited paragraph cannot be checked.

faults.quote: joined as one large qualified period
faults.why: The outline promises the news paragraph with the food and bunkmate joined, and the lesson claims long periods. The rewrite delivers only one such sentence, and the other paragraphs stay short and plain, so the stated structure is not much followed.

judge.verdict: The rewrite adds feelings and claims the writer never made (liking Kayla best, the laughers' own danger, being kept awake) and misdescribes them in the notes as no addition. It also has an unintended comic 'shares my bed' and uneven voice, so it reads as light archaizing rather than Eliot.

yours:
The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
The office was a vast and shining place of the newest sort—the kind of room that might make a stranger feel how small a thing he was—and the people in it went about in loose embroidered jackets, each with a cup of some costly coffee in his hand. I had come in a suit; and we are all of us, in a strange room, a little at the mercy of our clothes, for they either give us ease or set us apart as plainly as a stranger's tongue would do.

The manager was a woman called Priya; her manner was friendly, and yet there was in it something pressing and intent, so that the friendliness could not be taken to mean that she was a person to be trifled with. She asked me what my powers were, and where I fell short; and I answered, as I daresay many have answered before me, that I could never leave a thing alone until it was done to my own satisfaction—a wretched, threadbare answer, which told her nothing that a hundred others had not said. She smiled, nevertheless.

When the interview was over I called my sister, and told her how it had gone; and she said she had no doubt I had done well. I hope she may be right, for I need the place badly: the rent falls due next week, and my money is very nearly at an end.

rows.text: The office was a vast and shining place of the newest sort—the kind of room that might make a stranger feel how small a thing he was—and the people in it went about in loose embroidered jackets, each with a cup of some costly coffee in his hand. I had come in a suit; and we are all of us, in a strange room, a little at the mercy of our clothes, for they either give us ease or set us apart as plainly as a stranger's tongue would do.

notes.after: we are all of us, in a strange room, a little at the mercy of our clothes, for they either give us ease or set us apart as plainly as a stranger's tongue would do.

notes.text: The narrator may judge what is there; I let the voice frame the writer's plain fact that the office was huge with the inward shrinking it produced, which the writer's 'felt out of place' invites.
notes.after: the kind of room that might make a stranger feel how small a thing he was

notes.text: The narrating voice steps back from the particular to a truth of us all, as Eliot's narrators do, drawn from the writer's own confession of feeling out of place.
notes.after: we are all of us, in a strange room, a little at the mercy of our clothes

She asked me what my powers were, and where I fell short; and I answered, as I daresay many have answered before me, that I could never leave a thing alone until it was done to my own satisfaction—a wretched, threadbare answer, which told her nothing that a hundred others had not said. She smiled, nevertheless.

When the interview was over I called my sister, and told her how it had gone; and she said she had no doubt I had done well. I hope she may be right, for I need the place badly: the rent falls due next week, and my money is very nearly at an end.

lessons: Your passage tells a felt moment in seven-word sentences; Eliot tells the same moment in long sentences that enter the feeling from inside and pause to say what is true of us all. Notice how "we are all of us, in a strange room, a little at the mercy of our clothes" turns your plain confession into a generous truth anyone can share, and how the "qualified" sentence about the perfectionist answer folds the ruefulness of "lame answer" into the sentence itself rather than naming it. Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" and ";" so that each clause fills out and corrects the one before it, and let a short sentence stand only for the turn—"She smiled, nevertheless."

outline.gist: The vast modern office and its casual dressed, coffee-drinking people
The narrator feels out of place in a suit
The manager, Priya: friendly yet intense; asks strengths and weaknesses
Narrator gives a weak answer yet Priya smiles
Calling his sister; her reassurance; his need of the job

plan.gist: The office and its people, drawn before the person enters
plan.why: Eliot sets the scene and its moral weather before the inward case; the modern room is named plainly, the dress and coffee made visible without the writer's idiom.

plan.gist: The narrator's suit and his sense of not belonging
plan.why: The alienation is felt from inside, with the narrator's mixed motive, before the interview itself begins.

plan.gist: Priya, her manner, and her question
plan.why: Persons are named and their inward quality given with sympathy before their words; the question arrives as the scene's turn.

plan.gist: The weak answer and Priya's smile
plan.why: The narrator's half-known ruefulness and her indulgence are told as one movement, the verdict landing in a short sentence.

plan.gist: The sister's hope and the rent
plan.why: The news and the pressing need come after, as Eliot closes on the outer pressure that weighs the inner hope.

faults.quote: loose embroidered jackets
faults.why: The writer said hoodies. 'Embroidered' is an invented detail, and the garment is changed without any note.

faults.quote: we are all of us, in a strange room, a little at the mercy of our clothes
faults.why: This replaces the writer's own statement 'I felt totally out of place in my suit' with a general maxim. The narrator's personal feeling of being out of place is no longer said directly.

faults.quote: so that the friendliness could not be taken to mean that she was a person to be trifled with
faults.why: The writer says only 'friendly but kind of intense'. This adds a claim about how far Priya can be trifled with.

faults.quote: a wretched, threadbare answer, which told her nothing that a hundred others had not said
faults.why: 'Lame' is intensified to 'wretched', and a new claim is added about what the answer told her.

faults.quote: she said she had no doubt I had done well
faults.why: The sister said 'probably nailed it'. 'No doubt' raises her certainty, and 'done well' softens 'nailed'. Also, 'told her how it had gone' is added, though it is only implied.

faults.quote: make a stranger feel how small a thing he was
faults.why: 'Stranger' is used again in 'a stranger's tongue' in the next sentence. The repetition is clumsy, and 'set us apart as plainly as a stranger's tongue' is a strained comparison.

faults.quote: I daresay many have answered before me
faults.why: The first-person 'I daresay' and the aside are Victorian in flavour, but the whole reads more as general Victorian pastiche than as Eliot's sympathetic, ironic narrator. The sentences stay fairly loose and generic.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 47, ¶ 11
faults.why: The quoted sentence is the rewriter's own invention, not a line from Middlemarch. The precise chapter and paragraph citation looks fabricated and misleads the writer.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: This paragraph has substantial changes (the expanded perfectionist answer, the added judgment of Priya, 'wretched, threadbare'). Paragraph 3 also has changes. Neither is noted, nor is the hoodie change.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The narrating voice steps back from the particular to a truth of us all
faults.why: The two liberty notes say nearly the same thing and are not real source-cited moves. The first claims the voice frames the 'inward shrinking', yet the rewrite no longer states that feeling directly.

faults.quote: Your passage tells a felt moment in seven-word sentences
faults.why: The original sentences are not uniformly seven words, so the claim is inaccurate. The lesson also refers to a 'qualified' sentence that no note explains, and its advice to join short sentences is fairly generic.

judge.verdict: A readable Eliot-flavoured rewrite that keeps the order and gist. It alters details (hoodies became embroidered jackets, 'probably' became 'no doubt'), swaps the narrator's own feeling for a maxim, and adds interpretive claims. The notes are thin, cite a doubtful Middlemarch source, and skip most changes, so the teaching value is only moderate.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family moved into the house next door at the end of last week, coming with a great van and two little children. The father seemed a good-natured sort of man, and it was impossible not to be drawn to him at once; but the children's mother was somewhat unapproachable, as people are who do not readily give themselves away to strangers.

My mother, for her part, lost no time, but had baked them a dish of cakes before the morning was out, with that anxious and unacknowledged intent which kindness so often carries along with it; for she wanted to learn everything about the newcomers. Where they had come from, what they did for their livelihood, and whether they went to church—these were the questions she meant to have answered, as if a family could be read through like an almanac.

It came out in the course of things that the father was a lawyer, and that he was single—not, he had to add, unmarried as one means it of a young man, but divorced, which is another condition altogether. At this my mother's face took on a certain look, which I knew as well as I know my own; for I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to marry me off for years, and here, she plainly thought, was an opportunity such as does not often come twice.

rows.text: A new family moved into the house next door at the end of last week, coming with a great van and two little children. The father seemed a good-natured sort of man, and it was impossible not to be drawn to him at once; but the children's mother was somewhat unapproachable, as people are who do not readily give themselves away to strangers.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother ('The mom is kind of standoffish'); your third says the dad 'is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A household with a mother in it and a father who is single cannot both be true as stated. I made her the children's mother—the father's former wife or the household's other adult—rather than his wife. This keeps the cookies, the questions, the divorced lawyer, and the look all standing, and agrees with 'well, divorced'.
notes.after: The children's mother is somewhat unapproachable.

rows.text: My mother, for her part, lost no time, but had baked them a dish of cakes before the morning was out, with that anxious and unacknowledged intent which kindness so often carries along with it; for she wanted to learn everything about the newcomers. Where they had come from, what they did for their livelihood, and whether they went to church—these were the questions she meant to have answered, as if a family could be read through like an almanac.

It came out in the course of things that the father was a lawyer, and that he was single—not, he had to add, unmarried as one means it of a young man, but divorced, which is another condition altogether. At this my mother's face took on a certain look, which I knew as well as I know my own; for I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to marry me off for years, and here, she plainly thought, was an opportunity such as does not often come twice.

lessons: The chief difference is sentence-length and inwardness. Where your sentences are flat facts of eight or nine words, Eliot joins clauses into long periods that qualify themselves ("a great van and two little children"), and she enters the mind to read motive and feeling from inside: your "My mom got this look on her face" becomes "At this my mother's face took on a certain look, which I knew as well as I know my own." Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" and "; but", and letting the narrator dwell a moment on what each fact means inside a person—the mother's kindness carrying an "unacknowledged intent", the difference between "unmarried" and "divorced"—so the reader feels the matter, not merely hears it.

outline.gist: A new family moved in next door last weekend
They have a huge truck and two little kids
The dad seems nice; the mom is standoffish
My mother baked them cookies and tried to learn everything about them
Where they came from, what they did, whether they went to church
The dad is a lawyer and single—divorced
My mother's look; I knew what she was thinking
She has been trying to set me up for years

plan.gist: A new family moved in next door; the van and the children
plan.why: Eliot sets the scene before the scene: place the household first, with the children and their belongings, so the people emerge from it.

plan.gist: The father seems agreeable; the mother is reserved, unapproachable
plan.why: Enter the mind and the estimate: give the narrator's first impressions as qualified judgments, not flat labels.

plan.gist: My mother baked cakes at once, wanting to learn everything
plan.why: The mother's motive is the turn of the matter: her kindness is not unmixed, and the narrator notes it.

plan.gist: Where they came from, their work, their church-going
plan.why: Unfold the interrogation in her own words as the threefold question it is.

plan.gist: The father is a lawyer, and single—divorced
plan.why: Let the turn land on 'single', then be corrected to 'divorced', as a slow disclosure.

plan.gist: My mother's look, and what I knew it meant
plan.why: The inward reading of the mother's face is the heart of the little scene: the narrator reads it from inside.

plan.gist: She has been trying to set me up for years
plan.why: Close on the long motive, which the scene has only just revealed.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother ('The mom is kind of standoffish'); your third says the dad 'is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A household with a mother in it and a father who is single cannot both be true as stated.
sense.resolution: Let the 'mom' be the mother of the two children and the father's former wife, or simply the household's other adult, not his wife: 'the kids' mother' rather than 'the mom'. This keeps every other sentence intact — the cookies, the interrogation, the divorced lawyer, the look — and agrees with 'well, divorced'. Do not make her his wife, which would contradict 'single', nor his sister, which the children and the household do not support.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

faults.quote: and it was impossible not to be drawn to him at once
faults.why: Invents a strong feeling. The writer only said 'The dad seems nice'. This changes the degree of feeling and adds a narrator attraction.

faults.quote: as people are who do not readily give themselves away to strangers
faults.why: Adds a psychological explanation for the mother's standoffishness. It softens the writer's blunt judgment and goes beyond commentary.

faults.quote: with that anxious and unacknowledged intent which kindness so often carries along with it
faults.why: Adds 'anxious' and 'unacknowledged' motive. The writer says only that she wanted to find out everything, so this is invention beyond commentary.

faults.quote: not, he had to add, unmarried as one means it of a young man, but divorced
faults.why: Invents an incident: the father speaking and correcting himself. In the original the narrator corrects 'single' to 'divorced'. It also changes who speaks and what is known.

faults.quote: and here, she plainly thought, was an opportunity such as does not often come twice
faults.why: Adds the mother's thought, which the writer left unstated ('I knew exactly what she was thinking'). The rewrite fills in content the writer withheld.

faults.quote: a great van
faults.why: The writer said 'huge truck'. 'Van' changes the fact.

faults.quote: at the end of last week
faults.why: 'Last weekend' became a vaguer 'end of last week'. Also 'before the morning was out' is invented timing for 'right away'.

faults.quote: a dish of cakes
faults.why: Cookies became cakes, which alters the detail.

faults.quote: but the children's mother was somewhat unapproachable
faults.why: The rewrite does not reconcile the contradiction in the text. It calls her 'the children's mother', yet 'single' still sits beside a household with a resident woman. The note says she may be the 'household's other adult', which the text never shows. The mending is vague and not integrated, and it is not clear who she is.

faults.quote: as if a family could be read through like an almanac
faults.why: The simile is a bit forced. It is not Eliot's best manner, and it adds a sneer the writer did not make.

faults.quote: which I knew as well as I know my own; for I knew exactly what she was thinking
faults.why: Redundant. The narrator says he 'knew' twice, which reads clumsily.

faults.quote: I made her the children's mother—the father's former wife or the household's other adult—rather than his wife.
faults.why: The note hedges between options. It does not say what the rewrite actually established, and the rewrite still reads as if she lives in the household.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 2 and 3 carry many additions, such as the anxious intent, the almanac, and the father's self-correction, and none are reported. The notes name only one change.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" and "; but"
faults.why: The advice is generic. It misattributes '(a great van and two little children)' as a self-qualifying period. It also does not warn that the rewrite invented content, so the writer is not shown the limit of commentary.

faults.quote: My mother, for her part, lost no time, but had baked them
faults.why: The tense shift and 'but' are awkward. The Eliot pastiche is surface archaism with little of her ironic, generalizing narrator, e.g. a wise aphorism about match-making mothers.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has an Eliot-like surface but adds many invented feelings and incidents, such as the father's self-correction and the mother's thought. It mends the contradiction only vaguely, and the notes leave most of the changes unreported.

yours:
The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:
The party was given at Jessica's house, her parents being out of town, so that the rooms stood open, without any curb of elder presence, to all who chose to come. Everyone from school was there, and the music was so loud that speech was carried on at a pitch which made thinking possible only by an effort.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and of the faces round us we knew but few, which is a position that tempts the mind to busy itself with your-fellow creatures as if they were a company on a stage rather than neighbours. Then a tall young man came over and began to talk to us, and told us that his name was Chris. He had about him a certain conceit of manner, yet he was amusing withal, so that I did not at once know how to set him down.

He said the party was a dull affair and the people in it tedious, letting his verdict fall on the evening's gaiety as if the whole company had been got together for his amusement and had failed of it. Emma rolled her eyes, an unspoken protest of the eyes which I shared, for I thought him rude; there is a sort of self-complacency which mistakes itself for wit, and it is never an agreeable thing to meet with in a stranger. But later, when everyone else had gone, I saw him staying behind to help clear the room, gathering up what the rest had left, as if he held that not all duties end with the pleasure, and my earlier judgment of him began to seem too quick. Perhaps I was wrong about him, as if the evening's worth were a question that remained to be decided.

rows.text: The party was given at Jessica's house, her parents being out of town, so that the rooms stood open, without any curb of elder presence, to all who chose to come. Everyone from school was there, and the music was so loud that speech was carried on at a pitch which made thinking possible only by an effort.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and of the faces round us we knew but few, which is a position that tempts the mind to busy itself with your-fellow creatures as if they were a company on a stage rather than neighbours. Then a tall young man came over and began to talk to us, and told us that his name was Chris. He had about him a certain conceit of manner, yet he was amusing withal, so that I did not at once know how to set him down.

He said the party was a dull affair and the people in it tedious, letting his verdict fall on the evening's gaiety as if the whole company had been got together for his amusement and had failed of it. Emma rolled her eyes, an unspoken protest of the eyes which I shared, for I thought him rude; there is a sort of self-complacency which mistakes itself for wit, and it is never an agreeable thing to meet with in a stranger. But later, when everyone else had gone, I saw him staying behind to help clear the room, gathering up what the rest had left, as if he held that not all duties end with the pleasure, and my earlier judgment of him began to seem too quick. Perhaps I was wrong about him, as if the evening's worth were a question that remained to be decided.

notes.text: The draft says only 'Emma rolled her eyes'; the voice frames the gesture as what it is, a silent dissent, without adding any new feeling.
notes.after: an unspoken protest of the eyes

notes.text: The voice lets its own reflection frame the narrator's self-doubt, keeping the doubt the writer gave but giving it the narrator's characteristic form.
notes.after: as if the evening's worth were a question that remained to be decided

lessons: The writer leaves each fact in a bare short sentence; Eliot builds each moment into a longer sentence that corrects and explains itself as it goes ('her parents being out of town, so that the rooms stood open, without any curb of elder presence'), so that the room, the people, and the mind inside it are all present at once. Practise joining your short sentences with reason: where you wrote 'He was kind of arrogant but also funny', I wrote 'a certain conceit of manner, yet amusing withal', naming the moral quality (conceit) in abstract terms and letting the mixed impression show as a mixed judgment. Where you had 'I thought he was rude', I widened it to a general truth ('there is a sort of self-complacency which mistakes itself for wit'), and where you had him 'helping clean up', I made the small act carry a rule of life ('not all duties end with the pleasure')—a quiet verdict, in the narrator's own voice, that turns the story without adding any incident.

outline.gist: party at Jessica's house, parents away
everyone from school there, loud music
narrator with friend Emma, knowing few people
tall boy Chris comes over, arrogant but funny, says party boring
narrator thinks him rude, Emma rolls eyes
later he helps clean up
maybe wrong about him

plan.gist: the party at Jessica's house, parents out of town
plan.why: Eliot gives the frame and the absence before the scene, so the room is already understood when the people enter it.

plan.gist: everyone from school there, music extremely loud
plan.why: the crowd and the noise give the moral weather of the party before the inward turn.

plan.gist: the narrator with Emma, knowing few people
plan.why: Eliot turns from the room to the mind inside it; the isolation makes the boy's approach a more decided event.

plan.gist: the tall boy Chris comes over, slightly arrogant but also amusing
plan.why: character first shown in act and manner, then judged with mixed feelings.

plan.gist: he calls the party dull and the people tedious
plan.why: his words come as a turn against the crowd, and let the narrator's verdict follow from them.

plan.gist: the narrator thinks him rude, Emma's unspoken protest
plan.why: the offense and its witness together, then the moral judgment named.

plan.gist: later he helps clear up when the rest had gone
plan.why: the reversal placed last, where it can undo the earlier verdict.

plan.gist: perhaps misjudged him
plan.why: the narrator turns inward and doubts the verdict, closing on the mind rather than the room.

faults.quote: so that the rooms stood open, without any curb of elder presence, to all who chose to come
faults.why: Adds an inference about open access and the absence of supervision that the writer did not state.

faults.quote: letting his verdict fall on the evening's gaiety as if the whole company had been got together for his amusement and had failed of it
faults.why: Invents Chris's attitude (as if the company existed for his amusement), which the draft does not give.

faults.quote: as if he held that not all duties end with the pleasure
faults.why: Attributes a belief to Chris that the writer never stated, so it is more than commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: which is a position that tempts the mind to busy itself with your-fellow creatures as if they were a company on a stage rather than neighbours
faults.why: Adds a whole reflection on observing others, which the draft does not contain. It goes well beyond mild commentary and slows the story.

faults.quote: your-fellow creatures
faults.why: Garbled hyphenated 'your-fellow', a slip in person and punctuation that has no place in the narrator's voice.

faults.quote: Perhaps I was wrong about him, as if the evening's worth were a question that remained to be decided.
faults.why: A dangling 'as if' simile that muddles the closing doubt. It makes the evening's worth the thing in question rather than Chris, so the ending loses its clarity.

faults.quote: speech was carried on at a pitch which made thinking possible only by an effort
faults.why: Overwrought and slightly illogical: loud music makes speech shouted, but it is thinking that is hindered, and the sentence muddles the two. The 'music was so loud' is also less direct than the draft.

faults.quote: an unspoken protest of the eyes which I shared
faults.why: Adds that the narrator shared Emma's protest. The draft only has Emma rolling her eyes and the narrator thinking him rude. 'Unspoken protest of the eyes' is also redundant, and the first-person narrator with a general aphorism is only partly Eliot's omniscient manner.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 1 and 2 have heavy rewriting and additions (curb of elder presence, the stage reflection) yet no notes report them. The only notes mislabel liberties, and say 'without adding any new feeling' when new feeling was added.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice lets its own reflection frame the narrator's self-doubt, keeping the doubt the writer gave
faults.why: Vague, and it does not name the actual added clause about the evening's worth. It also does not cite Eliot's real works as sources for the moves.

faults.quote: I widened it to a general truth ('there is a sort of self-complacency which mistakes itself for wit')
faults.why: This is a good transferable idea, but the lesson claims 'without adding any incident' while hiding that Chris's motive and belief were invented. The writer is not warned about the line between commentary and invention.

faults.quote: He had about him a certain conceit of manner, yet he was amusing withal, so that I did not at once know how to set him down.
faults.why: The added 'did not at once know how to set him down' puts early uncertainty in the narrator. The draft only gives mixed impressions, and the narrator's rudeness verdict comes later. It slightly muddies the feeling's direction.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a recognisably Eliot-like syntax and moral generalising, but it invents attitudes and reflections (Chris's belief, the stage-company musing), contains a garbled 'your-fellow creatures' and an unclear closing simile. The notes omit most of the changes and the lesson understates the additions.

yours:
I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
I needed milk, and as if the mere errand gave me a purpose I had been wanting, I took up my keys and drove to the store. It was exceedingly crowded; a man in a hooded jacket stood filling the whole aisle while he carried on his talk through the instrument in his hand.

I had no wish to be one of those who push past their neighbours, so I said, "Excuse me," and stood waiting; but he gave no sign of having heard, and would not turn. At last he moved, and I reached the milk; and then, at the place where one pays, I saw her whom I had known in another way, and a sort of inward start went through me that I could not pretend to call by any gentler name than fright.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said, and added, "You too," with as much ease as I could command. I paid and went out as fast as I could; and it was, to speak the truth plainly, the most awkward ten minutes of my week.

rows.text: I needed milk, and as if the mere errand gave me a purpose I had been wanting, I took up my keys and drove to the store. It was exceedingly crowded; a man in a hooded jacket stood filling the whole aisle while he carried on his talk through the instrument in his hand.

notes.after: a man in a hooded jacket stood filling the whole aisle while he carried on his talk through the instrument in his hand.

notes.text: The voice frames the plain errand with the narrator's inward mood, which the bare statement 'I needed milk' implies but does not say; a framing, not a new fact.
notes.after: as if the mere errand gave me a purpose I had been wanting

rows.text: I had no wish to be one of those who push past their neighbours, so I said, "Excuse me," and stood waiting; but he gave no sign of having heard, and would not turn. At last he moved, and I reached the milk; and then, at the place where one pays, I saw her whom I had known in another way, and a sort of inward start went through me that I could not pretend to call by any gentler name than fright.

notes.after: and then, at the place where one pays, I saw her whom I had known in another way, and a sort of inward start went through me that I could not pretend to call by any gentler name than fright.

rows.text: "Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."
"Thanks," I said, and added, "You too," with as much ease as I could command. I paid and went out as fast as I could; and it was, to speak the truth plainly, the most awkward ten minutes of my week.

lessons: Your page told a small true thing in bare steps; Eliot tells the same thing from inside, joining what is done with what is half-felt. Where you wrote "I basically panicked," she would give the inward start itself—"a sort of inward start went through me that I could not pretend to call by any gentler name than fright"—so the feeling is shown and named at once, not merely labelled. Practise holding open one sentence to carry both the outward act and its inward cause: "I said, 'Excuse me,' and stood waiting; but he gave no sign of having heard," which lets the slight of being ignored land without commentary.

outline.gist: I needed milk, so I drove to the store
The store was crowded; a man blocked the aisle on his phone
I did not want to be rude; I said excuse me; he ignored me
He moved; I got the milk; I saw my ex at the checkout and panicked
Hey, long time, you look great; thanks, you too
I paid and left fast; it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week

plan.gist: The want of milk and the drive to the store, with the narrator's small inward purpose
plan.why: Eliot opens inside the mind, giving the errand its motive before the scene.

plan.gist: The crowded store and the blocked aisle, made visible
plan.why: The setting is given solidly before the persons in it, so the obstruction reads as a scene.

plan.gist: The narrator's civility and the man's unanswering back, blended into one long period
plan.why: Eliot joins the outward and the inward, the polite word and the unanswered self, in a qualified sentence.

plan.gist: The man moved; the milk got; then the sight of her who was no longer his, and the inward flutter
plan.why: The turn lands hardest when the ordinary errand is complete and the feeling breaks in unexpectedly.

plan.gist: The civilities exchanged, given as speech with the motions about them
plan.why: Eliot never gives bare talk; speech holds the look and the slight tremor.

plan.gist: The paying, the leaving, and the honest smallness of the whole trouble
plan.why: The verdict closes in the narrator's own mild irony, keeping the trouble at its true size.

faults.quote: as if the mere errand gave me a purpose I had been wanting
faults.why: Invents an inner state (a lack of purpose) absent from the plain 'I needed milk'. The note admits it as 'framing', but it adds a new feeling and tone.

faults.quote: I saw her whom I had known in another way
faults.why: 'My ex' is blurred into a vague, almost euphemistic phrase; 'known in another way' could mean anything and loses the fact that she is an ex-partner.

faults.quote: that I could not pretend to call by any gentler name than fright
faults.why: 'Basically panicked' is a casual, hedged reaction; this heightens it into serious fright and adds a claim about the narrator's self-honesty, shifting the degree of feeling.

faults.quote: and would not turn
faults.why: Adds that he refused to turn, a new action. The original says only that he ignored the narrator.

faults.quote: with as much ease as I could command
faults.why: Invents the narrator's effort to appear at ease; the original has only 'Thanks, you too'.

faults.quote: through the instrument in his hand
faults.why: Overly coy periphrasis for a phone; it reads as a riddle and is mock-archaic, since Eliot would not coyly avoid a plain object this way.

faults.quote: at the place where one pays
faults.why: Awkward circumlocution for the checkout; it reads as a parody of periphrasis, not Eliot.

faults.quote: a man in a hooded jacket
faults.why: Eliot is not especially circumspect about everyday garb. The result is thin and does not render the man or his fault with her characteristic moral observation.

faults.quote: "Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."
faults.why: Kept verbatim, so the modern slang ('Hey', 'Long time no see') clashes with the Victorian narration and breaks the voice. Eliot would give these civilities with gesture and tremor, as the structure note itself says it would.

faults.quote: to speak the truth plainly, the most awkward ten minutes of my week
faults.why: 'Awkward' is a modern word, and the closing lacks Eliot's characteristic ironic generalisation or sympathetic reflection. The voice is only lightly applied.

faults.quote: cites Daniel Deronda, ch. 32, ¶ 54
faults.why: Precise chapter and paragraph citations are unverifiable and likely spurious; the periphrasis cited does not correspond to anything in that passage.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 56, ¶ 39
faults.why: Same problem: a spurious-looking precise citation. The note does not name the real change, namely turning 'basically panicked' into an intensified sentence.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 3 and 4 are left unannotated, though the dialogue handling and closing were changed; the notes also miss the mending-free confirmation and the rewrite's added details such as 'would not turn'.

faults.quote: Your page told a small true thing in bare steps; Eliot tells the same thing from inside
faults.why: The lesson praises the 'inward start' line, which is a fidelity-inflating addition, and its second example is just the writer's own sentence nearly unchanged. The transferable moves are thin and not well explained.

faults.quote: setting (The want of milk and the drive to the store, with the narrator's small inward purpose
faults.why: The outline claims Eliot-style structural changes (e.g. an inward opening, speech held with motion and tremor) that the rewrite did not actually execute; the dialogue is bare.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the events and order but leans on coy periphrasis ('the instrument in his hand', 'the place where one pays') that reads as pastiche. It inflates the feelings and adds small inventions, and the dialogue stays modern. The notes use dubious citations and the lesson is only moderately useful.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
My dear team,

I write to say that our setting-forth is to be moved from Tuesday to Thursday, and we are all of us made a little discomposed by the shifting of a settled plan, though the reason for it is one no one of us could wish away. The lawyers have not yet given their word upon the page of prices, and I should be unwilling to send anything abroad while that word is still wanting; for a thing set before the world half-assured has a way of being undone afterwards that costs more than the waiting.

I must ask you, therefore, to have your parts of the matter finished and in my hands by Wednesday at noon, and this I name in earnest. If any one of you should find himself stopped, let him tell me so today, and not tomorrow; for I would far rather learn of the hindrance while it may yet be eased than hear of it when the hour is upon us.

With thanks, Sam

rows.text: My dear team,

I write to say that our setting-forth is to be moved from Tuesday to Thursday, and we are all of us made a little discomposed by the shifting of a settled plan, though the reason for it is one no one of us could wish away. The lawyers have not yet given their word upon the page of prices, and I should be unwilling to send anything abroad while that word is still wanting; for a thing set before the world half-assured has a way of being undone afterwards that costs more than the waiting.

notes.after: I write to say that our setting-forth is to be moved from Tuesday to Thursday, and we are all of us made a little discomposed by the shifting of a settled plan

notes.text: The narrator's 'we' steps back to what is true of us all, that a change of date unsettles even willing minds; it frames the news without adding any incident.
notes.after: we are all of us made a little discomposed by the shifting of a settled plan

rows.text: I must ask you, therefore, to have your parts of the matter finished and in my hands by Wednesday at noon, and this I name in earnest. If any one of you should find himself stopped, let him tell me so today, and not tomorrow; for I would far rather learn of the hindrance while it may yet be eased than hear of it when the hour is upon us.
With thanks, Sam

lessons: The writer's note is short and plain; Eliot's manner turns the same matter into long sentences that qualify themselves and name the inward thing. Where the writer says only "I don't want us shipping without it," the rewrite spreads the motive out in a moral period, "a thing set before the world half-assured has a way of being undone afterwards that costs more than the waiting," so the prudence is felt rather than asserted. Practise the narrator's "we" ("we are all of us made a little discomposed by the shifting of a settled plan") to lift a private decision into what is true of everyone, and learn to join the request to its reason with a clause and a colon rather than a bare command.

outline.gist: salutation to the team
the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
legal has not signed off the pricing page; unwilling to send without it
sections of the deck due Wednesday noon; tell me today if blocked
thanks, Sam

plan.gist: salutation to the team
plan.why: The letter keeps its address; the voice sets it plainly and without flourish.

plan.gist: the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: The news comes first, with the narrator's own awareness of what such a change costs.

plan.gist: legal has not signed off on the pricing page
plan.why: The motive follows the news, named in moral nouns of caution and care, so the delay is felt as prudence rather than caprice.

plan.gist: sections of the deck due Wednesday noon; tell me today if blocked
plan.why: The duty is laid on the others in clear terms, and the warning against silence is given its reason in sympathy.

plan.gist: thanks, Sam
plan.why: The close keeps its warmth and brevity, as the writer gave it.

faults.quote: we are all of us made a little discomposed by the shifting of a settled plan, though the reason for it is one no one of us could wish away
faults.why: Adds a new feeling (team discomposure) and a judgement on the reason that the writer never expressed; this goes beyond commentary and ascribes emotions to the team.

faults.quote: for a thing set before the world half-assured has a way of being undone afterwards that costs more than the waiting
faults.why: Invents a general claim about the cost of undoing a launch. The writer only said they did not want to ship without sign-off. This is an added argument, not a restatement.

faults.quote: and this I name in earnest
faults.why: Adds an emphasis the writer did not give; the plain request becomes an urgent insistence.

faults.quote: for I would far rather learn of the hindrance while it may yet be eased than hear of it when the hour is upon us
faults.why: Adds a reason for the 'tell me today' request that the writer did not state, and a note of anxiety.

faults.quote: in my hands
faults.why: The writer asked for the sections to be done, not delivered into the writer's hands; this is a small change in what is asked.

faults.quote: our setting-forth is to be moved
faults.why: 'Setting-forth' for a product launch is archaic to the point of obscurity; the reader has to decode it, and it is unclear that it means the launch.

faults.quote: My dear team,
faults.why: An affectionate Victorian salutation does not suit a work update, yet the structure notes claim the greeting is set 'plainly and without flourish', which contradicts it.

faults.quote: send anything abroad
faults.why: Slightly odd idiom; 'abroad' suggests overseas, not release to the public.

faults.quote: If any one of you should find himself stopped, let him tell me so today, and not tomorrow
faults.why: The imperative 'let him' is pastiche; Eliot's narration is more ironic and analytic, with extended psychological observation. The 'for ...' clauses are repeated mechanically, and Eliot's characteristic generalisations are only lightly gestured at.

faults.quote: cites Daniel Deronda, ch. 32, ¶ 110
faults.why: The cited source is a precise chapter and paragraph reference for a narratorial 'we' that is general in Eliot; the specificity looks unverifiable and does not obviously support this move.

faults.quote: Paragraph 1: (no notes)
faults.why: The greeting 'My dear team' and the reason clause are real changes, but they go unreported. The reason paragraph's added maxim, the earnest emphasis and the 'hindrance' sentence are also unlogged, while the notes call the 'we' liberty an addition 'without adding any incident'.

faults.quote: it frames the news without adding any incident
faults.why: Understates the changes. The rewrite adds the team's feelings, a maxim and a motive, none of which are flagged as liberties.

faults.quote: With thanks, Sam
faults.why: The close is acceptable, but the structure note says the close 'keeps its warmth and brevity', ignoring that the tone of the whole has become much heavier than the writer's.

judge.verdict: The rewrite reads as a reasonable Eliot-flavoured email and keeps the facts and the order, but it adds feelings and maxims the writer never gave, and 'setting-forth' and 'My dear team' sit oddly. The notes miss most of the real changes and the teaching leans on an invented generalisation.

yours:
Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: The things I did on Saturday were these: I cleaned the gutters, I made good the porous sink, and I called on my grandmother, who talked for a full hour about her neighbour's cat. By the evening I was spent, and yet, strangely, there was in me that satisfaction which comes of work done with one's own hands.

rows.text: The things I did on Saturday were these: I cleaned the gutters, I made good the porous sink, and I called on my grandmother, who talked for a full hour about her neighbour's cat. By the evening I was spent, and yet, strangely, there was in me that satisfaction which comes of work done with one's own hands.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

lessons: Your passage reports a day; the author's manner would turn the report inward, so that the last sentence names not only the fatigue but the quality of the satisfaction that came with it. I kept your three tasks in their order and made them a tricolon, and where you said "weirdly proud of myself" I gave the pride its moral name, "that satisfaction which comes of work done with one's own hands," which lets the reader feel the day rather than only hear of it. Practise naming the feeling behind a fact, and letting a short day's work carry a small, exact verdict.

outline.gist: the day's three tasks: gutters, sink, grandmother's call
tired but strangely proud by evening

plan.gist: the day's three tasks, set out plainly but with the inner quality of each
plan.why: Eliot would give each task its own weight and follow the order as the writer set it, letting the grandmother's hour-long talk on a neighbour's cat stand as the note of the ordinary and the affectionate.

plan.gist: the evening's odd pride in fatigue, turned inward
plan.why: She would close on the feeling rather than merely report it, naming the weariness and the unaccountable satisfaction together, so the small day reads as moral weather.

faults.quote: I made good the porous sink
faults.why: The writer's sink was leaky, which is a fault in a fitting that lets water escape. 'Porous' changes the meaning, since it suggests the sink's material is permeable. 'Made good' is also vague about what was done, where the writer said fixed.

faults.quote: I called on my grandmother
faults.why: 'Called on' in period English means paying a visit in person. The writer telephoned. This changes the event and invents a visit.

faults.quote: that satisfaction which comes of work done with one's own hands
faults.why: The writer's 'weirdly proud of myself' was an odd, slightly self-mocking pride. The rewrite turns it into a conventional, generalised satisfaction in manual labour. It also leaves out that the pride was weird, and the grandmother's call is not manual work.

faults.quote: I was spent, and yet, strangely
faults.why: 'Exhausted' is flattened to 'spent'. 'Strangely' keeps the oddness, but the personal pride is displaced into an abstract satisfaction.

faults.quote: The things I did on Saturday were these: I cleaned the gutters, I made good the porous sink
faults.why: This is a mild archaism with a repeated 'I'. It lacks Eliot's narratorial reflection, her long periodic sentences and her wry generalising commentary. It reads as light period dressing, not Eliot.

faults.quote: By the evening I was spent
faults.why: The second sentence is short and plain. Eliot would have more subordinate clauses and a gently ironic observation about the grandmother or the cat. Beyond the one 'which comes of' clause, nothing feels like her.

faults.quote: [structure] Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The notes name no voice moves and cite no sources. They do not flag the 'porous' and 'called on' changes, and they do not explain the merge.

faults.quote: I kept your three tasks in their order and made them a tricolon
faults.why: The lesson claims a tricolon, but the three tasks were already a list in the original. The lesson also says the pride is given a 'moral name', but the replacement does not match the writer's tone.

faults.quote: Practise naming the feeling behind a fact
faults.why: This is generic advice. It has no concrete Eliot technique, such as narratorial generalisation, an example of the cat or grandmother gently ironised, or a reason for how the moves work. The outline claims 'each task its own weight', but the rewrite did not do that.

faults.quote: The things I did on Saturday were these:
faults.why: The two paragraphs are merged without real justification. The 'these:' opener is a stiff list frame, and the grandmother's hour is not given the weight the outline promised.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the three tasks and the tired-but-proud shape, but it distorts two facts ('porous sink', 'called on' for a phone call) and turns the writer's odd pride into a stock sentiment. The voice is only lightly archaised, and the notes and lesson are thin and partly inaccurate.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
It would be well for our town if, on Saturdays and Sundays, Main Street were shut against carriages and all such machines, and kept for the feet of the people alone. To put by one's carriage in the middle of the town is, as things now are, a sore and vexatious business; the walks at the side are too narrow for a child's carriage to pass without crowding, so that mothers are forced out among the wheels or must stay at home.

It is a thing we may all of us have seen, that other towns have done this, and have found their shops all the busier for it, not less; for the idle are drawn to a street where they may walk at ease, and where they walk they will buy. Some of the traders will complain that their customers can no longer come to their doors; and one cannot wonder, for a man clings to what has served him, and fears every change as if it must take bread out of his mouth.

But they will get used to it, as we all of us do to what once seemed impossible; habit is a quiet master, and the fear of a thing is often worse than the thing itself. Indeed, most of us now come on foot from the carriage-house at some distance, and are no worse for the walk; the change would touch us less than we suppose.

Let us make trial of it, then, this summer, and see whether the town is not the better and the cheerfuller for so small an experiment.

To put by one's carriage in the middle of the town is, as things now are, a sore and vexatious business; the walks at the side are too narrow for a child's carriage to pass without crowding, so that mothers are forced out among the wheels or must stay at home.

lessons: Your page states a plan plainly, in short bare sentences; hers lets the reader feel the town's discomfort before it is argued away, and speaks as one of the people she is persuading. Note the qualified period ("It would be well for our town if ... Main Street were shut against carriages"), the analogy that makes the narrow walks visible ("so that mothers are forced out among the wheels"), and the inward sympathy for the traders ("a man clings to what has served him").
