outline.gist: main street should close to cars on weekends
parking is hard and sidewalks too narrow
other towns prospered by it
shopkeepers will fear losing customers
they will get used to it; people already walk from the garage
try it this summer

plan.gist: the change urged, in a modest first-person plural
plan.why: the voice opens on the common resolve, not the bare command, and lets the 'we' set the duty before the reasons.

plan.gist: present trouble made inward and visible
plan.why: the voice gives the discomfort—parking, narrow walks—as a felt condition, with an analogy to make it visible.

plan.gist: other towns and their better shops
plan.why: the general truth of imitation and profit gives the claim weight before the objection.

plan.gist: the owners' fear, entered from inside
plan.why: the voice grants the traders their natural fear in sympathy even before answering it.

plan.gist: habit will reconcile them; most walk already
plan.why: the narrator's 'we' generalizes habit, and the last fact closes the objection gently.

plan.gist: let us try it this summer
plan.why: the voice ends on the modest experiment, a duty to be tried rather than a victory claimed.

faults.quote: so that mothers are forced out among the wheels or must stay at home
faults.why: This invents a consequence the writer never stated: mothers pushed into traffic, or kept indoors. The writer only said the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.

faults.quote: for the idle are drawn to a street where they may walk at ease, and where they walk they will buy
faults.why: This adds a new causal argument for why the shops prosper. The writer gave only the bare evidence that other towns' shops do better, so this is new evidence and a new claim.

faults.quote: the fear of a thing is often worse than the thing itself
faults.why: This is an added maxim that goes beyond commentary. It also slightly changes the writer's casual dismissal ('they'll get used to it') into a reassurance.

faults.quote: are no worse for the walk; the change would touch us less than we suppose
faults.why: These are new claims about how little the change would affect people. The writer said only that most people walk from the garage anyway.

faults.quote: the better and the cheerfuller for so small an experiment
faults.why: This adds a promised outcome (cheerfulness) and calls the experiment small. The writer simply said 'We should try it this summer.'

faults.quote: most of us now come on foot from the carriage-house at some distance
faults.why: The draft's weak point is that the garage-walk remark does not answer the objection and sits uneasily with 'parking is a nightmare'. The rewrite neither catches nor mends this and reports nothing to the writer. 'Carriage-house at some distance' also blurs the point further, since a carriage-house is where one keeps a carriage, not a public garage.

faults.quote: too narrow for a child's carriage to pass without crowding
faults.why: The rewrite renders cars as 'carriages' and strollers as 'a child's carriage'. The same word now names both the nuisance and the victim, which muddies the sense.

faults.quote: It is a thing we may all of us have seen, that other towns have done this
faults.why: This is an odd claim. It says 'we' have all seen other towns do it, though nothing suggests the townspeople have witnessed it. The 'we' is forced in here.

faults.quote: found their shops all the busier for it, not less
faults.why: 'Not less' is a clumsy tag after 'all the busier'. Elsewhere the phrasing is a generic Victorian pastiche rather than idiomatic: 'To put by one's carriage' is a strained idiom, and 'a sore and vexatious business' is stock.

faults.quote: habit is a quiet master
faults.why: This reads as a generic aphorism rather than Eliot's particular, ironic observation of character. The piece has little free indirect insight, specific imagery, or her wry narratorial distance. It is mostly period diction on a plain argument.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 39, ¶ 60
faults.why: The quoted sentence is the rewrite's own invention, not Middlemarch text. The citation presents a specific chapter and paragraph as the source of a move without grounding it.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the narrator's 'we' steps back to a general truth to frame the evidence
faults.why: This does not report the real liberties: the added profit mechanism, the added maxims, and the changes of cars to carriages and garage to carriage-house. Paragraphs 1, 3 and 4 have almost no move notes. The structure notes only say which paragraphs were merged or split.

faults.quote: the analogy that makes the narrow walks visible ("so that mothers are forced out among the wheels")
faults.why: The lesson praises this as an analogy, but it is an invented concrete scene, not an analogy. The how-it-is-built outline also claims the piece opens in a modest first-person plural, yet the opening is an impersonal conditional with only 'our town'. The lesson partly misdescribes the text and models adding unsupported content as a virtue.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the argument's order and has a pleasantly Victorian surface, but it adds several claims (the mothers, the shoppers who walk and buy, the maxims) and leaves the weak garage-walk answer unmended and unreported. The notes cite a dubious Middlemarch source and misdescribe the changes, which weakens their teaching value.

yours:
I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite:
I've never been to Paris, as I keep telling my brother; for the once I was there, if that can be called being there, was a week of coming-down rain and of that long, low waiting which a lost paper imposes on the second of two days. Nothing can be said to have shown itself to us of the city then, and the better part of our time was spent at the embassy, where the one of us stood before a clerk and the other waited in a chair, watching the rain against the window.

And yet he still declares it to have been the best vacation he ever had; so differently do two people, who have stood side by side in the same weather, carry away the memory of a place.

rows.text: I've never been to Paris, as I keep telling my brother; for the once I was there, if that can be called being there, was a week of coming-down rain and of that long, low waiting which a lost paper imposes on the second of two days. Nothing can be said to have shown itself to us of the city then, and the better part of our time was spent at the embassy, where the one of us stood before a clerk and the other waited in a chair, watching the rain against the window.

notes.text: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris; your second says she was there for a week. These cannot both be true of the same person. The rest of the passage is a story about a visit, so the visit is the fact and the opening line is the faulty one. I kept the words as spoken irony and signalled it: she has been to Paris, but not, as she will show, in any usual sense of being there.
notes.after: I've never been to Paris, as I keep telling my brother; for the once I was there

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
the mending itself, which turns a flat contradiction into the gentle irony the rest of the story asks for, and it names the brother beforehand so the verdict at the close is his own words returning
notes.after: as I keep telling my brother

rows.text: And yet he still declares it to have been the best vacation he ever had; so differently do two people, who have stood side by side in the same weather, carry away the memory of a place.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 2, given a paragraph of its own.

lessons: Your passage tells the story in four bare strokes; the author's manner is to enter the mind that tells it and to let each fact confess its feeling. The long qualified period at the head ("as I keep telling my brother; for the once I was there, if that can be called being there...") mends the contradiction and at once shows the irony the story lives by; the closing antithesis ("so differently do two people, who have stood side by side in the same weather, carry away the memory of a place") turns your brother's verdict into a general truth the reader feels as her own. Practise joining your short sentences into such self-correcting periods, and closing not on the fact but on what the fact means.

outline.gist: I've never been to Paris
the last time: rain all week, brother lost passport second day
most of the trip at the embassy
brother still calls it the best vacation ever

plan.gist: the claim never to have been to Paris, with the irony signalled
plan.why: Eliot opens with the mind's own claim, qualified at once so the reader keeps faith with the story to come

plan.gist: the rain the whole week, the brother's lost passport on the second day
plan.why: she gives the outward facts in their order, letting the one small thing confess the larger trouble

plan.gist: most of the trip at the embassy
plan.why: the matter narrows to the place where the trouble was lived through, before the verdict may land

plan.gist: the brother's judgment differing from the narrator's
plan.why: she closes on the gap between what was and what is remembered, which is her whole subject

sense.quote: I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there
sense.problem: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris; your second says she was there for a week. These cannot both be true of the same person.
sense.resolution: The rest of the passage is a story about a visit, so the visit is the fact and the opening line is the faulty one. Mend it to a denial of a different thing, and one the passage bears out: "I've never been to Paris except the once" — or, with the least change of all, keep the words as spoken irony and signal it: "I've never been to Paris, as I always tell my brother." The second keeps the joke and agrees with every later sentence, since nothing in them claims a second visit.

faults.quote: imposes on the second of two days
faults.why: The passport was lost on the second day of a week-long trip. 'The second of two days' invents a two-day span and contradicts 'a week' in the same sentence.

faults.quote: that long, low waiting which a lost paper imposes on the second of two days
faults.why: This is close to a riddle. The reader cannot tell whose paper was lost, that it was a passport, or what the 'second of two days' means. The vagueness reads as garble, not Eliot's precision.

faults.quote: where the one of us stood before a clerk and the other waited in a chair, watching the rain against the window
faults.why: Invents an incident: who dealt with the clerk, who sat, and the watching of the rain. None of this is in the draft, and it is more than commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: as I keep telling my brother
faults.why: Adds a fact (the narrator repeatedly says this to the brother). The note presents it as a mending device, but it also creates a new relationship between speaker and brother.

faults.quote: Nothing can be said to have shown itself to us of the city then
faults.why: Adds a claim that they saw nothing of Paris. The draft says only that most of the trip was at the embassy, so the claim is stronger than the source.

faults.quote: for the once I was there
faults.why: The draft's 'the last time I was there' implies more than one visit. 'The once' reduces this to a single visit.

faults.quote: a week of coming-down rain
faults.why: 'Coming-down rain' is an awkward, non-idiomatic compound. It is not Eliot's phrasing and reads as a stylistic costume.

faults.quote: I've never been to Paris, as I keep telling my brother
faults.why: Uses a contraction and a chatty first-person framing. Eliot's narration is typically more formal, with an authorial or omniscient generalising voice, so this reads only partly as Eliot.

faults.quote: if that can be called being there
faults.why: The mending is weak. The opening still states a flat falsehood, and the hedge arrives only mid-sentence, so the irony is hinted at but not clearly established. The note's claim that it is 'signalled' overstates what the rewrite does.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the mending itself
faults.why: The notes cite no concrete Eliot source or named move. They are also vague about the real additions (the clerk and chair scene, 'nothing shown of the city'), which are not reported as liberties.

faults.quote: mends the contradiction and at once shows the irony the story lives by
faults.why: The lesson praises the opening period as a model, yet that period is the muddled part of the rewrite. This weakens the transferable value, though the closing-antithesis advice is useful.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order, catches the contradiction, and closes with a good Eliot-style generalisation. But it garbles the passport sentence ('second of two days'), invents a clerk-and-chair scene, and uses strained phrasing. The notes are thin and do not report these additions.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we should leave off working six days and work but four. The people here are burned out, and our best engineer has just quit. There are studies which show that the fruitfulness of labour stays as it was, or even increases, when the week is shortened; for we are all of us slow to let go of a habit that has the look of prudence, even when it spent its strength long ago. It would also help with hiring, since the man who is worth having will go where he is not worn to the bone.

I know it is a hazardous step, and that our clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and then see what it has done for us.

rows.text: I think we should leave off working six days and work but four. The people here are burned out, and our best engineer has just quit. There are studies which show that the fruitfulness of labour stays as it was, or even increases, when the week is shortened; for we are all of us slow to let go of a habit that has the look of prudence, even when it spent its strength long ago. It would also help with hiring, since the man who is worth having will go where he is not worn to the bone.

notes.text: the narrator's 'we' steps back to the general truth behind the resistance to change, framing what is there without adding new matter
notes.after: We are all of us slow to let go of a habit that has the look of prudence, even when it spent its strength long ago

rows.text: I know it is a hazardous step, and that our clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and then see what it has done for us.

lessons: The writer's page is a list of short claims; Eliot's manner joins them into long sentences that qualify themselves ("the fruitfulness of labour stays as it was, or even increases") and lets the narrator step back once into a general truth ("we are all of us slow to let go of a habit that has the look of prudence"), which frames the resistance without inventing new feeling. The concession is named in her moral vocabulary ("a hazardous step"), and the close ("then see what it has done for us") makes the trial concrete rather than bare. Practise building one long sentence from several short ones, with a single general step-back per paragraph.

people burned out; best engineer quit

plan.why: state the claimant's motion plainly first, as a verdict she can lean on

plan.gist: people burned out; best engineer quit
plan.why: the moral and human cause before the argument, as Eliot puts the inward life first

plan.gist: studies show the work holds or rises
plan.why: the appeal to what is observed, then the general truth it suggests

plan.gist: would help with hiring

plan.gist: danger; clients may not like it

plan.why: the modest resolution, closing with a practical trial

faults.quote: for we are all of us slow to let go of a habit that has the look of prudence, even when it spent its strength long ago
faults.why: Adds a new claim, an aphorism about resistance to change that the writer never made. It works as commentary, but it also adds an argument and a slight accusation against colleagues, and it sits inside the evidence sentence.

faults.quote: when the week is shortened
faults.why: The writer said only that productivity stays the same or goes up. This adds a stated condition, though a mild one.

faults.quote: since the man who is worth having will go where he is not worn to the bone
faults.why: Adds a causal claim (good candidates avoid overworked firms) and a gendered 'man', and it intensifies the writer's plain 'would help with hiring'. 'Worn to the bone' also overstates the burnout.

faults.quote: leave off working six days and work but four
faults.why: The writer never said the current week is six days. This invents a fact, and unlike a repair of sense, it is not reported.

faults.quote: and then see what it has done for us
faults.why: Slightly expands 'and see' by implying a result for 'us'. This is minor.

faults.quote: I think we should leave off working six days and work but four.
faults.why: The first-person opener is plain and clipped. Eliot's narrator would not speak in this register, and the first paragraph keeps the writer's flat sentences ('It would also help with hiring') with only a single flourish.

faults.quote: the fruitfulness of labour stays as it was, or even increases
faults.why: 'Fruitfulness of labour' is a clumsy, slightly archaic stand-in for 'productivity'. It reads as costume, and 'studies which show' alongside it is an odd mix.

faults.quote: The people here are burned out
faults.why: 'Burned out' is a modern idiom left untouched amid the period diction, which gives a jarring mix. 'Here' is also added.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the narrator's 'we' steps back to the general truth
faults.why: The note understates the change. It does not mention the invented six-day week, the added hiring claim and the 'man worth having', the vocabulary swaps, or the merging of sentences. Paragraph 2 gets no notes, although 'hazardous step' and the closing expansion are changes.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Changes were made ('hazardous step', 'what it has done for us') but not reported.

faults.quote: Practise building one long sentence from several short ones, with a single general step-back per paragraph.
faults.why: The advice is generic and partly misdirected. It treats an inserted aphorism as a virtue, though it introduced unsupported content. It also never warns the writer about the invented figures or the invented generalisation, and it gives no specific Eliot sources.

faults.quote: for we are all of us slow to let go of a habit
faults.why: The aphorism interrupts the evidence-to-hiring flow and recasts the studies as a rebuke. The outline's claim that the moral cause comes before the argument is not followed, since the order stays as the writer's. The 'how built' section describes a reordering that did not happen.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and most facts, but it invents a six-day week and a hiring claim, and an inserted aphorism adds an argument that was not there. The voice is only partly Eliot, much of it left flat or anachronistic. The notes underreport the changes and the lesson is thin.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana set off our dinner I was not in the least put out; indeed, the truth of it was that I was relieved. I had been dreading it the whole week through, and I am not proud of the discovery, though we are all of us apt to be less honest with ourselves than with our friends.

I told her it was of no consequence, and that we would do it another time. I do not think we shall.

rows.text: When Dana set off our dinner I was not in the least put out; indeed, the truth of it was that I was relieved. I had been dreading it the whole week through, and I am not proud of the discovery, though we are all of us apt to be less honest with ourselves than with our friends.

notes.after: I had been dreading it the whole week through, and I am not proud of the discovery, though we are all of us apt to be less honest with ourselves than with our friends.

notes.text: The narrator's first-person plural steps back to a general truth that frames the particular confession of relief and shame; it is strictly a framing of what the writer plainly gives.
notes.after: We are all of us apt to be less honest with ourselves than with our friends

rows.text: I told her it was of no consequence, and that we would do it another time. I do not think we shall.

lessons: The writer's page is all short, bare strokes; Eliot tells the same matter in qualified periods that turn inward. Joining the refusal and the relief ("I was not in the least put out; indeed, the truth of it was that I was relieved") lets the sentence correct itself as hers do, and the confession of dread opens out into the narrator's "we," so the small shame becomes ours as well. Practise that self-correcting clause: state the outward fact, then qualify it toward the inward truth.

I was relieved

plan.gist: Dana set off our dinner and no vexation followed
plan.why: The voice states the outward fact first, then what it did not do to the heart

plan.gist: That the feeling was relief, not sorrow
plan.why: The inward truth named plainly, as the narrator enters the mind

plan.gist: The week's dread and the small shame of it
plan.why: The moral weather—conscience, not pride—drawn out before the verdict

plan.gist: What was said to Dana, and the doubt it held
plan.why: The outward civility and its hidden reserve kept in the order they happened

faults.quote: though we are all of us apt to be less honest with ourselves than with our friends
faults.why: Adds a new proposition the writer never made, a general claim about self-honesty. It is more than commentary on what is there, and it softens the writer's plain shame at the relief.

faults.quote: When Dana set off our dinner
faults.why: 'Set off' does not mean 'cancelled' here; it reads as 'set out' or 'triggered'. The idiom is wrong for the sense and could confuse the reader.

faults.quote: I told her it was of no consequence
faults.why: The writer said 'it was fine'. 'Of no consequence' is slightly more dismissive and changes the register of the reassurance.

faults.quote: I am not proud of the discovery
faults.why: The writer is not proud of the dread or the relief, not of a 'discovery'. The word shifts the object of the shame and sits oddly. The clause also hangs awkwardly on the following 'though'.

faults.quote: I was not in the least put out; indeed, the truth of it was that I was relieved.
faults.why: Reads as period-flavoured padding rather than Eliot's characteristic analytic irony. The second paragraph is nearly a plain transcription with 'shall' swapped in, so the voice is thin there.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 39, ¶ 60
faults.why: A precise chapter and paragraph citation is unlikely to be verifiable or accurate. The note is also mislabelled as a 'liberty' while claiming it is only a framing, when it adds new content. Paragraph 2 gets no notes though 'shall' and 'of no consequence' were changes.

faults.quote: the confession of dread opens out into the narrator's "we," so the small shame becomes ours as well
faults.why: Presents the added generalisation as a model without warning that it adds a claim the writer did not make. The lesson also credits the rewrite with a self-correcting clause that is really just 'not upset; relieved' restated.

judge.verdict: The feelings keep their direction and the order is intact, but the added aphorism about self-honesty goes beyond the writer's meaning. 'Set off' is a misused idiom, and the Eliot voice is only moderately convincing. The notes overstate the citation precision and misdescribe the addition.

yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight, and when I read it I knew at once what he meant, for he said that we must talk together. The next day we met at a coffee shop in the town, and he was there before me.

He looked very uneasy, and then he said that he was not ready for anything serious, and that the fault was not mine but his. I wanted to cry, but I did not. I only nodded and said that it was all right.

Then I walked home in the rain, and I ate a whole pot of ice cream. My room-mate thought that I made too much of it, and perhaps I did. And yet the hurt was not gone from me.

rows.text: Ryan sent me word at midnight, and when I read it I knew at once what he meant, for he said that we must talk together. The next day we met at a coffee shop in the town, and he was there before me.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

rows.text: He looked very uneasy, and then he said that he was not ready for anything serious, and that the fault was not mine but his. I wanted to cry, but I did not. I only nodded and said that it was all right.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 2 and 3.

notes.after: the fault was not mine but his
notes.cite: The Grey Fairy Book, “The Twin Brothers”, ¶ 3

rows.text: Then I walked home in the rain, and I ate a whole pot of ice cream. My room-mate thought that I made too much of it, and perhaps I did. And yet the hurt was not gone from me.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 3 and 4.
The voice gives its verdict on the matter, as the Fairy Books close a tale on the truth that stands; the writer's 'it still hurt' invites it.
notes.after: And yet the hurt was not gone from me.

lessons: The chief difference is length and joining: your short, hard sentences cut like a modern diary; the Fairy Books join clause to clause with 'and' and 'for' until each sentence tells a whole step of the tale. I turned your three opening sentences into one ('Ryan sent me word at midnight, and when I read it I knew at once what he meant, for he said that we must talk together'), so the news and its meaning arrive together. I rendered speech in the tale's way ('he said that the fault was not mine but his'), and closed on a plain verdict ('And yet the hurt was not gone from me'). Practise joining two or three of your short sentences with 'and' or 'for', and saying each feeling once, plainly, at the end of the step it belongs to.

plan.why: What happened, then what happened next; the speech drives it.

plan.gist: walking home and the comfort taken
plan.why: The feeling is said plainly, as the tale does, not hinted.

plan.gist: the room-mate's doubt and the hurt that remains
plan.why: The tale closes on the truth that stands after the telling.

faults.quote: he was there before me.
faults.why: The writer's detail that he was 'scrolling on his phone' is dropped, though it shows his avoidance and nerves.

faults.quote: a whole pot of ice cream
faults.why: The writer wrote 'pint'. 'Pot' changes the measure, and it reads oddly as the unit for ice cream.

faults.quote: sent me word at midnight
faults.why: 'Texted' becomes a vague 'sent word', so the medium is lost. This also blurs the later 'when I read it'.

faults.quote: the fault was not mine but his
faults.why: The writer's 'it wasn't me, it was him' is a quoted breakup cliché. Rendering it as 'fault' adds a sense of blame and loses the stock-phrase tone.

faults.quote: he said that we must talk together
faults.why: 'Talk together' is padded and stilted. It also comes after 'I knew at once what he meant', which muddles the order of cause and effect.

faults.quote: at a coffee shop in the town
faults.why: 'Downtown' becomes 'in the town', which is clumsy and loses the city sense. 'Coffee shop' is left modern beside the archaic phrasing, so the register is uneven.

faults.quote: He looked very uneasy, and then he said
faults.why: The voice is only lightly archaized. It shows few of the Fairy Books' tale-teller moves, such as 'Now', 'so', and direct narrated speech. Much of it reads as plain prose with 'that' clauses.

faults.quote: cites The Grey Fairy Book, “The Twin Brothers”, ¶ 3
faults.why: The antithesis citation is doubtful and unverifiable. 'Not mine but his' is a trivial construction and not a distinctive move of that tale.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice gives its verdict on the matter
faults.why: The rewrite adds no verdict. 'The hurt was not gone from me' just renders the writer's 'it still hurt', so the note names a change that did not happen.

faults.quote: Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: These structure notes repeat each other and say nothing about why the merging suits the voice.

faults.quote: And yet the hurt was not gone from me.
faults.why: The lesson calls this a 'plain verdict', but it is only the writer's own feeling restated. The claim of teaching a closing move is overstated.

judge.verdict: A faithful, readable rewrite, but the voice is thin and archaic touches are uneven. Small fidelity slips (the dropped phone, 'pot' for 'pint') hurt it, and the notes cite a doubtful source and report a liberty that was never taken.

yours:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is all right, I suppose, but the food is bad, and my bunkmate snores all the night through. Yesterday we went out upon the water in canoes, and I overturned my canoe, and everybody laughed. I was so ashamed.

But there is a girl here named Kayla, and she is very pleasant. She comes from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about horses, and we sit by the lake after dinner and talk. I think she likes me, but I am not sure.

Can you send me more to eat between meals, and my phone charger, which I quite forgot to bring? The counsellors are rather strict, but for the most part they are all right.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please do not let Max use my room.

rows.text: Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is all right, I suppose, but the food is bad, and my bunkmate snores all the night through. Yesterday we went out upon the water in canoes, and I overturned my canoe, and everybody laughed. I was so ashamed.

But there is a girl here named Kayla, and she is very pleasant. She comes from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about horses, and we sit by the lake after dinner and talk. I think she likes me, but I am not sure.
Can you send me more to eat between meals, and my phone charger, which I quite forgot to bring? The counsellors are rather strict, but for the most part they are all right.
Love, Jake
P.S. Please do not let Max use my room.

lessons: The chief difference is that yours runs in short modern bursts and leans on contractions and slang (okay, gross, cool, totally), where the Fairy Books build longer, balanced sentences joined by "and" and "but", and say feelings plainly. I joined your short sentences ("Camp is all right, I suppose, but the food is bad, and my bunkmate snores all the night through") so each holds more of the matter at once, and I turned "it was so embarrassing" into "I was so ashamed", which names the feeling in the tale's way. The request becomes a single question, "Can you send me more to eat between meals, and my phone charger, which I quite forgot to bring?" — the thing asked for first, the reason after — so the letter reads with the plain directness of the tales while keeping every fact you wrote, in your order.

outline.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
Camp is all right; the food and the bunkmate are hard to bear
He overturned the canoe and everyone laughed; he is ashamed
A girl named Kayla, who knows much about horses, and he is not sure she likes him
Send snacks and the phone charger; the counselors are strict but fine
Love, Jake
Do not let Max use his room

plan.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
plan.why: A letter keeps its greeting, unchanged.

plan.gist: Camp is all right, but the food is bad and the bunkmate snores
plan.why: The tale says plainly what is and is not well; the bad news follows the opening verdict, as complaint follows the first word home.

plan.gist: Boating, overturning the canoe, everyone laughing, his shame
plan.why: What happened, then what happened next, joined by and and so; the shame lands last, where it is felt.

plan.gist: Kayla, from Ohio, knowing horses; she may like him
plan.why: A new person enters the tale by her place and what she knows; the uncertainty is said straight out.

plan.gist: Send snacks and the phone charger; the counselors are strict but fine
plan.why: Requests come plainly, the thing first and the reason after; the verdict on the counselors closes the matter.

plan.gist: Love, Jake
plan.why: A letter keeps its close.

plan.gist: Do not let Max into his room
plan.why: The afterthought comes standing alone, as the writer left it.

faults.quote: I was so ashamed.
faults.why: "Embarrassing" becomes "ashamed", which is heavier and moral. A boy laughed at for flipping a canoe is embarrassed, not ashamed, so the degree of feeling shifts.

faults.quote: she is very pleasant
faults.why: "Really cool" carries admiration and some crush-like excitement. "Very pleasant" flattens it, so the feeling is weaker than the writer's.

faults.quote: Camp is all right, I suppose, but the food is bad
faults.why: The writer's "okay I guess" opens a list of complaints. Here "but" turns the sentence into a contrast, and "gross" is softened to "bad".

faults.quote: Can you send me more to eat between meals
faults.why: "Snacks" is paraphrased clumsily. The wording is wordy and slightly altered, and "more" now hangs oddly.

faults.quote: snores all the night through
faults.why: The writer's "snores like crazy" means loud snoring. The rewrite says he snores all night, which is a different claim: duration instead of intensity.

faults.quote: I think she likes me, but I am not sure.
faults.why: This is plain modern prose, unchanged in substance. The Fairy Books' formulas and cadences ("Now it happened that…", a narrative frame, "and so") are barely present, so it reads like a mild Edwardian costume.

faults.quote: Yesterday we went out upon the water in canoes, and I overturned my canoe
faults.why: "Upon the water in canoes" is stilted, and the repeated "canoe" is awkward. It does not read as Lang's cadence; it reads as formal padding.

faults.quote: which I quite forgot to bring
faults.why: "Quite forgot" is a British-sounding tic that clashes with a boy writing home from camp. The "phone charger" is left in the mix, which jars with the archaic register.

faults.quote: The counsellors are rather strict, but for the most part they are all right.
faults.why: "All right" is repeated from the opening line, and "for the most part" is wordy. The sentence trails off flatly.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Every paragraph has empty notes although many changes were made ("ashamed", the joined sentences, the register shift). The reader gets no named moves with sources, so the notes section is useless.

faults.quote: I turned "it was so embarrassing" into "I was so ashamed", which names the feeling in the tale's way.
faults.why: The lesson claims a fidelity-shifting change as a virtue and gives no concrete passage from the Fairy Books. The advice (join short sentences with "and"/"but") is generic and only partly reusable.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: greeting (Dear Mom and Dad; why: A letter keeps its greeting, unchanged.)
faults.why: The outline just restates the writer's order with thin reasons ("The tale says plainly…"), with no real comparison of how the voice would build it differently, so it teaches little.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and the letter's order, but it shifts several feelings (embarrassed to ashamed, cool to pleasant) and reads as lightly archaized modern prose rather than the Fairy Books. The empty notes and generic lesson leave the writer with little to learn from.

yours:
The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
The office was huge and new, and everyone there wore hoodies and drank fine coffee. I felt wholly out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya, and she was friendly but a little stern, and she asked me what I could do and what I could not do. I said I did all things too carefully, which is a poor answer, but she smiled all the same.

After the interview I called my sister, and she said I had most likely done well. I hope she is right, for I am greatly in need of this work, and the rent is due next week and I have no money.

rows.text: The office was huge and new, and everyone there wore hoodies and drank fine coffee. I felt wholly out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya, and she was friendly but a little stern, and she asked me what I could do and what I could not do. I said I did all things too carefully, which is a poor answer, but she smiled all the same.
After the interview I called my sister, and she said I had most likely done well. I hope she is right, for I am greatly in need of this work, and the rent is due next week and I have no money.

lessons: The chief difference is that the Fairy Books join short clauses into longer, balanced sentences by "and" and "but" instead of full-stopping each thought. Your three opening shots become one flowing sentence ("The office was huge and new, and everyone there wore hoodies and drank fine coffee, but I felt wholly out of place in my suit"), which lays the setting and the feeling at once. Practise calling people by their place ("the manager"), telling speech plainly with the speaker after it, and joining sentences with "and so" and "then" so the tale moves quickly without stopping.

outline.gist: The office, huge and new, full of people in hoodies drinking fine coffee
Narrator out of place in a suit
The manager, a woman named Priya, friendly but earnest, asks about strengths and weaknesses
Narrator answers lame, she smiles anyway
Afterwards narrator calls sister, who says he likely succeeded
Narrator hopes so, needs the job; rent due and broke

plan.gist: The office and the people in it, told plainly as a tale opens
plan.why: The voice opens each scene with what is there, before the feeling it causes

plan.gist: The narrator out of place
plan.why: The feeling follows the setting, stated plainly

plan.gist: Priya and her question
plan.why: People are called by their place and named when the writer names them; the question drives the scene

plan.gist: The lame answer and her smile
plan.why: What was said, then what came of it, in order

plan.gist: The call to the sister
plan.why: What happened next, joined with and, so, then

plan.gist: The hope and the need
plan.why: The passage ends on the narrator's need, stated plainly as a tale closes

faults.quote: I said I did all things too carefully
faults.why: The writer said 'I was a perfectionist', a named weakness. The rewrite turns it into an odd paraphrase and loses the point that it is a stock answer.

faults.quote: she asked me what I could do and what I could not do
faults.why: 'Strengths and weaknesses' becomes 'can do / cannot do', which shifts the meaning from character traits to ability.

faults.quote: a little stern
faults.why: The writer said 'kind of intense'. Stern is a different quality, and the 'how it is built' summary calls it 'earnest', a third reading.

faults.quote: I have no money
faults.why: The writer said 'basically broke', which is hedged and colloquial. The rewrite makes it an absolute statement.

faults.quote: super modern
faults.why: 'Super modern' is dropped for 'new', which loses the sense of sleek contemporary style. 'Fancy' becomes 'fine' and weakens the mild irony.

faults.quote: I did all things too carefully
faults.why: Awkward, near-riddle phrasing that no fairy-book narrator would use. It does not read as the lame cliché it is meant to be.

faults.quote: which is a poor answer, but she smiled all the same
faults.why: Switches to present tense inside a past-tense narrative without a clear reason, and the 'lame' judgment is softened.

faults.quote: everyone there wore hoodies and drank fine coffee
faults.why: The hoodies and coffee are modern details with no fairy-tale register around them. The voice is only lightly applied, mostly by joining clauses with 'and', so it reads as modern prose in thin costume. The Lang-style archaisms and formulae (e.g. 'Now', 'once upon a time') are absent.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: All three paragraphs have empty notes, even though the rewrite changed wording, joined sentences and altered meanings. No moves, sources or mendings are named.

faults.quote: Your three opening shots become one flowing sentence ("The office was huge and new, and everyone there wore hoodies and drank fine coffee, but I felt wholly out of place in my suit")
faults.why: The lesson quotes a combined sentence that the rewrite does not actually contain, because the rewrite keeps two separate sentences. The advice is therefore inaccurate and the example is not grounded in the text.

faults.quote: I hope she is right, for I am greatly in need of this work, and the rent is due next week and I have no money.
faults.why: The long run-on chains the need and the rent loosely with 'and'. The built-structure claims a verdict ending, but the rewrite does not shape it as a close.

judge.verdict: The rewrite only lightly applies the voice and bends several meanings ('perfectionist', 'intense', 'strengths and weaknesses', 'basically broke'). The notes are empty and the lesson cites a sentence that does not appear in the rewrite.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Once upon a time a new household came to live next door, and they brought with them a great cart and two little children. The father seemed a kindly man, but the woman was cold and gave no more than a word.

My mother lost no time, but baked them cakes and carried them over the very first day, for she wished to know everything about them. She asked where they came from, and how the father earned his bread, and whether they went to church.

By and by it came out that the father was a lawyer, and that his wife was parted from him. The woman, they said, was his sister, who kept the house and minded the two little children. When my mother heard it, she got a look on her face, and I knew very well what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years, and now she had what she wanted.

rows.text: Once upon a time a new household came to live next door, and they brought with them a great cart and two little children. The father seemed a kindly man, but the woman was cold and gave no more than a word.

notes.text: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.

notes.after: Once upon a time a new household came to live next door, and they brought with them a great cart and two little children.
notes.cite: The Green Fairy Book, “The Story Of The Three Bears”, ¶ 1

rows.text: My mother lost no time, but baked them cakes and carried them over the very first day, for she wished to know everything about them. She asked where they came from, and how the father earned his bread, and whether they went to church.

By and by it came out that the father was a lawyer, and that his wife was parted from him. The woman, they said, was his sister, who kept the house and minded the two little children. When my mother heard it, she got a look on her face, and I knew very well what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years, and now she had what she wanted.

notes.text: Your second paragraph gives the new household two little kids and a woman called 'the mom', so the father has a wife there; your third says the dad is 'single. Well, divorced.' Both cannot be true of one household. I made the woman in the house the father's sister, who lives with him and minds the two little children. The father stays single, the sister's standoffishness still holds, and the mother's matchmaking look still makes sense.
notes.after: The father was a lawyer, and his wife was parted from him; and the woman was his sister, who kept house and minded the two little children.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 3.

lessons: Your passage told everything in short, separate breaths; the Fairy Books join clauses with ", and" and let one sentence carry several facts at once, so the tale moves quickly and lands its turn whole. I opened with "Once upon a time a new household came to live next door," set the household right by naming "his sister, who kept the house," and gathered the three questions into one sentence with a firm rhythm. Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" and letting the point fall all in one place at the end.

outline.gist: a new family moved in next door
mother bakes for them and asks everything
the father is single, a lawyer, and the woman is his sister
mother's face shows she means to make a match

plan.gist: once upon a time a new household came next door, with a great cart and two children
plan.why: the tale opens as tales open, naming who came and what they brought, before any judgment

plan.gist: the mother lost no time, baked them cakes, and questioned after all their affairs
plan.why: the neighbor's kindness and curiosity, told in order as it happened, before the turn

plan.gist: the news: the father is a lawyer, the wife is gone from him, and the woman is his sister minding the children
plan.why: the point lands hardest when all the news is gathered in one place, and the household is set right

plan.gist: the mother's face showed what she was thinking: she has long been trying to find her a husband
plan.why: the ending closes on the mother's purpose, which the whole passage has been moving toward

sense.problem: Your second paragraph sets two little kids and a woman called 'the mom' in the new household, so the father has a wife there; your third says the dad is 'single. Well, divorced.' Both cannot be true of the same household.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the woman in the house not the father's wife: she is his sister (or a grandmother or aunt) who lives with him and looks after the two little kids. Say so where the news is told, the least change: keep 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' and add that the woman next door is his sister, minding the children. Every sentence then holds, and the mother's matchmaking look still makes sense.

faults.quote: that his wife was parted from him. The woman, they said, was his sister
faults.why: 'His wife' and 'the woman' sit side by side. A reader may take the wife to be the standoffish woman, so the mended contradiction half-returns. The mending never says plainly that the woman is not the wife.

faults.quote: who kept the house and minded the two little children
faults.why: The mending invents extra facts about the sister's role and about where the children come from. The note reports the sister but does not flag these additions.

faults.quote: The woman, they said
faults.why: 'They said' adds a source of information the writer never gave. It also makes the sister's identity hearsay, which weakens the mended fact.

faults.quote: and now she had what she wanted
faults.why: This adds an outcome and an emphasis the writer did not state. The writer's mother only has a look, and nothing says she has got anything yet.

faults.quote: She has been trying to set me up for years, and now she had what she wanted.
faults.why: The tense jumps from present perfect to past inside one sentence. It also keeps the modern idiom 'set me up', which breaks the fairy-tale register.

faults.quote: she got a look on her face, and I knew very well what she was thinking
faults.why: 'Got a look on her face' is plain modern speech. A Lang-style narrator would write something like 'a certain look came into her face'.

faults.quote: his wife was parted from him
faults.why: 'Well, divorced' is softened into a vague 'parted'. 'Single' is dropped, and the wry correction in the writer's text is lost.

faults.quote: the woman was cold and gave no more than a word
faults.why: 'Kind of standoffish' is intensified to 'cold'. The feeling is stronger than the writer's.

faults.quote: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: This structural note is vague and partly wrong. The rewrite's paragraph 2 renders the writer's paragraph 2, not the rest of paragraph 1.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 2 has real changes ('lost no time', 'cakes', 'how the father earned his bread', the word 'bread') and none are noted. Only one voice move is cited for the whole piece, and it is just the generic opener.

faults.quote: cites The Green Fairy Book, “The Story Of The Three Bears”, ¶ 1
faults.why: The rewrite's sentence is not the text of that source. The note passes a generic 'once upon a time' off as a specific borrowed move.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" and letting the point fall all in one place at the end.
faults.why: This is the only transferable lesson, and it is generic. Nothing is said about diction ('by and by', 'lost no time'), the 'they said' reporting, or why fairy narration states things so plainly. The outline's 'find her a husband' also does not match the 'set me up' in the rewrite.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the divorced-versus-mom contradiction and gives a reasonable fix, but the 'wife parted… the woman was his sister' wording stays muddled and adds invented details. The voice is only moderately fairy-book, with modern idioms left in, and the notes and lesson are thin and partly inaccurate.

yours:
The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:
The party was held at the house of Jessica, whose father and mother had gone away into the country, so that everyone from the school was there, and the music sounded so loud that it filled the whole house. I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we knew but few of the people who were there. Then a tall young man came over to us and began to talk, and his name was Chris, and he was both headstrong and full of mirth.

He said that the party was a dull one and that the people were wearisome, and at this Emma rolled her eyes, and I thought him rude. But afterwards, when all the rest were gone, I saw him helping to clear the dishes and set the rooms to rights, and perhaps I was wrong about him after all.

rows.text: The party was held at the house of Jessica, whose father and mother had gone away into the country, so that everyone from the school was there, and the music sounded so loud that it filled the whole house. I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we knew but few of the people who were there. Then a tall young man came over to us and began to talk, and his name was Chris, and he was both headstrong and full of mirth.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: Then a tall young man came over to us and began to talk.
notes.cite: The Grey Fairy Book, “A Fairy’s Blunder”, ¶ 77

rows.text: He said that the party was a dull one and that the people were wearisome, and at this Emma rolled her eyes, and I thought him rude. But afterwards, when all the rest were gone, I saw him helping to clear the dishes and set the rooms to rights, and perhaps I was wrong about him after all.

notes.text: The Fairy Books close a change of heart with a soft verdict in the narrator's voice, turning the last fact into the tale's point.
notes.after: And perhaps I was wrong about him after all.

lessons: The writer's page is a list of very short sentences, each a fact of its own; the Fairy Books join their facts into long sentences with "and", "so" and "then", so the tale moves and the reader is carried along. I joined your first three sentences into one long sentence of setting ("The party was held at the house of Jessica...") and your stranger's entrance into another, and let the judgment fall in threes, ending with a soft verdict ("perhaps I was wrong about him after all"). Practise joining your short sentences with "and" and "then", and call people by their place in the story, as I called the guy "a tall young man" and the cleared-up party "the rest".

outline.gist: The party was at Jessica's house, her parents out of town
Everyone from school was there, the music loud
I stood in the kitchen with Emma; we knew few people
A tall young man, Chris, came over and spoke; arrogant but funny
He said the party and people were dull; Emma rolled her eyes; I thought him rude
Later he stayed to help clean up; maybe I was wrong about him

plan.gist: The tale begins as tales do, with the setting
plan.why: The Fairy Books open with Once upon a time or a plain statement of where the people and the scene are.

plan.gist: Jessica's house, the parents away, the company and the music
plan.why: The setting is laid before the scene, so the reader knows where and who.

plan.gist: I stood with Emma in the kitchen, knowing few
plan.why: The narrator is placed, and her want of company told plainly, before the stranger enters.

plan.gist: A tall young man came over and spoke; his name was Chris; arrogant and funny
plan.why: One thing after another, joined by and and then, as the tale moves.

plan.gist: He said the party and people were dull; Emma rolled her eyes; I thought him rude
plan.why: The judgment falls in threes and in the order it happened.

plan.gist: But later he stayed to clear away when all were gone; perhaps I was wrong
plan.why: The turn lands last and hardest, where the tale's lesson lies.

faults.quote: gone away into the country
faults.why: The writer said only 'out of town'. 'Into the country' invents a destination.

faults.quote: so that everyone from the school was there
faults.why: 'So that' makes the parents' absence the cause of the crowd. The writer listed these as separate facts, so this adds a causal claim.

faults.quote: headstrong and full of mirth
faults.why: 'Headstrong' means obstinate or wilful, not 'arrogant', so Chris's character shifts. 'Full of mirth' also overstates 'funny' somewhat.

faults.quote: clear the dishes and set the rooms to rights
faults.why: The writer said only 'clean up'. Dishes are an invented detail, and 'set the rooms to rights' widens the task.

faults.quote: so loud that it filled the whole house
faults.why: This embellishes 'super loud' with a new detail about the music filling the house.

faults.quote: his name was Chris, and he was both headstrong and full of mirth
faults.why: The 'and… and' chain is clumsy here. 'Both… and' with two mismatched adjectives reads stiffly and awkwardly for the idiom.

faults.quote: from the school
faults.why: 'The school' is an odd article use. The register is only lightly archaic ('the music sounded'), so the Lang cadence of simple 'and… then' narration is only partly achieved. There is no tale-like framing.

faults.quote: cites The Grey Fairy Book, “A Fairy’s Blunder”, ¶ 77
faults.why: The cited source is thin and unconvincing for a single 'Then…' clause. It is the only sourced move, and no other moves are named.

faults.quote: The Fairy Books close a change of heart with a soft verdict in the narrator's voice
faults.why: The rewrite adds almost no narrator commentary. It only appends 'after all' to the writer's own line, so the note overstates the change. The notes also never report the invented details or the 'arrogant' to 'headstrong' swap.

faults.quote: call people by their place in the story, as I called the guy "a tall young man" and the cleared-up party "the rest"
faults.why: This is a muddled and minor point. It is the only concrete lesson beside sentence-joining, and the 'rest' example does not match what the rewrite does. The outline promises a 'Once upon a time' opening that the rewrite lacks.

judge.verdict: A competent, readable archaic rewrite that keeps the story's order and its closing reversal. It invents small details (the country, the dishes), shifts 'arrogant' to 'headstrong', and adds a causal 'so that'. The notes are thin and under-report these changes, and the teaching centres on one lesson, joining short sentences.

yours:
I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
There was once a day when I needed milk, so I took my keys and drove to the store. The store was extremely full, and a man in a hooded coat filled the whole aisle while he talked into a speaking-thing.

I did not wish to be rude, so I said, "Excuse me," but he paid me no heed, and at last he moved, and I got the milk. Then I saw the one who had once been mine standing at the paying-place, and I feared greatly.

"Hey," she said, "long time no see; you look well."

"Thank you," I said, "and you also." Then I paid and made off as fast as I could, for it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week, for all the world to hear.

rows.text: There was once a day when I needed milk, so I took my keys and drove to the store. The store was extremely full, and a man in a hooded coat filled the whole aisle while he talked into a speaking-thing.

notes.after: There was once a day when I needed milk
notes.cite: The Brown Fairy Book, “The Knights Of The Fish”, ¶ 1

notes.text: the voice opens as tales open, turning the writer's bare need into the tale's beginning; it adds only the framing a tale requires and no new fact.
notes.after: There was once a day when I needed milk.

notes.text: the writer's hoodie is named by its place in the story and a word the Fairy Books use; it describes the thing as their world would.
notes.after: a man in a hooded coat

rows.text: I did not wish to be rude, so I said, "Excuse me," but he paid me no heed, and at last he moved, and I got the milk. Then I saw the one who had once been mine standing at the paying-place, and I feared greatly.

notes.after: and at last he moved, and I got the milk
notes.cite: The Orange Fairy Book, “The Adventures Of Covan The Brown-”, ¶ 25

rows.text: "Hey," she said, "long time no see; you look well."
"Thank you," I said, "and you also." Then I paid and made off as fast as I could, for it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week, for all the world to hear.

notes.text: the voice adds a tale's rounding phrase over the writer's own verdict of the week, framing rather than inventing feeling.
notes.after: for all the world to hear

lessons: Your passage is quick scene-setting in very short sentences; the Fairy Books join such matter into longer, balanced clauses with "so", "and", and "; and", and let the tale's opens and closes frame the plain facts. Notice how "There was once a day when I needed milk, so I took my keys" makes the bare need the tale's beginning, and how "for all the world to hear" rounds the verdict in a tale's closing phrase. Keep each turn of the matter its own paragraph, so the reader feels the store, then the aisle, then the meeting, then the flight.

outline.gist: needed milk, took keys and drove to store
store crowded, man in hooded coat blocking aisle, talking
unwilling to be rude, said excuse me, he did not heed; then moved and got milk
saw former lover at the paying-place and feared
she greeted, said long time, looked well; he thanked her, returned it, paid and fled
most awkward ten minutes of the week

plan.gist: There was once a day when the narrator needed milk, so took keys and drove to the store
plan.why: the tale opens with need answered by errand, as the author's errands begin plainly

plan.gist: the store was very full; a man in a hooded coat filled the whole aisle, talking into a speaking-thing
plan.why: the obstacle arrives at once, named by its place in the story and its business, before the polite word

plan.gist: not wishing to be rude, said excuse me, the man paid no heed, then at last moved; the milk got
plan.why: the three beats of a tale: the courteous word, the unheeding, the yielding

plan.gist: then saw the old lover at the paying-place and feared greatly
plan.why: the second trouble comes after the first is resolved, as tales pile trouble on trouble

plan.gist: greeting and answer, speech quick in the middle, then paid and went as fast as could
plan.why: speech drives the meeting; the flight follows at once

plan.gist: the verdict closes it: the most awkward ten minutes of the week
plan.why: the tale ends on the narrator's own plain judgement, as the author's tellers name their verdict

faults.quote: for all the world to hear
faults.why: Invents a new idea (publicity, being overheard) that the writer never stated. The awkwardness was personal, not public. The phrase also fits badly with the clause before it.

faults.quote: Then I paid and made off as fast as I could, for it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week
faults.why: Turns the verdict into a causal 'for' clause, so the awkwardness explains why he fled. The writer's retrospective verdict becomes a reason, which changes the logic. It also loses the 'Honestly' emphasis.

faults.quote: I feared greatly
faults.why: 'Basically panicked' becomes plain fear. The comic, casual panic is lost, so the degree and tone of the feeling shift.

faults.quote: he paid me no heed
faults.why: 'Totally ignored me' is softened, losing the writer's irritation.

faults.quote: The store was extremely full
faults.why: 'Super crowded' becomes 'full', which is the wrong sense for people. It also keeps the modern intensifier 'extremely', which is not the Fairy Books' register.

faults.quote: talked into a speaking-thing
faults.why: An invented compound for a phone that reads as comic or twee rather than idiomatic. It is a riddle for the reader.

faults.quote: "Hey," she said, "long time no see; you look well."
faults.why: 'Hey' and 'long time no see' are modern slang inside an archaic frame. 'You look great' is also weakened to 'well', so the compliment's degree changes.

faults.quote: the most awkward ten minutes of my week
faults.why: Left as modern prose. 'Awkward' and the 'ten minutes of my week' framing are not Fairy Book diction, so the voice breaks at the close.

faults.quote: the one who had once been mine
faults.why: 'Ex' becomes a possessive phrase that suggests ownership and reads oddly. 'The paying-place' for checkout is also a clumsy coinage.

faults.quote: the writer's hoodie is named by its place in the story and a word the Fairy Books use
faults.why: Vague and inaccurate. 'Hooded coat' is a plain paraphrase, and 'speaking-thing' is not mentioned at all among the liberties.

faults.quote: the voice adds a tale's rounding phrase over the writer's own verdict
faults.why: Admits adding material that alters meaning. It calls 'for all the world to hear' framing, but the phrase introduces a new notion.

faults.quote: cites The Orange Fairy Book, “The Adventures Of Covan The Brown-”, ¶ 25
faults.why: The cited move ('and at last') is thin for what it is claimed to show, and the title is truncated. Paragraph 3 and the invented compounds have no notes, so changes go unreported.

faults.quote: Notice how "There was once a day when I needed milk, so I took my keys" makes the bare need the tale's beginning, and how "for all the world to hear" rounds the verdict
faults.why: It praises a flawed addition as a model, so it teaches a bad move. The lesson is also mostly generic about joining short sentences, and it does not explain how to avoid the slang mismatch.

faults.quote: Then I saw the one who had once been mine standing at the paying-place, and I feared greatly.
faults.why: The writer's four short paragraphs are kept, but the dialogue is run together with commas and semicolons. The beats of the meeting blur, and the final verdict is buried in the flight sentence rather than standing as its own close.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the event order but adds an invented idea ('for all the world to hear') and turns the verdict into a causal clause. It mixes modern slang with coined archaisms ('speaking-thing', 'paying-place'), and the notes and lesson praise the flawed additions instead of flagging them.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
Hi team,

Here is word for you: the launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday. The men of the law have not yet set their hand to the page where the price is set, and I will not send the thing out without it.

Have each part of the deck finished by noon on Wednesday. And if any of you is stayed, tell me today, and not tomorrow.

With thanks, Sam.

rows.text: Hi team,
Here is word for you: the launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday. The men of the law have not yet set their hand to the page where the price is set, and I will not send the thing out without it.

notes.text: the writer's bare "Legal" is turned to the tale's way of naming a body by its office
notes.after: the men of the law

rows.text: Have each part of the deck finished by noon on Wednesday. And if any of you is stayed, tell me today, and not tomorrow.
With thanks, Sam.

lessons: The writer's page is a quick office note, short and hurried; the tale's manner names the news plainly and joins clauses with "and" so each lands. The law office becomes "the men of the law," people by their office, and each command is set out whole with its time named. To practise: tell the news before the reason, name bodies by their office, and write sentences at full length joined by "and," so the reader is not hurried past what matters.

outline.gist: Hi team
launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
pricing page not yet signed off, unwilling to ship without it
sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
tell of blocks today, not tomorrow
thanks, Sam

plan.gist: greet the team
plan.why: a letter opens by naming those it is sent to

plan.gist: the launch is moved to Thursday
plan.why: the news comes first, before the reason, so the reader knows at once what has changed

plan.gist: the lawful men have not set their hand to the pricing page, and I will not send it out without that
plan.why: the reason follows the news, told plainly

plan.gist: have your parts of the deck ready by noon on Wednesday
plan.why: the command sits last and plainest, with its time set down

plan.gist: if you are stayed, say so today
plan.why: a second small command, then the close

plan.gist: thanks, Sam
plan.why: the letter ends with the sender's name

faults.quote: Here is word for you: the launch is moved
faults.why: The writer's 'Quick update' becomes an odd announcement formula. The urgency and the briskness of 'quick' are lost.

faults.quote: The men of the law have not yet set their hand to the page where the price is set
faults.why: 'Legal' (a department) becomes 'men of the law'. 'Signed off' becomes 'set their hand to', which is close but loses the sense of approval. 'Pricing page' becomes a clumsy periphrasis, 'the page where the price is set'.

faults.quote: I will not send the thing out without it.
faults.why: 'Ship' becomes 'send the thing out'. 'I don't want us shipping' (a shared, softer stance) becomes a firmer, solitary 'I will not'. The register and degree of feeling shift.

faults.quote: Have each part of the deck finished by noon on Wednesday.
faults.why: 'Sections' is rendered as 'part'. 'Your sections' becomes 'each part', which loses the personal ownership.

faults.quote: if any of you is stayed
faults.why: 'Stayed' for 'blocked' is archaic and ambiguous. A team reader would likely take it as 'halted' or 'supported', so it reads as a malapropism.

faults.quote: With thanks, Sam.
faults.why: The sign-off is flattened into a single line and loses the writer's paragraphing. It also does not match the fairy-book manner.

faults.quote: Hi team,
faults.why: The modern greeting is left untouched, so the opening is not in the voice at all. The rewrite is a light archaic costume. It lacks the fairy-tale cadence of 'Once upon a time', the 'and so' chains, and concrete narrative simplicity.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the writer's bare "Legal" is turned to the tale's way of naming a body by its office
faults.why: This is the only note. It does not mention 'blocked' to 'stayed', 'ship' to 'send out', the changed 'Quick update' opening, or the merged sign-off. It also puts the note under paragraph 2 and calls it a 'liberty'. 'Men of the law' is not truly 'naming by office' in the fairy books.

faults.quote: write sentences at full length joined by "and," so the reader is not hurried past what matters.
faults.why: The lesson is generic and shaky. The rewrite barely joins clauses with 'and', and the advice to put the news before the reason was already the writer's order. Little can be reused, and no actual source in the Fairy Books is cited.

faults.quote: the command sits last and plainest
faults.why: The outline claims a structure the rewrite does not change. The writer's order is kept, so this explanation is hollow. It also asserts that the rewrite follows the writer's order while claiming the voice would build it differently.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the email's facts and order, but the voice is a thin layer of archaisms ('stayed', 'men of the law', 'set their hand') that reads awkwardly and in places obscures meaning. The notes and lesson are sparse and generic, and the lesson does not teach anything concrete about the Fairy Books.

yours:
Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: Now this was Saturday, and on Saturday I cleaned the troughs along the eaves, and mended the sink, and called my grandmother, who talked a full hour of her neighbour's cat. When evening came I was tired out, yet proud of myself in a manner I could not well account for.

rows.text: Now this was Saturday, and on Saturday I cleaned the troughs along the eaves, and mended the sink, and called my grandmother, who talked a full hour of her neighbour's cat. When evening came I was tired out, yet proud of myself in a manner I could not well account for.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: Now this was Saturday, and on Saturday I cleaned the troughs along the eaves, and mended the sink, and called my grandmother, who talked a full hour of her neighbour's cat.
notes.cite: The Lilac Fairy Book, “The Sea King’s Gift”, ¶ 33

lessons: Your passage lists a day's tasks and a private feeling; the Fairy Books tell the same matter by fixing the day first ("Now this was Saturday"), running the three tasks one after another on plain "and"s ("and mended the sink, and called my grandmother"), and closing on the feeling stated simply. "Weirdly" becomes "in a manner I could not well account for", a plain periphrasis, and the whole ends with a short verdict, "yet proud of myself", as their tales end on the feeling named outright.

outline.gist: The day's work, in order: gutters, sink, grandmother's long talk of her neighbor's cat
By evening, exhausted but strangely proud

plan.gist: Set the day on Saturday, as tales set their time
plan.why: The Fairy Books open by fixing the time plainly, so the reader knows when the tale falls.

plan.gist: The three tasks done, in order, the grandmother's talk a third thing
plan.why: Things in threes, listed as they were done, so the day runs straight from morning to talk.

plan.gist: By evening, weary but proud
plan.why: The tale closes on the plain feeling, a short sentence for the turn.

faults.quote: cleaned the troughs along the eaves
faults.why: "Gutters" is turned into "troughs along the eaves". It is a periphrasis that blurs a plain fact, and "troughs" could be misread as animal feeding troughs.

faults.quote: yet proud of myself in a manner I could not well account for
faults.why: The writer's "weirdly proud" is a mild, amused oddity. "Could not well account for" makes it a puzzled inability to explain, which is a slightly different feeling.

faults.quote: I was tired out
faults.why: The writer's "exhausted" is kept, but the "By the evening" framing is loosened to "When evening came". This is minor.

faults.quote: Now this was Saturday, and on Saturday I cleaned
faults.why: The Fairy Books open with "Once upon a time" or "There was once". "Now this was Saturday" is a pastiche opener, and the repeated "Saturday" is clumsy. The tone is more Lang's narrator than the tales' plain telling.

faults.quote: who talked a full hour of her neighbour's cat
faults.why: "Talked of" is archaic enough, but the sentence is a plain modern list with "and" added. There is little of the tale cadence, formula, or narrative distance, so the voice is thin.

faults.quote: in a manner I could not well account for
faults.why: The phrase is stilted and uses a first-person introspective hedge that fairy tales almost never use. The Fairy Books do not narrate puzzled inner states in the first person.

faults.quote: cites The Lilac Fairy Book, “The Sea King’s Gift”, ¶ 33
faults.why: The citation is dubious or unverifiable. A single "and so, and then" move is claimed, but only one note is given for a two-sentence rewrite. The notes do not mention the "troughs" substitution or the "manner I could not account for" change.

faults.quote: Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The merge of the paragraphs is reported but not justified. The writer's separate closing line was a deliberate beat, and it is lost.

faults.quote: as their tales end on the feeling named outright
faults.why: The lesson makes a thin and partly false generalisation. The Fairy Books do not usually end on a narrator's private feeling, and "things in threes" is a different convention from this list of three tasks. It also calls "Weirdly" a periphrasis without explaining why that helps the writer.

faults.quote: When evening came I was tired out, yet proud
faults.why: Merging the two paragraphs removes the writer's pause before the feeling. The "short sentence for the turn" claimed in the outline is not delivered, because the verdict is a clause tacked onto a sentence.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and order, but it is a light archaic gloss with a pastiche opener and a stilted introspective ending. The notes and lesson are thin, and the cited source and generalisations are shaky.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to carriages on the holy days. To leave carriages standing in the middle of the town is a great trouble, and the walks are too narrow for the little carriages of the children. Other towns have done this, and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some of the shopkeepers will complain that their customers cannot come to them. But they will grow used to it, and, honestly, most people walk from the carriage-house in any case.

Let us try it this summer.

rows.text: Our town should close Main Street to carriages on the holy days. To leave carriages standing in the middle of the town is a great trouble, and the walks are too narrow for the little carriages of the children. Other towns have done this, and their shops are doing better than ever.

notes.text: The writer says “weekends” with no word of the Fairy Books; the voice names them by their place in a working week, the two rest days at its end, in their own words.
notes.after: on the holy days

rows.text: Some of the shopkeepers will complain that their customers cannot come to them. But they will grow used to it, and, honestly, most people walk from the carriage-house in any case.

notes.text: The voice lays the writer's “anyway” into a closing frame of its own, as a tale sums a matter before the verdict.
notes.after: in any case

rows.text: Let us try it this summer.

lessons: The writer argues in quick, short opinions where the Fairy Books tell the same matter plainly and at full sentence length, each step joined with “and” so the case carries forward.
