I joined the writer's short objection-and-answer into “But they will grow used to it, and, honestly, most people walk from the carriage-house in any case,” one plain sentence that answers the doubt as a tale answers a doubter. I also called people by their place — “the shopkeepers” — and laid the close short and firm as “Let us try it this summer,” which works because a tale ends on its resolution, not on a suggestion.

outline.gist: Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends.
Parking downtown is a nightmare; sidewalks too narrow for strollers.
Other towns have done this and their shops do better than ever.
Some business owners will complain customers can't get to them.
They'll get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.
We should try it this summer.

plan.gist: The town should close Main Street to carriages on the holy days.
plan.why: The tale opens straight on the matter, as a tale opens on its business, with the proposal first.

plan.gist: To leave carriages in the middle of the town is a trouble, and the walks are too narrow for the little carriages.
plan.why: The reason follows the proposal at once, told as plain fact, so the reader sees the trouble.

plan.gist: Other towns have done this, and their shops thrive as never before.
plan.why: The proof of other towns comes third, as testimony in a tale comes after the setting of the case.

plan.gist: Some of the shopkeepers will say their customers cannot come to them.
plan.why: The objection is spoken in the voice's words and answered at once, as a tale deals plainly with a doubter.

plan.gist: But they will grow used to it, and most folk walk from the carriage-house in any case.
plan.why: The answer runs the objection into the ground in one plain sentence.

plan.gist: Let us try it this summer.
plan.why: The close proposes the deed, short and firm, as a tale ends on its resolution.

faults.quote: close Main Street to carriages on the holy days
faults.why: 'Cars' becomes 'carriages' and 'weekends' becomes 'holy days'. The holy days are a different thing from weekends (they would not be Saturday), and the rewrite adds a religious meaning the writer never had.

faults.quote: To leave carriages standing in the middle of the town is a great trouble
faults.why: The writer says parking downtown is a nightmare. 'Leaving carriages standing in the middle of the town' changes the problem to the location of the carriages, and 'great trouble' weakens 'nightmare'.

faults.quote: the little carriages of the children
faults.why: Strollers become 'little carriages of the children'. This is a clumsy approximation, and strollers carry babies, not children.

faults.quote: from the carriage-house in any case
faults.why: A garage is a parking structure, but a carriage-house is a private outbuilding. The meaning shifts, and it clashes with the earlier claim that carriages are a nuisance in the middle of town.

faults.quote: and, honestly, most people walk
faults.why: 'Honestly' is a modern colloquial word that the Fairy Books would not use. It breaks the voice, and the 'carriage' costume is otherwise only a word swap.

faults.quote: Our town should close Main Street
faults.why: The opening is the writer's own sentence with a few nouns swapped. There is no 'Once upon a time' manner, no plain narrative cadence, and no 'and... and' chaining, so it reads as modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: most people walk from the carriage-house in any case
faults.why: The anachronism makes the logic odd. If the town is closing the street to carriages, the carriage-house is the garage, but the rewrite does not clarify this.

faults.quote: the voice names them by their place in a working week, the two rest days at its end, in their own words
faults.why: The note describes 'holy days' as 'two rest days', which is inaccurate, and it does not mention that 'cars' became 'carriages'. The note is also vague and gives no source.

faults.quote: The voice lays the writer's “anyway” into a closing frame of its own, as a tale sums a matter before the verdict.
faults.why: The note is vague and does not describe the real change ('anyway' to 'in any case'). The 'closing frame' is not in the text, and Paragraph 3 has no notes though 'Let us try' is a change.

faults.quote: I joined the writer's short objection-and-answer into “But they will grow used to it, and, honestly, most people walk...”
faults.why: The lesson claims a Fairy Books move that is not in the text, since the writer already had these as one sentence structure. It also claims the rewrite 'called people by their place', but it was already 'business owners'. The advice is generic and thinly grounded.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: proposal (...) → reason (...)
faults.why: The outline just repeats the writer's order with claimed reasons about tales that are vague and generic. It offers no real structural improvement.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is mostly the original with period nouns swapped in, and several swaps ('holy days', 'carriage-house', 'little carriages of the children') change or muddle the meaning. The Fairy Books cadence is barely present, and the notes and lesson misdescribe what changed.

yours:
I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite: I have only once been to Paris. That time it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day; and we spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best holiday he ever had.

rows.text: I have only once been to Paris. That time it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day; and we spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best holiday he ever had.

notes.text: Your first sentence says you have never been to Paris; your second says the last time you were there it rained. I kept the anecdote, which plainly tells of a visit, and made the first sentence agree: you have been only once.
notes.after: I have only once been to Paris.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

lessons: Your passage begins with two sentences that cannot both be true, and leans on short clauses where the Fairy Books join things with ", and". I made the first sentence agree with the anecdote ("I have only once been to Paris"), and joined your events in one long movement — "it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day; and we spent most of the trip at the embassy" — so the misfortune and its consequence roll on as the tale does. I also put "holiday" for "vacation", their word, and closed on the brother's verdict, which lands hardest last.

outline.gist: the narrator has never been to Paris
the one visit: rain all week, brother lost his passport on the second day
most of the trip spent at the embassy
the brother still calls it his best holiday

plan.gist: the narrator's one visit to Paris
plan.why: the tale opens with the state of things, plainly, before the events

plan.gist: rain the whole week, the brother lost his passport on the second day
plan.why: the misfortune comes first, told flatly as the tale tells wonders, joined with and

plan.gist: most of the trip spent at the embassy
plan.why: what came of the misfortune, the next thing that happened

plan.gist: the brother still says it was the best holiday he ever had
plan.why: the tale closes on the brother's happy sentence, the point where it lands

sense.problem: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris; your second says ‘The last time I was there it rained the whole week.’ Both cannot be true of the same person.
sense.quote: I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week
sense.resolution: Mend with the least change, as the rest of the passage points: the anecdote is plainly about a visit to Paris, and the brother's fond memory depends on that visit having happened, so keep the second sentence and change the first to agree — e.g. ‘I've only been to Paris once.’ If instead the writer means the first sentence as a joke (the narrator forgetting, or meaning some other city), the joke must be made plain in the words, for as written the two sentences merely contradict.

faults.quote: I have only once been to Paris.
faults.why: The mending turns 'never' into 'only once', an invented count. It also loses the possible joke or irony (never really saw Paris, only the embassy). The writer's 'the last time' implies more than one visit, so 'only once' contradicts that too.

faults.quote: and we spent most of the trip at the embassy
faults.why: The writer's separate, deadpan sentence is merged into a ', and' chain. 'We spent most of the trip at the embassy' was a distinct beat, and merging it weakens the comic timing and the relation to the final verdict.

faults.quote: That time it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day; and we spent most of the trip at the embassy.
faults.why: This is plain modern prose with a semicolon, not Lang's fairy-book manner. There is no 'once upon a time' framing, no formulaic diction, no 'now' or 'so' transitions, and no first-person naïveté. The costume is thin.

faults.quote: He still says it was the best holiday he ever had.
faults.why: Only 'vacation' became 'holiday'. The sentence is otherwise unchanged and carries no Fairy Books cadence.

faults.quote: I kept the anecdote, which plainly tells of a visit, and made the first sentence agree
faults.why: The fault was resolved by the least interesting option (altering the fact). It was not considered that the line could be kept as a joke, or the 'never been' read as 'never really seen Paris'. 'Only once' conflicts with the retained 'the last time'.

faults.quote: That time it rained the whole week
faults.why: 'That time' is an awkward replacement for 'The last time I was there'. It is slightly off idiomatically and dropped the 'last time' meaning.

faults.quote: Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The note says 'your paragraphs 1 and 2', but the writer's first paragraph holds two sentences, so it misreports the merge. It also gives no reason, and the paragraph break had a function, setting up the punchline.

faults.quote: My brother lost his passport on the second day; and we spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says
faults.why: Merging the paragraphs removes the beat before the punchline. The structure note claims the misfortune and consequence 'roll on as the tale does', but the result is a run-on that mixes ';' and ', and'.

faults.quote: leans on short clauses where the Fairy Books join things with ", and"
faults.why: The lesson claims a Fairy Books trait with no cited source or example. It is thin and generic, and the one transferable move (chaining with 'and') is poorly demonstrated by the rewrite, which uses a semicolon.

faults.quote: I also put "holiday" for "vacation", their word
faults.why: No move is listed in the notes for this change, and calling 'holiday' 'their word' is an unsupported claim. It is a minor Briticism swap rather than a voice move.

judge.verdict: The rewrite makes only minimal edits, changing 'never' to 'only once' and swapping a word, so it barely sounds like the Fairy Books. Its fix of the contradiction invents a fact and loses the writer's deadpan structure. The notes and lesson are thin.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite: I say we should keep no more than four days in the week. The people are worn out with labour, and the best of our hands has gone away from us. There are reports which show that the work done stays the same, or grows greater; and it would help us, too, in taking on new people. I know it is a risky thing, and that our customers may not take kindly to it; but we might try it for three months, and see.

rows.text: I say we should keep no more than four days in the week. The people are worn out with labour, and the best of our hands has gone away from us. There are reports which show that the work done stays the same, or grows greater; and it would help us, too, in taking on new people. I know it is a risky thing, and that our customers may not take kindly to it; but we might try it for three months, and see.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: we might try it for three months, and see
notes.cite: The Olive Fairy Book, “The Silent Princess”, ¶ 79

notes.after: and it would help us, too, in taking on new people
notes.cite: The Violet Fairy Book, “The Story Of A Gazelle”, ¶ 48

notes.text: the voice gives the plain 'we' of the passage a fuller opening, as a tale opens directly with the speaker's proposal
notes.after: I say we

lessons: Your passage says its six points in short, bare lines; the Fairy Books join clauses into longer, even sentences, so each point lands with the next. I kept your order and all your matter, but turned your four-day week into "no more than four days in the week," and your engineer into "the best of our hands," naming people by their place in the story rather than their trade. The three months are kept as a pattern of three, and the doubt is named before the trial, as a tale names the danger before the venture.

outline.gist: we should keep only four days in the week
people are worn out and the best hand has left
reports say the work done stays as much or grows
it would help in taking on new people
it is risky and customers may not take to it
try it for three months and see

plan.gist: we should keep only four days in the week
plan.why: the tale states its point first, plainly, so the hearer knows the matter

plan.gist: people are worn out and the best hand has left
plan.why: the reason follows the claim, as consequences follow a deed

plan.gist: reports say the work done stays as much or grows
plan.why: the proof is set down flatly as fact, in support of the claim

plan.gist: it would help in taking on new people
plan.why: a second short reason, joined with 'and', keeps the matter moving

plan.gist: it is risky and customers may not take to it
plan.why: the doubt is named honestly before the trial, as a tale names the danger before the venture

plan.gist: try it for three months and see
plan.why: the tale closes with the trial laid out, three for the pattern of threes

faults.quote: I say we should keep no more than four days in the week.
faults.why: The writer proposes 'switch to a four-day week'. 'Keep no more than four days' reads as a cap, not a switch, and 'keep' implies it is the existing arrangement. The sense is slightly blurred.

faults.quote: The people are worn out with labour
faults.why: 'Burned out' is rendered as plain tiredness. 'Burnout' carries a sense of exhaustion from the job that 'worn out with labour' only loosely covers.

faults.quote: the best of our hands has gone away from us
faults.why: 'Quit' becomes 'gone away from us', which loses the sense of a voluntary resignation and could be read as death or departure. 'Engineer' is lost, so the specific skill is dropped.

faults.quote: There are reports which show that the work done stays the same, or grows greater
faults.why: 'Studies' become 'reports', which is weaker. The sense of 'productivity' as output is acceptable, but 'studies' is the evidence claim and it is softened.

faults.quote: in taking on new people
faults.why: Rendering 'hiring' this way is stiff and a little awkward. It is closer to modern bureaucratic phrasing than to fairy-tale diction.

faults.quote: the best of our hands
faults.why: 'Hands' for workers is a Victorian idiom for factory labourers, not the fairy-tale register. It is somewhat odd in a collegial proposal.

faults.quote: I know it is a risky thing, and that our customers may not take kindly to it; but we might try it for three months, and see.
faults.why: The Fairy Books favour plain parataxis with 'and' and simple narrative. Here the semicolon and 'but' make a modern argumentative balance. There is no fairy-tale colour, such as 'now' or 'once upon a time', so it reads as mildly archaic business prose.

faults.quote: I say we should keep no more than four days in the week.
faults.why: The voice is third-person narrative. First-person 'I say' and the argumentative stance are not Lang's narrative voice, and there is no attempt to bridge this.

faults.quote: Things in threes: “we might try it for three months, and see”
faults.why: This is not a thing in threes. It is one three-month period, and a pattern of three is not formed. The cited move does not match the quoted text.

faults.quote: And so, and then: “and it would help us, too, in taking on new people”
faults.why: A single 'and' is a weak example of the move. The citation of 'The Story Of A Gazelle' as a source for it is not shown to be apt.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the voice gives the plain 'we' of the passage a fuller opening, as a tale opens directly with the speaker's proposal
faults.why: The note claims a fuller opening, but the text changes only 'I think we should' to 'I say we should'. It is inaccurate and self-contradictory (a fuller opening versus a direct one).

faults.quote: the Fairy Books join clauses into longer, even sentences, so each point lands with the next
faults.why: The rewrite is barely longer than the original and several sentences stay short. The lesson claims a change that was largely not made, and it gives the writer little reusable technique.

faults.quote: three, for the pattern of threes
faults.why: The structure notes justify 'three months' by a pattern of threes. That is a spurious reason, since the number comes from the writer, and it teaches a false lesson.

faults.quote: as a tale names the danger before the venture
faults.why: The 'how it is built' claims reordering reasons as a tale would, but the order is unchanged and the explanations are generic. The outline adds no real contrast between the writer's build and the voice's.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and order but is only lightly archaized, with a few drifting renderings ('keep no more than four days', 'gone away from us'). The notes cite moves that are not in the text (a pattern of threes from a single three-month trial) and the lesson claims changes that were not made, so the teaching value is poor.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana scratched our dinner, I was not at all upset. The truth is, I was relieved. I had been dreading it all week, and I am not proud of that.

I told her it was of no matter, and that we would do it another time. But I do not think we shall.

rows.text: When Dana scratched our dinner, I was not at all upset. The truth is, I was relieved. I had been dreading it all week, and I am not proud of that.
I told her it was of no matter, and that we would do it another time. But I do not think we shall.

notes.text: The voice lets the closing verdict stand as the tale's quiet ending, set off against the polite answer that went before it.
notes.after: But I do not think we shall

lessons: Your passage is honest but spoken in the shorthand of a text, full of contractions and short fragments. The Fairy Books unfold the same matter in long, plain clauses joined by "and", and state feeling as flat fact: "I had been dreading it all week, and I am not proud of that." Learn the habit of joining clauses with "and" and letting each sentence carry its whole weight, so the honest close, "But I do not think we shall," lands with the quiet force of a tale's ending.

outline.gist: Dana called off the dinner, and I felt nothing.
I was relieved, not sorry.
I had dreaded it all week, and am ashamed of that.
I told her it was fine and we would meet another time.
I do not think we ever will.

plan.gist: Dana scratched the dinner, and I felt nothing.
plan.why: The tale names the event plainly first, so the feeling that follows lands against a solid fact.

plan.gist: The truth is I was relieved.
plan.why: The honest verdict comes next, said flatly, as the voice tells any wonder.

plan.gist: I had dreaded it all week, and that shames me.
plan.why: The confession of dread and shame belongs with the feeling it explains, before the polite answer.

plan.gist: I told her it was of no matter, another time would do as well.
plan.why: The kind lie is reported as speech, quick and courteous, as the tale reports all speech.

plan.gist: But I do not think we shall.
plan.why: The quiet truth ends the piece, as a tale ends, leaving the reader with the real thing.

faults.quote: When Dana scratched our dinner, I was not at all upset. The truth is, I was relieved.
faults.why: The sentences are nearly the writer's own with the contractions expanded. Lang's fairy books use plain narrative with 'and' chains and 'Now,' or 'it came to pass' framing, and none of that is here. This reads as modern prose in a light costume.

faults.quote: scratched our dinner
faults.why: 'Scratched' is racing or cricket slang for withdrawing an entry. It is an odd, slightly comic word for cancelling a dinner and is not a fairy-book idiom.

faults.quote: it was of no matter
faults.why: This is a stilted, archaic-sounding phrase placed in a first-person modern confession, so the register is mixed. It also slightly changes 'it was fine'.

faults.quote: I am not proud of that.
faults.why: The line is left nearly unchanged from the draft. The voice would give a tale-like phrasing, and the modern confessional tone stays.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: The voice lets the closing verdict stand as the tale's quiet ending
faults.why: No liberty was taken, because the closing verdict is the writer's own and was kept as written. The note mislabels it and names no actual change, such as 'scratched', 'of no matter', or 'shall'. Paragraph 1 has no notes even though the wording changed.

faults.quote: The Fairy Books unfold the same matter in long, plain clauses joined by "and"
faults.why: The lesson claims long 'and'-joined clauses, but the rewrite stays in short sentences and joins almost nothing with 'and'. The lesson does not match the output. The quoted line is the writer's own sentence, so it does not show the voice's habit.

faults.quote: and that we would do it another time. But I do not think we shall.
faults.why: This is small: 'But' is added, and 'we'd do it another time' becomes a reported 'that we would'. The change is minor and harmless to the feeling, but it is unreported.

faults.quote: event (Dana scratched the dinner, and I felt nothing.; why: The tale names the event plainly first
faults.why: The outline claims the voice reorders or reshapes the beats, but the order is identical to the writer's. The 'as the voice would build it' section also says 'felt nothing', which is not what the draft says (not upset, then relieved). The outline offers no real structural lesson.

judge.verdict: Faithful in feeling and order, but it is the original with contractions expanded and a few odd archaisms ('scratched', 'of no matter'). It barely sounds like the Fairy Books, and the notes and lesson misdescribe what was done.

yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant.

And it came to pass on the morrow, that we met at a coffee store in the midst of the city; and he was there before me, moving over the charger of his phone. And his countenance was troubled, and he was sore ill at ease. And he said unto me, I am not ready for that which is weighty: and he said, It is not thou, it is I.

And I would have wept, but I wept not: for I bowed my head and said, It is well. And I went home in the rain, and I ate a whole measure of ice cream.

And my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter. Peradventure I did: but it grieved me still.

rows.text: And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant.

notes.text: No fault of sense: Ryan, the narrator, and the roommate are consistent, and the order of events is clear. Nothing to mend. Nothing changed for sense.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant.

rows.text: And it came to pass on the morrow, that we met at a coffee store in the midst of the city; and he was there before me, moving over the charger of his phone. And his countenance was troubled, and he was sore ill at ease. And he said unto me, I am not ready for that which is weighty: and he said, It is not thou, it is I.

notes.text: The passage echoes, faintly, the scene of Ruth's refusal to leave ('whither thou goest, I will go', Ruth 1), but inverted: here it is the other who leaves, and the narrator is the one told to go. The prodigal son (Luke 15) is weaker: the narrator comes home to ice cream and a roommate's judgment, not to a welcome. The rewrite may take from Ruth the plain, bare dialogue and the grief carried in the going, but must not import Ruth's fidelity; the story's point is its opposite.
notes.after: And he said unto me, I am not ready for that which is weighty: and he said, It is not thou, it is I.
and he said, It is not thou, it is I.
And he said unto me, I am not ready for that which is weighty: and he said, It is not thou, it is I.

notes.text: The voice frames the old cliché in its own words, giving the verdict plainly without the writer's modern idiom; the framing is the voice's, the fact is the writer's.
notes.after: and he said, It is not thou, it is I

rows.text: And I would have wept, but I wept not: for I bowed my head and said, It is well. And I went home in the rain, and I ate a whole measure of ice cream.
And my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter. Peradventure I did: but it grieved me still.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short, clipped sentences become long sentences built of clauses joined by 'and', so that the grief is carried in the going rather than stated. My rewrite joins the message and the foreboding into one movement ('And at midnight Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together; and I knew straightway what that word meant'), and gives feeling by its sign rather than its name ('I would have wept, but I wept not', 'my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter'). Practise laying clause beside clause with 'and', and giving the sign of a feeling in short, old, concrete words, so that the reader carries the weight instead of being told to.

outline.gist: Ryan texted at midnight, said we needed to talk; I knew what it meant
next day at a coffee shop downtown; he was there, nervous
he wasn't ready for something serious; it wasn't me, it was him
I wanted to cry but didn't; nodded and said okay; walked home in rain, ate a pint of ice cream
roommate thought I was overreacting; maybe I was; but it still hurt

plan.gist: the message at midnight and the knowing of its meaning, joined as one long sentence
plan.why: the voice lays one clause beside another with 'and', so the message and the foreboding land together as one continuous movement

plan.gist: the setting the next day, then the man found already there
plan.why: the setting comes before the scene, and the man is found where the voice first sees him, with no waste

plan.gist: his words given in full, plainly, with the two halves parallel
plan.why: the voice brings speech in by 'said unto' and gives it whole; the doubled refusal echoes the writer's two sentences

plan.gist: the grief kept in, the bare assent, the going home in the rain and the eating of the ice cream
plan.why: feeling is given by its sign, gravely; the walk and the ice cream are one sentence joined by 'and', so the grief is carried in the going, as in Ruth

plan.gist: the roommate's judgment, the narrator's half-yielding, and the closing hurt
plan.why: the verdict of another, then the brief self-doubt, then the short sentence that closes: the point lands hardest at the end

sense.problem: No fault of sense: no contradiction, no unclear person or time, no missing step the reader needs. Ryan, the narrator, and the roommate are consistent throughout, and the sequence noon-to-afternoon is clear.

Echo: the passage echoes, faintly, the scene of the servant who refuses to leave — 'whither thou goest, I will go' (Ruth 1) — but inverted: here it is the other who leaves, and the narrator is the one told to go. The prodigal son (Luke 15) is a weaker echo: the narrator comes home to ice cream and a roommate's judgment, not to a welcome.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from Ruth the plain, bare dialogue and the steadfast refusal to dramatize — words spoken and kept, grief carried in the going — but must not import Ruth's fidelity; the story's point is its opposite.
sense.quote: He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

faults.quote: moving over the charger of his phone
faults.why: A garbled rendering of 'scrolling'. In the KJV a 'charger' is a platter, so the phrase reads as a riddle or unintended comedy and does not convey that he was scrolling.

faults.quote: moving over the charger of his phone
faults.why: The idle, distracted scrolling is lost. The phrase now suggests something about a charging device.

faults.quote: a coffee store
faults.why: 'Coffee store' is a modern, odd compound that does not belong in KJV diction, and it mistakes 'coffee shop' for a place that sells coffee.

faults.quote: he was sore ill at ease
faults.why: 'Ill at ease' is modern idiom, and the clause repeats 'his countenance was troubled'. The writer's single 'nervous' becomes two overlapping statements.

faults.quote: a whole measure of ice cream
faults.why: 'Pint' becomes the vague 'measure', which blurs the concrete detail. 'Measure' reads as grain or meal, not ice cream.

faults.quote: And I went home in the rain
faults.why: The writer 'walked' home. The walking, which the outline says carries the grief, is replaced by the neutral 'went'.

faults.quote: my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart
faults.why: 'Roommate' becomes 'friend', which adds a relationship the writer did not state. 'Said in her heart' also makes the roommate's thought more confessional than the plain 'thought'.

faults.quote: for I bowed my head and said, It is well.
faults.why: 'For' makes the nodding the cause of not weeping, which the writer did not say. 'It is well' also shades 'okay' toward serene acceptance, where the writer's tone is stifled hurt.

faults.quote: I am not ready for that which is weighty
faults.why: 'Weighty' is a loose rendering of 'serious' and a coinage in the voice's costume. 'Ready for a covenant/a bond' would be more KJV-like. The phrase is stiff and vague.

faults.quote: The passage echoes, faintly, the scene of Ruth's refusal to leave ('whither thou goest, I will go', Ruth 1), but inverted
faults.why: Nothing in the text resembles Ruth or the prodigal son. It is a false 'sense' note, and its claim that the narrator is 'told to go' invents an event. It is filed under sense although no sense fault exists.

faults.quote: cites 2 Samuel 15:26
faults.why: The cited verse ('Behold, here am I...') does not model the 'not thou, it is I' parallelism, so the source is not apt.

faults.quote: cites 1 Kings 17:2
faults.why: A bare verse reference with no specific correspondence to 'sent word... saying' clauses laid with 'and'. The source feels arbitrary.

faults.quote: The voice frames the old cliché in its own words, giving the verdict plainly
faults.why: This claims a liberty that was not taken, since the cliché is carried over directly. It misdescribes the change.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 3:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 3 and 4 carry the weakest renderings ('measure', 'it is well', 'friend', 'peradventure') and none of these changes is explained or flagged.

faults.quote: gives feeling by its sign rather than its name ('I would have wept, but I wept not', 'my friend that dwelleth with me said in her heart that I made too much of the matter')
faults.why: The roommate's judgment is not a sign of feeling, so the second example does not illustrate the lesson. The outline's talk of Ruth also confuses the writer.

judge.verdict: The shape and the 'and'-chained cadence are right, and the facts and their order are largely kept. The 'charger' garble, the modern 'coffee store' and 'ill at ease', and the vague 'measure' hurt both fidelity and naturalness. The notes cite irrelevant or inapt sources (a Ruth echo that isn't there) and leave the weakest paragraphs unexplained.

yours:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Unto my father and my mother, greeting.

The camp is well enough, I suppose: but the food is gross, and he that sleepeth beside me maketh a great noise in the night. And it came to pass yesterday that we went upon the water in a canoe, and the canoe was turned, and all that were there laughed. And I was ashamed.

But, behold, there is a damsel whose name is Kayla, and she is cool, and she is from Ohio, and she knoweth much of horses. And after dinner we sit by the lake and talk of many things; and I think she liketh me, but I know not.

Can ye send me more to eat? and the charger of my phone, which I wholly forgot. The counsellors are strict somewhat, yet for the most part well enough.

The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand.

Moreover, I beseech you, let not Max use my room.

rows.text: Unto my father and my mother, greeting.

notes.after: Unto my father and my mother, greeting.

rows.text: The camp is well enough, I suppose: but the food is gross, and he that sleepeth beside me maketh a great noise in the night. And it came to pass yesterday that we went upon the water in a canoe, and the canoe was turned, and all that were there laughed. And I was ashamed.

notes.after: And it came to pass yesterday that we went upon the water in a canoe, and the canoe was turned

rows.text: But, behold, there is a damsel whose name is Kayla, and she is cool, and she is from Ohio, and she knoweth much of horses. And after dinner we sit by the lake and talk of many things; and I think she liketh me, but I know not.

notes.after: But, behold, there is a damsel whose name is Kayla, and she is cool,

rows.text: Can ye send me more to eat? and the charger of my phone, which I wholly forgot. The counsellors are strict somewhat, yet for the most part well enough.

notes.after: Can ye send me more to eat?
the charger of my phone

rows.text: The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand.
Moreover, I beseech you, let not Max use my room.

lessons: The chief difference is that the Bible lays clause beside clause with "and" and gives feeling by its sign, where the writer's page is short and loose. Notice "the canoe was turned, and all that were there laughed: and I was ashamed" — the deed first, then the shame, in the plainest words. Practise joining short sentences with "and" until they run long and even, and naming a feeling by the thing it shows, as "I was ashamed" instead of "so embarrassing."

outline.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
Camp is okay; food gross, bunkmate snores
Canoe flipped, everyone laughed, embarrassing
A girl Kayla, cool, from Ohio, knows horses
We talk at the lake; she may like me, unsure
Send snacks and phone charger
Strict but fine
Love, Jake
Do not let Max use my room

plan.gist: Unto my father and my mother
plan.why: The epistle opens with a salutation, plain and fixed in form.

plan.gist: Camp as it is, the food and the bunkmate
plan.why: The voice states the case gravely before any story; the complaint rises from the fact.

plan.gist: The canoe overturned and all laughed, to his shame
plan.why: The deed first, then the shame: the voice sets the scene, then the feeling upon it.

plan.gist: A damsel named Kayla, and what she knoweth
plan.why: The voice marks the turn with behold; the new person comes with her name and her quality.

plan.gist: The lake at evening, and his uncertainty
plan.why: The voice gives feeling by its sign; unsureness is spoken plainly, not coyly.

plan.gist: Send food and the charger of his phone
plan.why: The counsel ask plainly; the charger comes with the thing he wholly forgot.

plan.gist: The counsellors
plan.why: A short verdict after the long asking: strict in part, yet well enough.

plan.gist: The salutation of Jake with his own hand
plan.why: The letter closeth in the epistle's own form, and his hand below.

plan.gist: Moreover, keep Max from his room
plan.why: The afterword holdeth a further charge, as an afterthought in an epistle.

faults.quote: I think she liketh me, but I know not.
faults.why: The original says she likes him but he is unsure. The rewrite is close, but 'hang out' and 'talk about stuff' are rendered as 'sit by the lake', which loses the sense of hanging out.

faults.quote: and she is cool
faults.why: 'Really cool' is flattened to a modern slang word left in the Bible text. The intensity is lost and the register is wrong.

faults.quote: Love, Jake
faults.why: The affection of the closing is replaced by 'The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand' (a Pauline formula). It drops the love and gives a formal greeting, so the feeling no longer points the same way.

faults.quote: The counsellors are strict somewhat, yet for the most part well enough.
faults.why: 'Kind of strict but mostly fine' is kept, but 'well enough' repeats the earlier 'well enough' for the camp and blurs the verdicts.

faults.quote: Can ye send me more to eat?
faults.why: 'Snacks' becomes 'more to eat', and the question form stays modern. 'Ye' is plural, but 'Can ye' is also a weak request form for the voice.

faults.quote: the food is gross
faults.why: 'Gross' is modern slang in an otherwise archaic sentence. This is the costume-slip the voice would never allow.

faults.quote: The camp is well enough, I suppose:
faults.why: 'I suppose' is modern and hedging, not Biblical. 'Camp' with a definite article is plain modern prose.

faults.quote: Can ye send me more to eat? and the charger of my phone
faults.why: 'Phone' and 'charger' are left as modern nouns, which is understandable, but the construction is clumsy. A question mark followed by a lowercase 'and' is a punctuation oddity.

faults.quote: he that sleepeth beside me maketh a great noise in the night
faults.why: This is serviceable, but 'snores like crazy' is rendered with no sign of the original hyperbole. 'In the night' is added.

faults.quote: The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand.
faults.why: 'Of me Jake' is an awkward garble. In the Pauline form it would be 'The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand', but placing it before the postscript and in place of the love makes an odd close.

faults.quote: strict somewhat
faults.why: The word order is unidiomatic for the KJV, which would say 'somewhat strict'.

faults.quote: And I was ashamed.

judge.verdict: The rewrite gets the basic Biblical markers (unto, behold, -eth, 'it came to pass') but leaves slang like 'gross' and 'cool', garbles the close, and loses the 'Love'. The notes cite verses that do not clearly support the moves, and the lesson misdescribes the rewrite.

The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
And the office was exceeding great and new, and the men and the women within it bore hoodies upon them, and drank coffee of the finer sort. And I in my suit was like a man set among them that were not of his kind, and I was wholly out of place.

And, behold, she that had the charge of the place was a woman named Priya, and she was friendly, but somewhat sharp. And she asked of me my strengths and the things wherein I was weak; and I said that I was one that would make all things perfect, which was a lame answer. And she smiled upon me notwithstanding.

And it came to pass, after the interview, that I called my sister; and she said that I had done well, and had gotten the place. And I hope that she is right, for I have need of this work; and the rent falleth due the next week, and I am empty and have nothing.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage runs in short, breathless sentences, while this voice joins clause to clause with "and" and lets a turn land at a verse's end: "And the office was exceeding great and new, and the men and the women within it bore hoodies upon them." You also tell feeling by its slang name ("totally out of place", "basically broke"); the voice gives it by its sign and its consequence, "I am empty and have nothing," so the reader feels it rather than is told of it. Practise joining two of your sentences into one long verse and closing with the heaviest fact last.

faults.quote: I am empty and have nothing

faults.quote: I was one that would make all things perfect
faults.why: 'Perfectionist' becomes a claim of making all things perfect, a shift in meaning. It is also awkward and loses the sense of the self-description as a cliché answer.

faults.quote: somewhat sharp
faults.why: 'Kind of intense' is rendered as 'sharp', which implies a different quality (keen or cutting) and not intensity. The how_it_is_built says 'keen', which doesn't match either.

faults.quote: exceeding great and new
faults.why: 'Super modern' becomes 'new', and the manager's greeting 'friendly but kind of intense' is also softened. Modernity is flattened.

faults.quote: which was a lame answer
faults.why: 'Lame' is a modern slang word left standing in an otherwise archaic sentence, so it reads as costume.

faults.quote: hoodies
faults.why: The word is left as is, which is unavoidable, but 'bore hoodies upon them' reads awkwardly. The wording doesn't sound like KJV.

faults.quote: And I hope that she is right, for I have need of this work; and the rent falleth due the next week
faults.why: The tense shifts from past to present and the mixing of 'hope', 'is' and 'falleth' is uneven. 'The next week' is not idiomatic; 'in the next week' or 'on the morrow of the week' would be. 'Had gotten' is an American form that the KJV would not use.

faults.quote: And I in my suit was like a man set among them that were not of his kind, and I was wholly out of place.
faults.why: The simile is added and then the plain statement is repeated, which is redundant and clunky.

faults.quote: cites Esther 2:3
faults.why: The cited verses do not demonstrate the claimed moves. Luke 14:2 is not an apt 'behold' example, Genesis 35:18 is not a typical 'it came to pass', and Acts 20:7 is not parallelism of that kind. The citations look unreliable.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the voice gives the feeling by a comparison the matter invites
faults.why: The notes disclose the simile but not the invented 'had gotten the place'. That is the real fidelity change, and it goes unreported.

faults.quote: so the reader feels it rather than is told of it
faults.why: The lesson praises 'I am empty and have nothing' as showing, but it is just a different statement of the feeling and an exaggeration. The advice is shaky, and the outline claims 'friendly but keen' when the text says 'somewhat sharp'.

faults.quote: and had gotten the place
faults.why: It introduces a contradiction of sense: if the place were already got, the narrator's need and hope would be pointless. No fault was in the draft, so this one is new.

judge.verdict: The KJV cadence is present, but the rewrite invents that the sister said the job was won, overstates poverty, and leaves modern slang ('lame') in place. The cited sources look dubious and the notes do not report the real change.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours, with a great truck and two little children. And the father of them seemed good: and his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near.

And my mother baked them cakes straightway, for she desired to know all their matters: whence they came, and what they did for their work, and whether they went up to the house of God.

And it came to pass that the father of them was a lawyer and had put away his wife, and was single. And a look came upon the face of my mother, and I knew the thought of her heart: for she hath sought these many years to set me unto a man.

rows.text: And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours, with a great truck and two little children. And the father of them seemed good: and his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother — 'The mom is kind of standoffish' — but your third says of the same household that 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A single, divorced father cannot at once have a wife; and nothing tells the reader who the standoffish one is. I made the standoffish one his sister who came with him, the least change that lets the father stay single and divorced, which the mother's scheming over him requires.
notes.after: And his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near.
And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours
his sister that was with him was aloof unto them that drew near

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences run very short and modern, where the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with 'and' until each sentence carries a whole turn of the matter. I opened your story with 'And it came to pass', joined your three neighbourly questions with 'and' into one breath, and made the standoffish one the father's sister so the divorce stands. Practise giving feeling by its sign — 'a look came upon the face of my mother' — rather than by telling, and joining deeds with their reasons in one long sentence, for that is how this voice lets a scene gather weight.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother: 'The mom is kind of standoffish.' Your third paragraph says of the same household that 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A man who is single — divorced — cannot at the same time have a wife who is the mom of his household; and nothing tells the reader who this mom is.
sense.resolution: Make the standoffish one not the father's wife: since the household is a single divorced father's with two little kids, she is most fitly his sister who lives with him, or the children's grandmother — the least change is 'His sister is kind of standoffish.' Then the dad may be divorced and single, and the mother's scheming over him stands. (If you would rather keep a mom, the mending must go the other way — the dad is married — but that undoes the whole point about setting you up, so the passage itself points to the sister.)
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

faults.quote: to set me unto a man
faults.why: The writer says only 'set me up'. The rewrite assumes the narrator is a woman and drops the link to the new neighbour, which is the point of the closing beat. It also adds an unreported gender.

faults.quote: had put away his wife
faults.why: The writer says only 'divorced'. 'Put away his wife' makes the father the one who ended the marriage, a fact the draft never gives. It also loses the narrator's self-correction ('Well, divorced').

faults.quote: A new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours
faults.why: 'Last weekend' is dropped, so the recency of the move-in is lost. 'Right away' survives only as 'straightway'.

faults.quote: was aloof unto them that drew near
faults.why: 'Aloof' is a modern word that does not appear in the King James text, and it is not a biblical idiom. It also loses the softening 'kind of'.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that the father of them was a lawyer
faults.why: 'It came to pass' marks an event, but here it stands for the writer's 'It turns out', a discovery. The formula is used mechanically, and 'the father of them' is clumsy and ambiguous.

faults.quote: And the father of them seemed good
faults.why: 'Seemed good' in the Bible means 'pleased' or 'was decided', as in 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost'. It does not mean 'seemed a nice man', so the sense of the writer's 'seems nice' is slightly distorted.

faults.quote: cites 1 Samuel 17:41
faults.why: That verse (the shield-bearer going before Goliath) is not an apt source for a parallelism move, and the 'parallelism' named is not really parallel in the rewrite.

faults.quote: cites Mark 5:14
faults.why: The verse is a loose match for a list of clauses joined by 'and'. The notes do not show the pattern in it.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice gives feeling by its sign
faults.why: This is a generic comment, not a real liberty, and it has no source. The notes never report the real changes: 'set me unto a man', 'put away his wife', 'cakes' for cookies, and the lost 'last weekend'.

faults.quote: The father seemeth good... The mother baketh cakes straightway
faults.why: The structure outline describes a present-tense archaic style ('seemeth', 'baketh'), but the rewrite is in the past tense. It also says 'countenance', where the rewrite says 'face'. The outline does not match the output.

faults.quote: joining deeds with their reasons in one long sentence
faults.why: The lesson praises long sentences, but the rewrite keeps short, simple paragraphs, so the example does not match the advice.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is readable and cleanly structured, and it catches and reports the mother/divorced contradiction. But it adds unreported facts ('put away his wife', 'a man'), uses some non-biblical diction ('aloof'), and has loose or inaccurate source citations and an outline that does not match its own output.

The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:
The company was at the house of Jessica, and her father and her mother were gone out of the city; and all they of the school were there, and the air was exceeding loud. And I stood in the room with Emma my friend, and we knew not many that were there. And, behold, there came unto us a man of great stature, and he began to talk with us; and his name was Chris. He was proud in his manner, yet also one that made mirth.

And he said that the company was lame, and the people therein were dull. And Emma rolled her eyes at his words; but I thought him rude. Yet afterward I saw him helping to cleanse the house when all the rest were departed; and I thought, Perhaps I was wrong concerning him.

lessons: Your page tells in short, flat sentences with modern idiom; the Author's manner lays clause beside clause with "and," so every turn lands. Your final "Maybe" becomes a spoken thought, "Perhaps I was wrong concerning him," which the voice gives as the doubt itself rather than a shrug; and your three short opening sentences become one, "and the air was exceeding loud," so the setting and the scene are one breath. Practise joining your sentences with "and" instead of full stops, and giving feeling by its sign, as in "Emma rolled her eyes; but I thought him rude."

plan.why: The voice sets the scene before the scene, placing each person and the whole company in one; this is where the matter opens.

plan.why: The encounter follows the setting; the matters are joined with ands so each clause lands.

plan.why: The speech is brought in plainly, and the feeling is given by its sign, not told at length.

plan.why: The turn of the matter closes on the writer's own 'maybe,' stated as the speaker's uncertainty, which is the weight of the piece.

faults.quote: the air was exceeding loud
faults.why: The writer said the music was loud. 'Air' replaces 'music', so the source of the noise is lost and the sentence reads oddly.

faults.quote: gone out of the city
faults.why: The writer said only 'out of town'. 'Out of the city' is nearly the same, but it is an addition and changes the meaning slightly.

faults.quote: He was proud in his manner, yet also one that made mirth.
faults.why: 'Arrogant but also funny' is softened. 'One that made mirth' says he makes others laugh, not that he is funny, and 'kind of' is dropped.

faults.quote: Yet afterward I saw him helping to cleanse the house when all the rest were departed
faults.why: 'Cleanse' means to purify, not to tidy. The writer's 'clean up' becomes ritual cleansing, which is a mismatch.

faults.quote: in the room with Emma my friend
faults.why: The writer said 'kitchen'. 'Room' makes the place vague for no reason. 'Emma my friend' is a stilted word order.

faults.quote: he said that the company was lame
faults.why: 'Lame' is a modern slang word and breaks the KJV register. A KJV word such as 'weak' or 'without savour' would fit. 'Company' used for both 'party' and 'people' is also confusing.

faults.quote: and the air was exceeding loud
faults.why: The KJV does not use 'loud' like this. It would say 'a great noise' or 'a loud voice'. The line reads as an archaic costume over modern prose.

faults.quote: Perhaps I was wrong concerning him.
faults.why: 'Perhaps' is not a KJV word. 'Peradventure' would be the right choice. The doubt is also less direct than the writer's own thought.

faults.quote: And, behold, there came unto us a man of great stature
faults.why: 'Tall guy' becomes 'a man of great stature', which is fine. But 'behold' is added decoration that sits oddly on a casual party scene.

faults.quote: Behold, lo, verily: “And, behold, there came unto us a man of great stature...” — cites Luke 2:10
faults.why: The note claims 'verily' and 'lo' but the text has only 'behold'. The cited verse is an angel's proclamation, a weak parallel.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “And, behold, there came unto us a man of great stature, and he began to talk with us.” — cites Matthew 26:22
faults.why: Neither 'thereof' nor 'wherefore' appears in the quoted line. Matthew 26:22 is the disciples asking 'Lord, is it I?', which does not match 'unto'. This note is padded.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “And Emma rolled her eyes at his words; but I thought him rude.” — cites Isaiah 6:10
faults.why: This is a contrast, not parallelism. Isaiah 6:10 ('make the heart of this people fat') is an unrelated verse. The note does not describe a real move.

faults.quote: cites Matthew 9:23
faults.why: Matthew 9:23 is the minstrels and the noisy crowd at the ruler's house. It is a loose match for the note's claim about laying clauses side by side with 'and'.

faults.quote: giving feeling by its sign, as in “Emma rolled her eyes; but I thought him rude.”
faults.why: The writer already wrote this, so it teaches nothing new. The lesson also claims 'three short opening sentences become one', but the rewrite makes two sentences. The advice amounts to 'join with and', which is thin.

faults.quote: and the people therein were dull
faults.why: The writer said 'boring'. 'Dull' is fine, but 'therein' is stiff, and 'Chris said the people were boring' is turned into a report where he speaks to them. The change is minor.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the events and order and its structure is sound. It has several wrong or shaky word choices ('air' for music, 'cleanse', 'lame', 'perhaps'), and its notes cite verses that do not support the moves they name. The lesson is thin and partly inaccurate.

I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
I had need of milk, and I caught up my keys and drove unto the store. And the place was exceeding full of people: and a man in a garment with a hood stood in the midst of the passage, so that none might go by, and he spake upon his phone.

And I would not be rude, and I said unto him, Let me pass, I pray thee. But he regarded me not at all, neither did he hear me: and at the last he moved, and I took the milk.

And it came to pass, as I went, that I saw her that had been my companion at the place of paying, and my heart was troubled within me.

And she said unto me, Hail: it is long since I have seen thee, and thou lookest well. And I said, I thank thee, and thou also.

And I paid, and departed in all the haste that I could: and it was the most grievous ten minutes of my week.
