plan.why: the voice states a need plainly, then opens the journey, joining the two clauses with and

plan.gist: the crowd and the man blocking the way
plan.why: the voice gives the scene before the obstacle, then the man, all in one breath

plan.gist: saying excuse me, being ignored, and the way made clear
plan.why: the voice lays the three turns clause beside clause with and, ending where the milk is gotten

plan.gist: seeing the former companion and being troubled
plan.why: the voice turns the story with And it came to pass, and the feeling is given by its sign

plan.gist: the greeting and the short answer
plan.why: the voice brings speech in by said unto, giving it in full and without quotation marks

plan.gist: paying, departing in haste, and the verdict
plan.why: the voice closes the matter and gives the narrator's judgment plainly

faults.quote: I saw her that had been my companion at the place of paying
faults.why: The original says the narrator saw his ex at the checkout. 'Her that had been my companion' at the place of paying reads as if she had been his companion at the checkout, which garbles the relationship and the location.

faults.quote: my heart was troubled within me
faults.why: The original 'basically panicked' is milder and more comic. 'Troubled' softens the panic, and the biblical flourish changes the degree of feeling.

faults.quote: Hail: it is long since I have seen thee, and thou lookest well.
faults.why: 'Hail' is not 'Hey', and it is stiff and odd as a greeting from an ex. 'You look great' is weakened to 'lookest well'.

faults.quote: I thank thee, and thou also.
faults.why: 'You too' is a reply to the compliment ('you look great too'); 'thou also' is ambiguous and does not clearly mean that she looks great.

faults.quote: Let me pass, I pray thee.
faults.why: The writer says 'excuse me' and also says he did not want to be rude. The added 'I pray thee' is acceptable, but the sentence says nothing about his wish to avoid being rude beyond 'I would not be rude', which reads as a refusal rather than a reluctance to offend.

faults.quote: and it was the most grievous ten minutes of my week
faults.why: 'Awkward' becomes 'grievous', which is far heavier than the writer's wry sense, and 'Honestly' is lost. 'Was ... ten minutes' is also ungrammatical in number.

faults.quote: in a garment with a hood
faults.why: The hoodie is rendered as a garment with a hood, which is clumsy rather than idiomatic KJV. 'Super crowded' becomes 'exceeding full of people', which is fine.

faults.quote: and he spake upon his phone
faults.why: 'Phone' is an anachronism that is left unadapted, and 'spake upon' is not idiomatic. The phrase reads as costume.

faults.quote: neither did he hear me
faults.why: The original says he ignored the narrator, not that he failed to hear. This adds a claim the writer did not make.

faults.quote: And I would not be rude, and I said unto him
faults.why: The repeated 'And' at the start of every sentence is mechanical, and 'I would not be rude' in the KJV sense means 'I refused', which misreads the writer's reluctance.

faults.quote: cites Genesis 32:16
faults.why: The same citation is given for two different moves, and 'Unto, thereof, wherefore' lists words that do not appear in the example. The sources look decorative rather than apt.

faults.quote: cites John 14:9
faults.why: John 14:9 is not an apt source for 'said unto me' dialogue. Psalms 81:11 and 1 Samuel 18:19 are tenuous matches for the moves cited.

faults.quote: the voice turns the writer's 'panic' into the sign of feeling, as the Bible does, though the degree stands as the writer's
faults.why: The claim that the degree stands is false, since 'troubled' is milder than 'panicked'. The note also does not report the dropped detail 'ex' or the loss of 'Honestly' and 'super'.

faults.quote: And it came to pass, as I went, that I saw her
faults.why: The original has the narrator at the checkout when he sees her, not 'as I went'. Mid-journey blurs the sequence of getting the milk and then seeing her, and the paragraph split is arbitrary. The speech also keeps colons rather than the quotation-free voice claimed, with 'Long time no see' reworked.

faults.quote: Practise joining your turns with "and" and saying each feeling by its sign
faults.why: The advice is somewhat generic, and the example 'my heart was troubled' is a weaker rendering of the original. The outline offers only vague 'why' reasons that restate the content.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has an archaic surface and a few apt moves, but it garbles the ex's identity ('my companion at the place of paying'), weakens the panic and awkwardness, adds that the man did not hear, and uses an odd 'Hail'. The notes' citations and claims are shaky and partly inaccurate.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
Unto the team, greeting.

And know ye that the launch passeth from the second day unto the fourth day of the week; for the lawyers have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price, and I would not that we go forth without it.

Have ye your several parts of the writing made ready by the sixth hour of the fourth day; and if any be hindered, let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow.

I thank you; and so I rest your servant, Sam.

rows.text: Unto the team, greeting.

notes.after: Unto the team, greeting.

rows.text: And know ye that the launch passeth from the second day unto the fourth day of the week; for the lawyers have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price, and I would not that we go forth without it.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And know ye that the launch passeth from the second day unto the fourth day of the week
for the lawyers have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price, and I would not that we go forth without it

rows.text: Have ye your several parts of the writing made ready by the sixth hour of the fourth day; and if any be hindered, let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow.

notes.after: let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow

rows.text: I thank you; and so I rest your servant, Sam.

lessons: Your note is hurried and telegraphic; the author's manner is slow and full, clause laid beside clause. I opened the letter with a salutation ("Unto the team, greeting") and joined your news to its cause with "for," so the reading moves as the Bible moves. Your charge I doubled into parallel halves ("let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow"), which gives the command weight and a place to land. Practise laying one clause against another with "and" and "for" instead of stacking short sentences.

outline.gist: greet the team
the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
legal has not signed off the pricing page, he will not ship without it
have sections done by Wednesday noon; if blocked, say today
thanks, Sam

plan.gist: salutation to the team
plan.why: the epistle opens with a direct salutation, as Paul's letters do

plan.gist: the launch moves to Thursday
plan.why: the news comes first, plainly, before the reason for it

plan.gist: the lawyers have not approved the pricing page, and he will not go without it
plan.why: the cause follows the news, so the reader sees why it turned

plan.gist: finish your parts by Wednesday noon; if hindered, say so today
plan.why: the charge and the condition, joined, land hardest at the end before the close

plan.gist: thanks and the writer's name
plan.why: the epistle ends with thanks and the sender's own hand

faults.quote: by the sixth hour of the fourth day
faults.why: Wednesday noon becomes 'sixth hour of the fourth day'. Wednesday is the fourth day only if the week starts on Sunday, and the rewrite counts Tuesday as 'second day' and Thursday as 'fourth day', which does not hold. Tuesday=third, Wednesday=fourth, Thursday=fifth under Sunday-first counting. So the dates are wrong and inconsistent.

faults.quote: from the second day unto the fourth day of the week
faults.why: Tuesday to Thursday is mis-numbered, and the rewrite then uses 'the fourth day' for the Wednesday deadline. That makes the launch and the deadline fall on the same day, creating a real contradiction that the rewrite introduced and never reported.

faults.quote: for the lawyers have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price
faults.why: 'Legal' is a department, and 'the page of the price' is an awkward rendering of 'pricing page'. The 'sign off' sense is only loosely kept, though it is acceptable.

faults.quote: I thank you; and so I rest your servant, Sam.
faults.why: 'Rest your servant' is a garbled sign-off. 'Thanks' becomes a tidy formula, and the writer's manager-to-team relationship is turned into servanthood, which shifts the tone.

faults.quote: and not tarry unto the morrow
faults.why: The sense is 'tell me today, not tomorrow'. 'Tarry' means to delay, so the sentence reads as 'do not delay until tomorrow', which shifts the meaning from telling to waiting.

faults.quote: Have ye your several parts of the writing made ready
faults.why: 'Have ye ... made ready' is a question-like or garbled imperative, and 'the writing' for 'the deck' is vague and odd. Real KJV would use 'Make ye ready'.

faults.quote: and I would not that we go forth without it
faults.why: 'Go forth' for shipping is a stretch. The construction is passable KJV (I would not that ye...), but 'go forth without it' is unclear.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “for the lawyers have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price, and I would not that we go forth without it” — cites Zechariah 11:12
faults.why: The quoted sentence contains no thou/thee or -est form, so the note names a move that is not in that passage. The Zechariah citation is also not apt.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “Unto the team, greeting.” — cites Deuteronomy 1:42
faults.why: The note lists 'thereof, wherefore', which do not appear in the rewrite. The Deuteronomy 1:42 citation has no connection to a salutation.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “let him tell me this same day, and not tarry unto the morrow” — cites 1 Samuel 14:9
faults.why: The 1 Samuel verse is not a parallel of this construction, and the cite looks arbitrary. The note also omits the big changes: the invented date numbering and the closing line, which has no note at all (Paragraph 4: none).

faults.quote: cites Ezekiel 31:1
faults.why: Ezekiel 31:1 is a dating verse and is cited for 'clauses laid side by side with and', which is not what the quoted sentence shows.

faults.quote: joined your news to its cause with "for,"
faults.why: The lesson is short and generic ('lay clause against clause'), and it does not warn that the date mapping broke. It also claims the rewrite 'doubled' the charge into parallel halves, when the original already had that two-part shape.

faults.quote: Unto the team, greeting.
faults.why: A KJV epistle would say 'Sam, unto the team: grace and peace', or similar. A bare 'greeting' is thin and modern in shape. Overall the voice is also mostly 'ye/unto/passeth' sprinkled on, with little KJV rhythm, and the 'and' + 'for' chains are shallow.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a plausible archaic surface, but it mis-numbers the days so that the launch and the deadline collide, and it contains an awkward sign-off and a garbled imperative. The notes name moves (thou/thee, thereof, wherefore) that are not in the text and cite verses that do not match, so the teaching is weak.

yours:
Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: On the seventh day I made clean the gutters, and I restored the sink that ran with water, and I called my grandmother: and she talked with me for the space of an hour of her neighbour's cat. And the evening found me spent, yet my heart was lifted up in a strange pride of myself.

rows.text: On the seventh day I made clean the gutters, and I restored the sink that ran with water, and I called my grandmother: and she talked with me for the space of an hour of her neighbour's cat. And the evening found me spent, yet my heart was lifted up in a strange pride of myself.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: of her neighbour's cat

notes.text: the voice frames the writer's own state (exhausted, weirdly proud) by its sign and its verdict: to be spent, and the heart lifted up, is the Bible's way of giving the feeling without naming it modernly
notes.after: And the evening found me spent, yet my heart was lifted up in a strange pride.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer lists in a modern idiom, while the King James Bible lays one deed beside the next with "and" and gives the day's close as a balanced turn. "And the evening found me spent, yet my heart was lifted up in a strange pride of myself" gives the weariness and the pride as parallel halves, so each lands with weight; practising that balance of a state given by its sign and a verdict in plain words will serve the writer in their own voice.

outline.gist: the day named: Saturday
the three works done, and the grandmother's hour of talk of the neighbour's cat
by evening, worn out yet strangely proud of himself

plan.gist: the day named
plan.why: the voice names the time first, plainly, before the deeds of the day

plan.gist: the works in order, each done, and the grandmother's talk
plan.why: the voice lays deed beside deed with and, in the order they were done, and gives the call and the talk at the full

plan.gist: by evening spent yet proud
plan.why: the voice closes with the state at evening, the weariness and the pride in balance, and a verdict in its own words

faults.quote: On the seventh day
faults.why: The writer said Saturday. Calling it 'the seventh day' is defensible but loads in a Sabbath/creation allusion, which makes the work-day sound like the day of rest. The note does not report this change.

faults.quote: I restored the sink that ran with water
faults.why: The writer fixed a leaky sink. 'Ran with water' is what a sink should do, so it loses the fault. The leak is gone, and it reads as if the sink was merely running, not leaking.

faults.quote: I made clean the gutters
faults.why: The meaning is kept, but 'made clean' is a clumsy calque and not a natural KJV construction for the task. 'Cleansed' would be more idiomatic.

faults.quote: talked with me for the space of an hour
faults.why: The writer says she talked, implying a monologue, while 'with me' implies conversation. This shifts the sense, and the mild humor of her talking on about the cat is lost.

faults.quote: spent, yet my heart was lifted up in a strange pride of myself
faults.why: 'Weirdly proud' becomes a 'strange pride', which is acceptable. 'Lifted up' carries scriptural overtones of sinful pride, so the feeling tilts away from the writer's gentle self-satisfaction. 'Pride of myself' is not KJV idiom.

faults.quote: in a strange pride of myself
faults.why: This is garbled. 'Pride of myself' is ungrammatical in either KJV or modern English. 'Proud of myself' or 'a strange pride in my doing' would be better.

faults.quote: And the evening found me spent
faults.why: 'Evening found me' is a modern literary conceit. The KJV would say 'and the evening came' or 'when evening was come'. The KJV also has 'thy' and 'hath' forms, and this rewrite has few archaisms (no 'did', 'unto', 'wherein'), so it reads thin.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “of her neighbour's cat” — cites Ezekiel 18:6
faults.why: The citation looks spurious or inapt. Ezekiel 18:6 concerns defiling a neighbour's wife, so it is not a model for this construction. The 'move' is also trivial, because 'of her neighbour's cat' is just a plain 'about'.

faults.quote: the Bible's way of giving the feeling without naming it modernly
faults.why: The note claims the feeling is shown by a sign, but the rewrite still names 'pride' and 'spent'. The note is vague and does not report the changes to the sink and the day.

faults.quote: practising that balance of a state given by its sign and a verdict in plain words will serve the writer
faults.why: The lesson is abstract and muddled, and it contradicts itself ('sign' and 'plain words'). It names no reusable technique beyond 'and' parataxis. It also praises a sentence that is itself flawed.

faults.quote: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The writer's two paragraphs, a list and then a turn, are merged. This loses the pause before the closing reflection and is not explained.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the three tasks in order and the weary-yet-proud turn, but it loses the 'leaky' fault of the sink, adds a Sabbath overtone, and contains the garbled 'pride of myself'. The notes cite an inapt verse and the lesson is vague, so the writer gets little to reuse.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to cars upon the days of rest. For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children. Other towns have done this thing, and their booths do better than ever before.

And some of the keepers of booths shall complain, that the guests cannot come unto them. But they will be used to it in time. For the most part, the people do walk from the store of waggons even as it is.

And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer.

rows.text: Our town should close Main Street to cars upon the days of rest. For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children. Other towns have done this thing, and their booths do better than ever before.

notes.text: the writer says the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers; the voice says walkways and carriages of children, naming the thing by its use rather than keeping words it never wrote
notes.after: and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children

rows.text: And some of the keepers of booths shall complain, that the guests cannot come unto them. But they will be used to it in time. For the most part, the people do walk from the store of waggons even as it is.

notes.after: the guests cannot come unto them
the keepers of booths

rows.text: And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer.

notes.after: And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer.

notes.text: the voice turns the story of the other towns with its usual formula, showing the change of scene
notes.after: And it shall come to pass

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short modern sentences are joined into clauses laid side by side with "and," so each reason lands as a turn of the story: "For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the walkways thereof are too narrow for the carriages of children." The voice gives the complaint and its answer as the writer ordered them, but in its old words—"the keepers of booths," "the guests cannot come unto them"—and closes on its formula, "And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer." Practise building one sentence of two balanced halves with a colon or "and," and turning every modern phrase into a plain thing named by its use.

outline.gist: close Main Street to cars on weekends
parking a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow for strollers
other towns' shops doing better
owners will complain customers can't reach them
they'll get used to it; most walk from garage anyway
try it this summer

plan.gist: close Main Street to cars on weekends
plan.why: open with the call, grave and plain, as the writer does

plan.gist: parking a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow
plan.why: lay the grievance beside the proposal with and, in two parallel halves

plan.gist: other towns' shops doing better
plan.why: better is better than ever, in the voice's comparative manner

plan.gist: owners will complain
plan.why: an objection, then its answer, each opened with and as the turns come

plan.gist: they will get used; most walk from the garage
plan.why: answer first the complaint, then the fact that undoes it

plan.gist: try it this summer
plan.why: a short verdict to close

faults.quote: For the laying down of waggons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream
faults.why: The writer said parking is a nightmare. 'Laying down of waggons' is an odd rendering of parking, and 'as an evil dream' weakens 'is a nightmare' into a simile. The sense of parking trouble is blurred.

faults.quote: the carriages of children
faults.why: Strollers become 'carriages of children', which is vague. The notes claim this names the thing by its use, but it is not clear and sounds like a coach carrying children.

faults.quote: their booths do better than ever before
faults.why: 'Shops' becomes 'booths', which changes the meaning and sounds like market stalls. 'Than ever before' also shifts the writer's 'than ever'.

faults.quote: the store of waggons
faults.why: The garage becomes a 'store of waggons', which wrongly suggests a warehouse or shop. It is an unclear and misleading rendering.

faults.quote: But they will be used to it in time.
faults.why: The writer's 'they'll get used to it' is kept in modern idiom, and 'be used to it' is not KJV diction. The writer's dismissive 'Honestly' is lost.

faults.quote: And it shall come to pass that we should try it this summer.
faults.why: The writer's plain call 'We should try it this summer' becomes a prophecy that something shall come to pass. This changes the force from a proposal to a prediction, and 'shall ... should' is clumsy.

faults.quote: upon the days of rest
faults.why: Weekends are rendered as 'days of rest', which is plausible but loses the plain fact. The first sentence is otherwise unchanged modern prose, so the voice is thin there.

faults.quote: the guests cannot come unto them
faults.why: 'Guests' for customers is wrong for KJV. 'Cannot' is also modern where the KJV would use 'cannot' only sparingly, and the passage lacks KJV parallelism or 'verily' and 'behold' moves.

faults.quote: the people do walk from the store of waggons even as it is
faults.why: 'Do walk' is an emphatic auxiliary, and 'even as it is' is awkward and not KJV idiom.

faults.quote: And some of the keepers of booths shall complain, that the guests cannot come unto them.
faults.why: 'Shall complain' with a comma before 'that' reads stiffly. Sentence-initial 'And' on every turn is mechanical.

faults.quote: cites 1 Samuel 9:6
faults.why: The cited verses are given as support for generic features such as 'unto' and 'of'. They do not show the specific phrases used, so the citations are decorative and not apt.

faults.quote: the voice turns the story of the other towns with its usual formula, showing the change of scene
faults.why: This is inaccurate. The 'come to pass' formula is applied to the final call, not to the other towns, and the call is not a change of scene.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the writer says the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers
faults.why: The note says 'words it never wrote' but the rewrite adds 'waggons', 'booths' and 'guests', which are not reported. Several liberties go unreported.

faults.quote: Practise building one sentence of two balanced halves with a colon or "and,"
faults.why: A colon is not a KJV device and the rewrite does not use one. The lesson also says short sentences are joined, but the rewrite still has the same short sentences, so the advice does not match the text.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: proposal (close Main Street to cars on weekends; why: open with the call, grave and plain, as the writer does)
faults.why: The outline says nothing was reordered and gives vague reasons such as 'better is better than ever'. It teaches little about structure and misdescribes the rewrite.

judge.verdict: The rewrite swaps in odd archaisms (waggons, booths, guests, store of waggons) that blur the meaning, and the voice is mostly modern syntax with a few thees. Notes cite verses loosely, misdescribe the 'come to pass' use, and the lesson does not match what was done.

yours:
I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite: I have never seen Paris aright, but once was I there, and it rained the whole week. And it came to pass that on the second day my brother lost his pass, and we spent the most part of the journey at the embassy. And my brother saith even now that it was the best journey he ever had.

rows.text: I have never seen Paris aright, but once was I there, and it rained the whole week. And it came to pass that on the second day my brother lost his pass, and we spent the most part of the journey at the embassy. And my brother saith even now that it was the best journey he ever had.

notes.text: The opening says you have never been to Paris, but the next sentence says the last time you were there it rained all week; both cannot be true of you. I narrowed the opening to say you have never truly seen Paris, that you were there but once and it rained the whole week, which removes the contradiction with the least change and lets the embassy and the brother's verdict stand as written.
notes.after: I have never seen Paris aright, but once was I there, and it rained the whole week

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
the verdict needed to be narrowed to remove the contradiction; 'aright' is the voice's plain way of granting the visit happened while denying it was truly seen.
notes.after: I have never seen Paris aright

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's four short sentences are laid out as clauses joined by "and", each opened with a turn of the voice. I joined the visit and the mishap with "And it came to pass", turned "most of the trip" into "the most part of the journey", and closed with the brother's verdict in the voice's cadence: "the best journey he ever had." To practise: let a story turn on "And it came to pass", and let each clause stand beside the next rather than underneath it.

outline.gist: I have never been to Paris
last visit, it rained all week and brother lost his passport on day two
most of the trip spent at the embassy
brother still calls it his best vacation

plan.gist: the narrator has never truly seen Paris
plan.why: the voice opens with the verdict that frames the matter, then turns to the story with And it came to pass

plan.gist: the one time there, it rained all week and the brother lost his passport the second day
plan.why: the setting and the mishap laid side by side with and, each clause given its place

plan.gist: they spent most of the journey at the embassy
plan.why: the time spent is the natural turn the mishap led to

plan.gist: the brother still says it was the best journey he ever had
plan.why: the point where it lands hardest, closed with his word

sense.problem: Your first sentence says you have never been to Paris; your second says the last time you were there it rained all week. Both cannot be true of you.
sense.resolution: Keep the anecdote and narrow the opening claim, which is the sentence the passage does not need: say you have never truly seen Paris, or never been back since (e.g. “I have never seen Paris but once, and then it rained the whole week”). This removes the contradiction with the least change and lets the embassy and the brother's verdict stand exactly as written.
sense.quote: I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week

faults.quote: I have never seen Paris aright, but once was I there
faults.why: The rewrite changes the writer's claim 'never been' into 'never seen aright' and so alters the meaning. The mending is plausible but sits awkwardly with 'the last time', which implies several visits; 'but once' invents a single visit.

faults.quote: my brother lost his pass
faults.why: 'Pass' for passport is a loose or archaic-sounding substitution that could mean a mountain pass or a permit. It blurs a precise fact.

faults.quote: the best journey he ever had
faults.why: 'Vacation' is turned into 'journey' and 'trip' into 'journey' too. The brother's pleasure in a holiday is flattened into travel, and the repeated 'journey' is clumsy.

faults.quote: the most part of the journey
faults.why: The phrase is a stilted pseudo-archaic form; the KJV would say 'the more part' or 'the greater part'. It reads as a malapropism.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that on the second day my brother lost his pass, and we spent
faults.why: 'Pass' sits next to 'came to pass', producing an unintended pun. The clause is also overloaded and loses the comic deadpan of the original.

faults.quote: but once was I there
faults.why: The inversion is more Shakespearean or poetic than KJV, and the prose is thin on KJV parallelism and diction ('and he said', 'in those days').

faults.quote: saith even now
faults.why: 'Saith' in a first-person narrative about a living brother is a costume gesture. 'Even now' is acceptable, but the whole passage is only lightly KJV.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the verdict needed to be narrowed to remove the contradiction
faults.why: This note is confused: it speaks of narrowing 'the verdict' when the opening claim was changed. It duplicates the sense note.

faults.quote: Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The rewrite removes the paragraph break and the deadpan beat of the second paragraph without explaining the loss.

faults.quote: turned "most of the trip" into "the most part of the journey"
faults.why: The lesson praises a phrase that is not authentic KJV idiom.

faults.quote: the point where it lands hardest, closed with his word
faults.why: The how_it_is_built claims the structure was reordered, but the order is the same as the writer's. The description is generic and the lesson gives little reusable guidance beyond 'use and'.

faults.quote: And my brother saith even now that it was the best journey he ever had.
faults.why: The writer's separate closing paragraph, which delivered the punchline, is merged into one run-on string of 'and' clauses, which weakens the comic turn.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the contradiction and mends it, but the mending is strained ('aright', 'but once'). The KJV costume is thin and uses odd phrases ('the most part', 'pass' beside 'came to pass'). The notes are muddled and the lesson is generic.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we should turn from the week of five days unto a week of four. For the people are wearied, and the week seemeth long unto them; and our best soul is gone from us, even he that was first among them. There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater. It would also help us in the taking of men.

I know it is wild, and they that are our clients may not love it; yet we could try it for the space of three months, and see.

rows.text: I think we should turn from the week of five days unto a week of four. For the people are wearied, and the week seemeth long unto them; and our best soul is gone from us, even he that was first among them. There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater. It would also help us in the taking of men.

notes.after: For the people are wearied, and the week seemeth long unto them; and our best soul is gone from us, even he that was first among them.
There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater.
It would also help us in the taking of men.
I think we should turn from the week of five days unto a week of four.

rows.text: I know it is wild, and they that are our clients may not love it; yet we could try it for the space of three months, and see.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: I know it is wild, and they that are our clients may not love it; yet we could try it for the space of three months, and see.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage states each point in a short modern sentence, while the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with "and" and "for" until the reasons gather weight: your three short reasons become one long sentence, "For the people are wearied, and the week seemeth long unto them; and our best soul is gone from us." I gave your "burned out" its sign rather than its name; practice that, giving feeling by what is seen ("the people are wearied"), so the reader feels the weariness with you.

outline.gist: switch to a four-day week
people burned out, best engineer quit
studies show productivity stays or rises
helps hiring
risky, clients may not like it
try three months and see

plan.gist: I think we should turn to a week of four days
plan.why: The voice opens plainly with the speaker's judgment, the claim before the reasons.

plan.gist: the people are spent and the best engineer is gone
plan.why: The grievance comes first, the strongest reason, laid out in parallel halves.

plan.gist: there are works shewing the work stays or waxes
plan.why: The proof follows the reason, reported gravely.

plan.gist: it would also help the taking of men
plan.why: A shorter reason after the long proof, joined with also.

plan.gist: I know it is wild, and clients may not love it, yet we could try for three months
plan.why: The voice grants the risk before the modest ask, and closes on the turn of trying.

faults.quote: and the week seemeth long unto them
faults.why: Invented content. The writer never says the week seems long; this is added beyond the writer's 'burned out'.

faults.quote: even he that was first among them
faults.why: Embellishment. 'Best engineer' becomes 'first among them', which shifts the meaning and adds a clause. 'Best soul' also drops the engineer's role.

faults.quote: There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater.
faults.why: 'Studies' becomes 'works', which is vague and misleading. 'Productivity' becomes 'the work of the week', which is clumsy. 'Stays the same or goes up' is kept but reads as strained.

faults.quote: It would also help us in the taking of men.
faults.why: 'Hiring' becomes 'taking of men', which suggests seizing or conscripting people. It is also gendered, and the sense is changed.

faults.quote: I know it is wild
faults.why: 'Risky' becomes 'wild', which is a different meaning and a different degree. 'Wild' is also not a KJV sense here.

faults.quote: our best soul is gone from us
faults.why: 'Best soul' for an engineer is odd and slightly comic. 'Gone from us' is also a softer tone than 'quit'.

faults.quote: they that are our clients may not love it
faults.why: 'Love' is an odd verb for clients' approval. 'May not' is modern, and 'they that are our clients' is padded.

faults.quote: I think we should turn from the week of five days unto a week of four.
faults.why: 'I think' is modern, not KJV. The writer's 'switch to a four-day week' is rendered as 'week of five days', which adds the five-day detail.

faults.quote: There be works that shew
faults.why: 'Be' is archaic but not KJV usage. The sentence mixes 'stayeth' and 'groweth' with a modern frame. Overall the voice is thin, with few 'and' chains, no 'behold' or 'verily', and 'unto' used sparingly.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “There be works that shew the work of the week stayeth as it was, or groweth greater.” — cites Revelation 2:19
faults.why: The note names thou/thee, but the sentence contains neither. The cited verse is not an apt source for the move.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “It would also help us in the taking of men.” — cites Psalms 60:11
faults.why: The citation is dubious and does not support the claim. The 'taking of men' phrase is not tied to the verse.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “I think we should turn from the week of five days unto a week of four.” — cites Matthew 14:17
faults.why: The sentence has no 'thereof' or 'wherefore'. Matthew 14:17 is about loaves and fishes and is a mismatched source.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “For the people are wearied... — cites Psalms 44:10
faults.why: The note does not report the added content ('week seemeth long', 'first among them'). The cited verse is not about weariness.

faults.quote: I gave your "burned out" its sign rather than its name
faults.why: The lesson claims the three short reasons became one long sentence, but the rewrite does not do this. It also praises an invented image ('the week seemeth long') as if it were a transferable move. The lesson is vague on reuse.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the broad order of the argument but adds invented phrases, distorts 'hiring' and 'risky', and has weak KJV texture. Its notes cite mismatched verses and name features such as thou/thee that are not present, so the teaching value is low.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
And when Dana had put off our dinner, it touched me not at all; and my heart was light within me. For I had feared it all the week, and this is no thing to be proud of.

And I said unto her, It is well, and we shall do it another time. But I do not think that we shall.

rows.text: And when Dana had put off our dinner, it touched me not at all; and my heart was light within me. For I had feared it all the week, and this is no thing to be proud of.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And when Dana had put off our dinner, it touched me not at all; and my heart was light within me.
it touched me not at all; and my heart was light within me

notes.text: the voice gives the relief by its sign, gravely and plainly, as it gives every feeling
notes.after: and my heart was light within me

notes.text: the writer's 'I'm not proud of that' becomes the narrator's plain verdict upon his own heart, the manner the voice takes for confession
notes.after: and this is no thing to be proud of

rows.text: And I said unto her, It is well, and we shall do it another time. But I do not think that we shall.

notes.after: And I said unto her, It is well
And I said unto her, It is well, and we shall do it another time.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short staccato confessions become one grave turn: I joined the cancelling and the relief in a single sentence set clause beside clause with "and," and gave the feeling by its sign, "my heart was light within me," where the writer said "relieved." The writer should practise joining what happened with what it stirred, as in "it touched me not at all; and my heart was light within me," for it lets each fact land with the other's weight.

outline.gist: Dana cancelled dinner; the narrator was not upset
honestly, relief
had dreaded it all week, not proud
told her it was fine, another time
does not think they will

plan.gist: the cancelling, then the relief, set as one turn
plan.why: the voice joins what happened and what it stirred in one sentence, clause beside clause

plan.gist: the week of dreading, the shame of it
plan.why: the narrator's verdict on his own feeling comes as a plain admission, not an aside

plan.gist: what he told her, and what he thinks
plan.why: the reply is kept, and the last thought lands as the turn

faults.quote: it touched me not at all; and my heart was light within me
faults.why: The writer said 'I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved.' 'Touched me not at all' suggests indifference and loses the upset/relief contrast. The 'Honestly' emphasis is gone.

faults.quote: For I had feared it all the week, and this is no thing to be proud of.
faults.why: 'Dreading' becomes 'feared', which is stronger and different in kind. 'I'm not proud of that' was a personal admission, but it now reads as a generalized maxim, and it loses the 'I'.

faults.quote: But I do not think that we shall.
faults.why: The 'I don't think we will' is kept, but 'we shall do it another time' now reads as a promise, so the tension with the narrator's inner doubt is blurred. 'It is well' is also more solemn than the casual 'it's fine'.

faults.quote: this is no thing to be proud of
faults.why: This is modern in rhythm with a stranded preposition, and 'no thing' is a clumsy negative. The KJV would say 'whereof I am not proud' or 'I glory not therein'.

faults.quote: But I do not think that we shall.
faults.why: The KJV does not use 'do not think' this way; it would say 'I think not' or 'I suppose not'. The 'do'-periphrasis is modern.

faults.quote: when Dana had put off our dinner
faults.why: 'Put off' for 'cancelled' is a modern idiom, and 'had put off' changes the sense toward postponing. It sits oddly with the 'another time' that follows.

faults.quote: all the week
faults.why: This is not idiomatic. The KJV would say 'all the week long' or 'all the days of the week'.

faults.quote: cites Daniel 10:10
faults.why: Daniel 10:10 is about a hand touching the speaker and has no relation to joining clauses with 'and', so the citation is inapt for the move named.

faults.quote: cites Psalms 143:4
faults.why: Psalm 143:4 ('my spirit is overwhelmed within me') is about distress, not a parallelism about relief. The rewrite's 'touched me not at all; and my heart was light' is not really parallelism.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “And I said unto her, It is well”
faults.why: The note lists 'thereof' and 'wherefore', which are not in the rewrite. It duplicates the next note, and the second use of Genesis 29:6 is padding.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the voice gives the relief by its sign
faults.why: This is vague, and it does not say that 'relieved' was replaced by 'light heart' and 'touched me not at all' replaced 'not upset'. The notes also omit the loss of 'Honestly' and the 'dreading' to 'feared' change.

faults.quote: it lets each fact land with the other's weight
faults.why: The lesson is vague, and the claim that the writer's staccato became one turn is not fully borne out because the rewrite still has several short sentences. The lesson about joining event and feeling is of limited transferable use and does not explain the sign-versus-name-of-feeling move concretely.

faults.quote: And when Dana had put off our dinner
faults.why: The 'Honestly' beat and 'I'm not proud of that' ending are flattened. Starting every sentence with 'And' or 'For' is fine, but the final sentence's bare 'But' loses the voice's closing weight.

judge.verdict: A competent but thin KJV pastiche that keeps the order and the feelings broadly intact, though 'touched me not at all' shifts relief toward indifference and several phrasings ('no thing to be proud of', 'do not think') are not true to the voice. The notes cite apt-sounding verses that do not support the moves named, and the lesson gives little reusable guidance.

yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and said we needed to talk. Here's the thing: I knew right away what those words meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown, and he was already there, looking at his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry, but I didn't. So I just said okay, and I didn't cry, and I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was making too much of it. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.

rows.text: Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and said we needed to talk. Here's the thing: I knew right away what those words meant.

notes.text: The voice turns to the listener to frame the foreboding the writer implies but does not state, a plain bridge into the scene.
notes.after: Here's the thing: I knew right away what those words meant.

rows.text: The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown, and he was already there, looking at his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.
I wanted to cry, but I didn't. So I just said okay, and I didn't cry, and I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

notes.text: The voice joins her restraint and her walk as a single measured sequence, the rhythm of building threes, adding no new feeling.
notes.after: So I just said okay, and I didn't cry, and I walked home in the rain.

rows.text: My roommate thought I was making too much of it. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.

lessons: The writer told the breakup in short, bare strokes; Obama stretches each beat into a spoken sentence that joins clauses with "and" and lets one moment stand for the whole. Notice the turn "I wanted to cry, but I didn't" — the antithesis holds her restraint and her grief in one breath — and the closing "Maybe I was. But it still hurt," where the honest verdict lands after the doubt. Practise joining your short sentences with "and" so the feeling builds rather than stops at each period.

outline.gist: A midnight message, and the foreboding it carries
The meeting at the coffee shop, and the words he uses to end it
The walk home, the crying she holds back, the ice cream
The roommate's doubt, and the hurt that remains

plan.gist: The midnight message and what it means
plan.why: Obama opens on the particular moment, then widens to what it told her; the foreboding before the scene.

plan.gist: The meeting, his nervousness, the two reasons he gives
plan.why: He gives the other person a fair hearing first, in his own words, before any judgement.

plan.gist: What she did and did not do, the walk home in the rain
plan.why: He keeps her feelings restrained and shown through action, not declared.

plan.gist: The roommate's doubt, and the hurt that stays
plan.why: He closes on the turn from what others said to what it still meant to her, landing on the honest hurt.

faults.quote: So I just said okay, and I didn't cry, and I walked home in the rain
faults.why: The writer's "nodded and said okay" loses the nod. "I didn't cry" is repeated, which adds redundancy not in the original. The nod is a real detail that was dropped.

faults.quote: So I just said okay, and I didn't cry, and I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.
faults.why: The "and… and… and" chain is clumsy and repeats the earlier "but I didn't". It reads as stumbling rather than a measured cadence.

faults.quote: Here's the thing: I knew right away what those words meant.
faults.why: "Here's the thing" is a stock imitation of a colloquial tic, which is not a strong Obama signature. It is tacked on and does not give the rhythm, reflection or widening to a larger point that the real voice has.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and said we needed to talk.
faults.why: The sentences are almost unchanged from the plain draft, with synonym swaps like "message", "looking at his phone" and "making too much of it". There are no Obama moves such as the reflective aside, the balanced triad, the gentle humor or the widening to the universal. It reads as modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: looking at his phone
faults.why: "Scrolling" is flattened to "looking", losing the specific image of idle distraction before the nervousness.

faults.quote: The voice turns to the listener to frame the foreboding
faults.why: There is no listener address in the rewrite. "Here's the thing" is not addressed to anyone in particular, and the notes overstate what was done. Paragraphs 2 and 4 are marked "no notes" although the "and" joining and "making too much of it" were changed.

faults.quote: the rhythm of building threes, adding no new feeling
faults.why: The sequence is not a true building three, because "said okay / didn't cry / walked home" repeats the restraint. The note flatters a clumsy change.

faults.quote: Obama stretches each beat into a spoken sentence that joins clauses with "and"
faults.why: The lesson is generic and rests on a questionable claim. It praises "I wanted to cry, but I didn't", which is the writer's own wording unchanged, and gives no reusable concrete move with a reason.

faults.quote: Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
faults.why: The structure is kept, and the outline claims Obama would widen the opening to what the moment told her, but the rewrite does not do that. The outline describes more than the text delivers.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is close to a light paraphrase of the original, with a few awkward changes (the repeated "didn't cry" chain, the stock "Here's the thing") and almost no real Obama cadence or reflection. The notes and lesson claim moves that are not actually present.

yours:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay, I guess—which is to say, it is fine, mostly. The food is not so good, and the boy in my bunk makes noise all night long. Yesterday we went out on the water, and I tipped the boat over, and everybody had a good time about it. It was so embarrassing.

But there is this girl named Kayla, and she is really cool. She is from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about animals. We go down to the lake after dinner and talk about things. I think she likes me, but I am not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I completely forgot. The counselors are a little strict, but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.

rows.text: Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay, I guess—which is to say, it is fine, mostly. The food is not so good, and the boy in my bunk makes noise all night long. Yesterday we went out on the water, and I tipped the boat over, and everybody had a good time about it. It was so embarrassing.

notes.text: The voice's plain reading of 'okay I guess,' setting the terms before the particulars; a frame the matter invites.
notes.after: which is to say, it is fine, mostly

rows.text: But there is this girl named Kayla, and she is really cool. She is from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about animals. We go down to the lake after dinner and talk about things. I think she likes me, but I am not sure.
Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I completely forgot. The counselors are a little strict, but mostly fine.
Love, Jake
P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's short, choppy sentences leave each fact standing alone, where Obama joins them and lets them build. I gathered the particulars into longer, spoken sentences that land on the feeling ("it was so embarrassing") and on the fair word ("mostly fine"), and I let one friend, Kayla, stand for the good of the place. Practise the turn from what happened to what it meant, and the antithesis "not so good…but fine" that lets a complaint and a fairness sit side by side.

outline.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
camp okay, food gross, bunkmate noisy
canoe flipped, everyone laughed, embarrassing
girl named Kayla, cool, from Ohio, knows horses, talk at lake, maybe likes me
send snacks and phone charger, counselors strict but fine
Love, Jake
don't let Max use my room

plan.gist: Dear Mom and Dad
plan.why: A letter keeps its greeting, set alone as the writer gave it.

plan.gist: camp, the food, the bunkmate
plan.why: The writer's order: the general verdict first, then the particular complaints; the voice lets the particulars carry the meaning.

plan.gist: the canoe turned over, everyone laughed, the embarrassment
plan.why: One child's story, told plainly, then what it felt like: the turn from what happened to what it meant.

plan.gist: Kayla, Ohio, horses, the lake, maybe she likes me
plan.why: One named friend standing for the good of the place; the feeling kept small and honest, not inflated.

plan.gist: snacks, charger, counselors
plan.why: The newspaper said the writer: the requests first, then the fair word on the counselors; the voice gathers the paragraph.

plan.gist: Love, Jake
plan.why: The close stays as given.

plan.gist: Max and my room
plan.why: The postscript stays as its own turn, kept last.

faults.quote: everybody had a good time about it
faults.why: The writer said everybody laughed and it was embarrassing; this softens the laughing into a pleasant time. It changes the feeling and reads as unintended comedy.

faults.quote: she knows a great deal about animals
faults.why: The writer said horses. Generalizing to animals drops a specific fact.

faults.quote: The food is not so good
faults.why: The writer said gross. This weakens the strength of the complaint, so the feeling is no longer to the same degree.

faults.quote: the boy in my bunk makes noise all night long
faults.why: The writer said the bunkmate snores like crazy. Losing the snoring drops the specific detail and the humor.

faults.quote: we went out on the water, and I tipped the boat over
faults.why: Canoeing and canoe are replaced with vague phrases. The fact is blurred without any gain.

faults.quote: which is to say, it is fine, mostly
faults.why: This adds a gloss the writer did not give, and it makes the opening verdict more positive than 'okay I guess'.

faults.quote: Camp is okay, I guess—which is to say, it is fine, mostly.
faults.why: This is the only Obama-like move in the piece. The rest is flattened, stiff, de-contracted prose with no real Obama cadence, such as anaphora, a rhetorical turn or warm self-deprecation, so it reads as a bland paraphrase.

faults.quote: it is fine, mostly
faults.why: The phrase is awkward and redundant after 'okay, I guess'. It also reads oddly as a child's letter, because 'is not so good' and 'I am not sure' sound stilted.

faults.quote: I think she likes me, but I am not sure.
faults.why: Dropping the contractions makes a kid's letter sound stiff, and it is not Obama's actual spoken register, which uses contractions freely.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice's plain reading of 'okay I guess,' setting the terms before the particulars; a frame the matter invites.
faults.why: The note is vague and covers only one change. It does not report the many substitutions (horses→animals, snores→noise, laughed→good time, gross→not so good, canoe→boat).

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Five of six paragraphs have no notes even though they contain substantive changes, so the notes do not name real changes accurately.

faults.quote: The chief difference is that the writer's short, choppy sentences leave each fact standing alone, where Obama joins them and lets them build.
faults.why: The rewrite does not do this. Sentences remain short and parallel, and the lesson claims a longer, built-up style and an antithesis 'not so good…but fine' that is not actually in the text. It teaches something the rewrite did not do.

faults.quote: The newspaper said the writer: the requests first, then the fair word on the counselors
faults.why: The structure description contains a garbled, irrelevant phrase. It also claims the voice gathers the paragraph, but the rewrite keeps the original order and structure unchanged.

judge.verdict: The rewrite blurs or alters several concrete facts (horses→animals, laughed→good time, snoring→noise) and barely sounds like Obama beyond one hedged opening. The notes and lesson describe changes that are not in the text, so the writer would learn little.

yours:
The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
The office was huge and thoroughly modern, and everyone in it wore sweatshirts and carried drinks that cost more than my lunch. I had shown up in a suit, and I felt completely out of place.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly, but there was an intensity about her all the same. She asked me about my strengths and my flaws, and I told her I was the kind of person who has to get every little thing right, which was not much of an answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview, I called my sister. She said I probably did just fine.

Here's the thing. I hope she's right, because I really need this job. The rent is due next week, and I am just about broke.

rows.text: The office was huge and thoroughly modern, and everyone in it wore sweatshirts and carried drinks that cost more than my lunch. I had shown up in a suit, and I felt completely out of place.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly, but there was an intensity about her all the same. She asked me about my strengths and my flaws, and I told her I was the kind of person who has to get every little thing right, which was not much of an answer. She smiled anyway.

notes.after: The manager was a woman named Priya.

rows.text: After the interview, I called my sister. She said I probably did just fine.

notes.text: Begins your paragraph 3, which the next paragraph finishes.

rows.text: Here's the thing. I hope she's right, because I really need this job. The rent is due next week, and I am just about broke.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 3, given a paragraph of its own.
the voice's plain turn to the listener, framing what follows
notes.after: Here's the thing.

lessons: Your draft moved in short, quiet beats; the voice builds each paragraph out of longer sentences that join clauses with “, and” and land on a verdict. I kept every fact and its order, but named the office’s people plainly (“sweatshirts,” “drinks that cost more than my lunch”), turned the lame answer into a small self-judgment (“which was not much of an answer”), and ended on the need that makes the hope matter (“I'm just about broke”). Practise joining two of your short sentences with “, and,” and saving a short sentence for the turn.

outline.gist: the modern office, hoodies and fancy drinks, the narrator out of place in a suit
the manager Priya, friendly but intense, the interview question and the lame answer
calling the sister, her reassurance
hoping she is right, rent due, broke

plan.gist: the office, the people in it, the narrator out of place
plan.why: the voice sets the scene plainly before the action, one detail standing for many

plan.gist: Priya, her manner, the question, the answer, her smile
plan.why: the particular story of one person carrying the meaning; the answer lands with its own verdict

plan.gist: the call to the sister and what she said
plan.why: the turn from what happened to what it means, and what the listener would say

plan.gist: hoping she is right, rent due, broke
plan.why: the voice lands on the need, plain and honest, the reason the hope matters

faults.quote: carried drinks that cost more than my lunch
faults.why: The writer said 'fancy coffee'. The rewrite drops coffee and invents a comparison to the narrator's lunch that the draft never makes.

faults.quote: wore sweatshirts
faults.why: 'Hoodies' is the writer's concrete, culturally specific detail. 'Sweatshirts' flattens it.

faults.quote: I was the kind of person who has to get every little thing right, which was not much of an answer
faults.why: The writer said 'perfectionist', a stock answer the writer calls 'lame'. The paraphrase hides that it was the cliché answer, and 'not much of an answer' is weaker than 'lame'. It also leaves unclear why the answer was poor.

faults.quote: She said I probably did just fine.
faults.why: The writer's sister said 'nailed it', which is stronger. 'Just fine' lowers the reassurance and the hope that follows.

faults.quote: She was friendly, but there was an intensity about her all the same.
faults.why: This is generic formal prose, not Obama's cadence. There are no rhetorical triads, no 'Now,' or 'Look,' and no reflective widening from the particular to the general. Apart from 'Here's the thing,' the voice barely shows.

faults.quote: Here's the thing.
faults.why: This is a stock Obama tag, but it is bolted on as its own paragraph and reads as costume. It leads into an unremarkable sentence and gives no real turn.

faults.quote: One American’s story: “The manager was a woman named Priya.” — cites Weekly Address, 21 April 2012, ¶ 1
faults.why: The sentence is identical to the writer's, so no move was made. The citation does not describe an actual change.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1 (renders the writer’s ¶1):
  (no notes)
faults.why: The paragraph changed substantially ('hoodies' to 'sweatshirts', the invented lunch comparison, merged sentences) but none of it is reported.

faults.quote: Structure: Begins your paragraph 3, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: The notes describe the paragraph split only mechanically and do not say why the break helps.

faults.quote: I kept every fact and its order
faults.why: This is untrue given the lost 'hoodies', 'coffee', 'perfectionist' and 'nailed it'. It misleads the writer about what changed.

faults.quote: Practise joining two of your short sentences with “, and,”
faults.why: The rewrite barely does this. Only the first sentence uses ', and', and the paragraphs remain short and plain. The lesson claims a pattern the text does not show.

faults.quote: (“I'm just about broke”)
faults.why: The rewrite reads 'I am just about broke', so the quote is inexact. The lesson also says the voice 'ends on the need', but the rewrite adds no new move there.

judge.verdict: A clean, readable rewrite that keeps the story's order but makes several small changes: an invented lunch comparison, dropped 'hoodies' and 'perfectionist', and a weakened 'nailed it'. It has only a faint Obama flavour, mostly 'Here's the thing'. The notes cite a move that changed nothing and omit real changes, and the lesson overstates what was done.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They came with a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice, and his sister is kind of standoffish.

My mother fired up the oven for them right away. She wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single. Well, separated. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years.

rows.text: A new family moved in next door last weekend. They came with a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice, and his sister is kind of standoffish.

notes.text: The first paragraph gives the new family a mother ('The mom is kind of standoffish'), and the last says the dad is single, well, divorced. Those cannot both be true of one household. I made the second adult the dad's sister, so that a cold aunt and a warm father can share the house, and the dad can still be single and divorced in the last paragraph — which is what the mother's plan needs.
notes.after: His sister is kind of standoffish.

rows.text: My mother fired up the oven for them right away. She wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.
It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single. Well, separated. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years.

lessons: Your passage told the story in short, flat strokes; Obama builds each paragraph into a sentence or two that gathers the details and lands on what they mean. I turned your one-line observations into a single balanced sentence ("The dad seems nice, and his sister is kind of standoffish") and folded the mother's questions into a three-part list that shows her curiosity rather than stating it, ending on the verdict — "she has been trying to set me up for years" — the way he ends a paragraph on the turn to what comes next. Practise gathering several short sentences into one with ", and" and a colon before a list, so the telling moves forward instead of pausing at each fact.

outline.gist: A new family moved in next door, with a truck and two kids
The dad seems nice; the woman colder
The mother bakes and asks everything about them
The dad is a lawyer, single — divorced
The mother's look, the matchmaking plan

plan.gist: A new family moved in last weekend
plan.why: Open with the fact, plainly, as the writer did; then fill in the particulars.

plan.gist: The truck, the two kids, the warm dad, the colder sister
plan.why: One household in one or two observations; keep the two adults distinct so the later truth about the dad can stand.

plan.gist: The mother bakes and asks everything
plan.why: The mother's character comes through her doing and her questions — shown, not just said.

plan.gist: The dad is a lawyer, single
plan.why: The news lands after the scene, and it turns on what the mother wants to know.

plan.gist: The look, the matchmaking
plan.why: End on what it means: the verdict, with a land on hope.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother — 'The mom is kind of standoffish' — and your last says the dad is single, well, divorced. Those cannot both be true of the same household: if the dad is single, the woman next door is not his wife (and if she were his ex-wife, she would not be living there as 'the mom' of the household).
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the second adult someone who could share a household with a single, divorced father. Least change: 'The dad seems nice. His sister is kind of standoffish.' (His mother, an aunt, a roommate would serve equally.) This keeps the observational first paragraph — someone in the house is cold, someone is warm — and keeps 'the mom' out of the family, so the last paragraph's 'single... divorced' stands and the mother's matchmaking plan still works. Since the passage points toward the narrator and the widowed/divorced dad, the 'mom' can't be the dad's estranged wife in residence; a sister is the cleanest answer.

faults.quote: My mother fired up the oven for them right away.
faults.why: The original says she baked them cookies. 'Fired up the oven' drops the cookies, so the gift is lost and the gesture changes meaning.

faults.quote: Well, separated.
faults.why: The writer wrote 'divorced'. The rewrite changes the marital status without a note. 'Separated' also weakens the mother's matchmaking hope, and it clashes with the note, which says he is 'single and divorced'.

faults.quote: his sister is kind of standoffish
faults.why: The mending invents a sister. The woman's identity is a guess, and the rewrite does not offer it as one. It also fixes the contradiction, but a smoother fix would have been to make her a relative or to drop the 'mom' reading. The note states the invention as settled.

faults.quote: I made the second adult the dad's sister, so that a cold aunt and a warm father can share the house
faults.why: The note does not tell the writer that this is an invented fact they need to confirm. The other changes are unreported: 'came with' for 'have', 'fired up the oven' for 'baked cookies', 'separated' for 'divorced'. 'Paragraph 2: (no notes)' is false, since the paragraph was altered.

faults.quote: A new family moved in next door last weekend. They came with a huge truck and two little kids.
faults.why: This is almost the writer's own text. There is no Obama cadence: no balanced periods, no reflective widening to a larger point, no self-deprecating wit, no 'Now,' or 'Look,' turn. It reads as modern prose with a few words changed.

faults.quote: My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years.
faults.why: This only joins two sentences with a comma and a colon. Obama's characteristic moves are absent: the rueful aside, the tricolon building to a turn, the gentle generalisation about neighbours or mothers.

faults.quote: Practise gathering several short sentences into one with ", and" and a colon before a list
faults.why: The lesson claims the draft was reshaped into Obama-style periods, but the changes are minimal. It overstates what was done and teaches a thin, generic tip. 'Fired up the oven' is also not a list, and the three-part list was already the writer's.

faults.quote: My mother fired up the oven for them right away. She wanted to find out everything about them
faults.why: The outline promises a scene shown through her doing and her questions, but no scene is added. The 'how it is built' claims a restructure that the text does not carry out.

faults.quote: fired up the oven for them
faults.why: This is an odd, vague idiom. The reader is left to infer a gift, and the 'for them' sits oddly with the hospitality the sentence is meant to show.

judge.verdict: It catches the contradiction and mends it with a sister, but it never signals that the sister is an invention. It also drops the cookies, changes 'divorced' to 'separated', and barely touches the voice, so it reads as the writer's own text with small edits. The notes and lesson overclaim what was changed.

The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:
The party was at Jessica's house, and her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there, and the music was loud enough to shake the floor.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we didn't know many people. Then a tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris, and he was proud of himself, but he was funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes, and I thought he was rude. But later, after everyone else had left, I saw him helping clean up. Maybe I was wrong about him.

rows.text: The party was at Jessica's house, and her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there, and the music was loud enough to shake the floor.
I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we didn't know many people. Then a tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris, and he was proud of himself, but he was funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes, and I thought he was rude. But later, after everyone else had left, I saw him helping clean up. Maybe I was wrong about him.

lessons: The writer's sentences were short and staccato, while Obama builds long sentences by joining clauses with ", and" and lets the paragraph land on a turn. I merged the short sentences into balanced pairs — "The party was at Jessica's house, and her parents were out of town" — and ended on the turn from what happened to what it means in "Maybe I was wrong about him." To practise: join related facts into one sentence and let the last sentence of a paragraph carry the meaning.

outline.gist: Party at Jessica's house while her parents are away; everyone from school, loud music
Narrator stands in the kitchen with Emma, knowing few people; a tall guy Chris comes over, proud but funny
Chris insults the party; Emma rolls her eyes; narrator thinks him rude
Narrator sees Chris cleaning up alone and reconsiders

plan.gist: Party at Jessica's house, parents away, crowd and loud music
plan.why: The voice sets the scene plainly first, so the reader knows where we are before anyone speaks.

plan.gist: Narrator and Emma in the kitchen, knowing few; Chris arrives
plan.why: Name the people and their place among the crowd before the turn, so the story rests on particular faces.

plan.gist: Chris insults the party; Emma rolls her eyes; narrator judges him rude
plan.why: Let the insult land, then answer it with the narrator's judgment, not this but that — then correct the judgment.

plan.gist: Seeing Chris clean up, the narrator reconsiders
plan.why: The voice ends on the turn from what happened to what it means, in a short verdict.

faults.quote: the music was loud enough to shake the floor
faults.why: The writer said 'super loud'. The rewrite adds an invented physical image and raises the intensity, so it goes beyond the voice's commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: he was proud of himself, but he was funny
faults.why: 'Kind of arrogant' becomes 'proud of himself'. This drops the hedge 'kind of' and softens 'arrogant' into something nearer to a compliment, which shifts the narrator's feeling.

faults.quote: The party was at Jessica's house, and her parents were out of town.
faults.why: This is the writer's own plain prose with a comma and 'and' in place of a full stop. Nothing in it is characteristic of Obama: no reflective framing, no 'not this but that' balance, no rhythmic build, no wry self-aware aside.

faults.quote: Emma rolled her eyes, and I thought he was rude.
faults.why: Another simple stitching of two sentences. Obama's manner of weighing a judgment, and the outline's own 'this but that' move, never appear in the rewrite.

faults.quote: Maybe I was wrong about him.
faults.why: The ending is unchanged from the draft. It gets no Obama-style widening of the reflection, so the rewrite reads as modern prose lightly dressed up.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: All three paragraphs have empty notes, yet the text was changed: sentences merged, 'super loud' replaced, 'arrogant' replaced, the cleanup clause reordered. None of these changes is reported or sourced.

faults.quote: Obama builds long sentences by joining clauses with ", and" and lets the paragraph land on a turn.
faults.why: This is a thin and partly inaccurate account of Obama's style. It gives no concrete or sourced move, and the rewrite does not show the others the outline promised. The writer gets only a comma-splice tip.

faults.quote: Narrator sees Chris cleaning up alone and reconsiders
faults.why: The outline's 'alone' is not in the writer's text, which says he helped clean up after everyone left. The 'as the voice would build it' column also describes moves ('not this but that') that the rewrite never makes.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is faithful in sequence but barely changes the text. It is not recognisably Obama, and it swaps in a few words that shift 'super loud' and 'kind of arrogant'. The notes are empty and the lesson is generic, so the writer learns little.
