plan.why: the short verdict to land the joke and the honesty

faults.quote: the party was lame
faults.why: 'Lame' is a modern teen word kept as it stood. It jars in a Huck-style register, and Twain would have found a period equivalent (dull, poor, a failure). The rewrite changes 'boring' to 'dull' but leaves 'lame'.

faults.quote: and he was kind of stuck up, and kind of funny, too.
faults.why: The 'cumulative' sentence only joins clauses with 'and'. It has no Twain-style comic specificity, simile, or exaggeration, and the joke the lesson promises does not land. 'But also funny' was a contrast, and it is flattened into a plain pile-up. The voice is thin, mostly dialect spelling plus conjunctions.

faults.quote: her folks were out of town ... the people was dull
faults.why: The dialect is applied inconsistently: 'folks were' and 'everybody had gone' stay standard while 'people was' and 'begun' are non-standard. The result is patchy rather than a steady voice.

faults.quote: the music went at it so a body couldn't hear himself think
faults.why: This adds a consequence (nobody could think) that was not in the draft's 'super loud'. It is mild commentary, but it is an addition, and the notes do not report it.

faults.quote: I judged he was impolite
faults.why: 'Impolite' softens 'rude' and 'judged' slightly changes 'thought', so the strength of the feeling is reduced a little.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 1 has real changes ('folks', 'a body couldn't hear himself think') that go unreported. This hides the voice moves that teach the most.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 29, ¶ 32
faults.why: The chapter and paragraph citation is over-precise and doubtful. The note also does not flag the dialect changes ('begun', 'people was') in the same sentence.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the narrator's aside, Huck's way, to mark a personal verdict that is not a fact.
faults.why: The draft already said 'I thought he was rude', so 'I judged' is a word swap, not a liberty or an aside. The note also does not mention the added 'I thought to myself'.

faults.quote: I put the verdict in the narrator's own mouth with "I judged,"
faults.why: The verdict was already in the narrator's mouth in the draft ('I thought he was rude'). The lesson claims a move that did not happen, and 'one sentence do the work of three' is generic advice that the rewrite only weakly shows.

faults.quote: later seen cleaning up alone
faults.why: The outline says 'alone', which is not in the draft. The outline also says Twain would build the piece in the same order, so it gives the writer no real structural contrast to learn from.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps all the facts and feelings and stays clear, but the Twain voice is light, mostly 'and' joins and a few dialect words, and 'lame' is left in. The notes and lesson misdescribe what changed (the 'I judged' liberty) and skip paragraph 1, so the teaching is partly hollow.

yours:
I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
I needed milk, so I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was crowded, packed and alive, and a man in a hooded coat was blocking the whole aisle whilst he talked on a telephone.

I didn't want to be rude, so I said excuse me, and he paid me no more mind than if I was a post. By and by he moved, and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the counter, and I reckon I was scared, and that is the truth of it.

"Hey," she said; "long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said; "you too." I paid and left as fast as I could, and it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week, or for a longer spell than that.

rows.text: I needed milk, so I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was crowded, packed and alive, and a man in a hooded coat was blocking the whole aisle whilst he talked on a telephone.

notes.text: hoodie has no word of his; the voice names the garment by what it plainly is
notes.after: a man in a hooded coat

rows.text: I didn't want to be rude, so I said excuse me, and he paid me no more mind than if I was a post. By and by he moved, and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the counter, and I reckon I was scared, and that is the truth of it.

notes.after: I saw my ex at the counter, and I reckon I was scared, and that is the truth of it.

notes.text: panicked must come out; the voice names the feeling as the narrator would own it, without any new degree of alarm
notes.after: I reckon I was scared

rows.text: "Hey," she said; "long time no see. You look great."
"Thanks," I said; "you too." I paid and left as fast as I could, and it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week, or for a longer spell than that.

lessons: The writer's page is a quick list of short facts; Twain's manner is a man telling it aloud, joining the facts in long "and ... and ..." runs that turn at the end. I joined the sentences into a few cumulative sentences ("I needed milk, so I grabbed my keys and drove to the store"), let the ignoring land in a tall, straight-faced comparison ("he paid me no more mind than if I was a post"), and ended on a deadpan verdict ("or for a longer spell than that"). Practise stringing the facts on "and" and putting the joke, un-announced, at the tail of the sentence.

outline.gist: needs milk, drives to store
store crowded, aisle blocked by man on phone
excuse me ignored, finally gets milk
sees ex at checkout, panics
greeting and compliments
pays, leaves, calls it the most awkward ten minutes of the week

plan.gist: need of milk, grab keys, drive to store
plan.why: the need comes first; the errand follows in one run

plan.gist: crowded, a man blocking the aisle talking on his telephone
plan.why: the obstruction set plainly, the man seen and heard at once

plan.gist: not wanting to be rude, saying excuse me, being ignored, then at last getting the milk
plan.why: the small ordeal strung out and then released in one movement

plan.gist: sighting the ex at the counter and the alarm of it
plan.why: the worst of the trouble lands after the minor one, so it lands hardest

plan.gist: her hey and compliments, his thanks and you too
plan.why: the civilities, kept short, as people actually talk

plan.gist: paying, leaving fast, the verdict on the ten minutes
plan.why: the escape and then the deadpan judgment to close

faults.quote: or for a longer spell than that
faults.why: The writer's verdict is simply 'the most awkward ten minutes of my week'. This tag adds a vague claim that the awkwardness lasted longer, which changes the meaning.

faults.quote: or for a longer spell than that
faults.why: The tail is garbled. It does not follow from 'most awkward ten minutes of my week' and reads as a riddle, not a deadpan joke. The lesson praises it as the ending, which makes the failure worse.

faults.quote: I reckon I was scared, and that is the truth of it
faults.why: 'Basically panicked' becomes 'scared', which is a weaker feeling. 'That is the truth of it' is added filler.

faults.quote: packed and alive
faults.why: The writer said 'super crowded'. 'Alive' is invented colour. 'Packed' also stands in for the intensifier without being named as a change.

faults.quote: "Hey," she said; "long time no see. You look great."
faults.why: The dialogue is left in modern idiom ('Hey', 'You look great', 'ex', 'checkout') and joined by an odd semicolon. It does not sound like Twain's dialogue, so the voice is only patchy.

faults.quote: whilst he talked on a telephone
faults.why: 'Whilst' is a British-leaning register that clashes with the American vernacular elsewhere ('reckon', 'by and by', 'if I was a post'). The narrator's voice is inconsistent.

faults.quote: I needed milk, so I grabbed my keys and drove to the store.
faults.why: The lesson promises long 'and… and…' runs, but the rewrite mostly just joins the writer's sentences with commas. The Twainian build-up and turn is thin.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 19, ¶ 32
faults.why: The citation is precise-looking but implausible, since nothing in that paragraph matches this line. A confident but unreliable source misleads the writer.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 3 and 4 carry no notes, yet the rewrite changed things there: the 'post' simile, 'by and by', the semicolon dialogue, and the new ending tag. Most real changes go unreported.

faults.quote: without any new degree of alarm
faults.why: The note claims the feeling's degree is unchanged, but 'panicked' became 'scared'. The note is inaccurate.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the story's order and has a couple of fair Twain touches ('no more mind than if I was a post', 'by and by'). But the closing tag is a garbled addition, 'panicked' is softened, the dialogue stays modern, and the notes are sparse and inaccurate with a doubtful citation.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
Hi, team—

Quick word of it: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday.

Legal has not signed off on the pricing page yet, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon, and if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks, Sam.

rows.text: Hi, team—
Quick word of it: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday.

notes.text: Begins your paragraph 2, which the next paragraph finishes.

rows.text: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page yet, and I don't want us shipping without it.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 2, given a paragraph of its own.
The narrator takes the writer's own wish and states it as his flat verdict; a voice may frame what is there.
notes.after: I don't want us shipping without it

rows.text: Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon, and if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.
Thanks, Sam.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's page is short, clipped, businesslike notes, where Twain would have the narrator talk it out in one run, joining the requests into a single cumulative "and ... and ..." breath. I joined the two requests into one sentence ("Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon, and if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow"), so the business reads as a man speaking it aloud rather than a list. I also let him say the absurd thing flatly—"Legal has not signed off ... yet, and I don't want us shipping without it"—so the mild joke that the law holds up a launch just sits there and lands at the end, never explained.

outline.gist: Hi team
launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal hasn't signed off on the pricing page; don't want to ship without it
please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
if blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow
Thanks, Sam

plan.gist: Hi team
plan.why: Keep the writer's greeting; it opens the letter as any letter opens.

plan.gist: launch moves Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: The news first, before the reason; tell them what is changed before why it changed, so no one is left wondering.

plan.gist: Legal hasn't signed off; I don't want us shipping without it
plan.why: The reason naturally follows the news, in a cumulative and-sentence, and it lands the mild irony that the law is what holds up a launch.

plan.gist: have your sections of the deck done Wednesday noon
plan.why: Now the work the news asks for, still in the same breath, so the business reads as one thing.

plan.gist: if blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow
plan.why: The second request is the shorter turn, the plain warning, saved for the end where it lands hardest.

plan.gist: Thanks, Sam
plan.why: Keep the writer's close, as the letter's form demands.

faults.quote: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page yet, and I don't want us shipping without it.
faults.why: This is nearly the writer's sentence with 'hasn't' expanded to 'has not'. There is no Twain syntax, vocabulary, hyperbole, dry understatement or vernacular. It reads as the original email lightly reformatted, not as Twain.

faults.quote: Quick word of it: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday.
faults.why: The only change is 'Quick update' to 'Quick word of it', which is a mild, unidiomatic tweak. It is not a recognizable Twain move.

faults.quote: Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon, and if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.
faults.why: The rewrite keeps the writer's words and only joins the two requests with a comma. It has no Twain cadence, digression or comic turn.

faults.quote: Quick word of it:
faults.why: 'word of it' is an odd phrase with no clear antecedent. It reads like a garble rather than idiomatic Twain or idiomatic email.

faults.quote: Hi, team—
faults.why: The added comma and em dash are awkward punctuation for a greeting. They do not sound like Twain and make the opening stilted.

faults.quote: Begins your paragraph 2, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: The notes say paragraph 2 is split across two paragraphs, but the rewrite's paragraph 2 and 3 do not actually split the writer's paragraph at a sentence boundary. They are the writer's own ¶2 sentences, and the 'which the next paragraph finishes' claim is confusing. The notes also point to a narrator, but the text has none.

faults.quote: The narrator takes the writer's own wish and states it as his flat verdict; a voice may frame what is there.
faults.why: No narrator exists in the rewrite, and the sentence is virtually unchanged, so this claims a liberty that was not taken. The notes name no real moves and cite no sources.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Most paragraphs have no notes, although the rewrite changed the wording ('update' to 'word of it', 'hasn't' to 'has not', the joined requests). The notes miss the actual changes.

faults.quote: I also let him say the absurd thing flatly—"Legal has not signed off ... yet, and I don't want us shipping without it"—so the mild joke that the law holds up a launch just sits there and lands at the end, never explained.
faults.why: The lesson claims a joke and a flat Twain delivery that are not in the text. The sentence is plain, and the joke does not land at the end because the request follows it. The lesson is also inaccurate about the rewrite, which does not read as a run of 'and ... and ...' clauses. It teaches nothing reusable.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam.
faults.why: The sign-off is collapsed onto one line. This loses the email's closing form (Thanks, then the name on a new line). The 'how it is built' also claims a cumulative single-breath structure that the rewrite splits into separate short paragraphs.

faults.quote: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page yet, and I don't want us shipping without it.
faults.why: The rewrite separates the news from the reason into their own paragraphs, while the stated plan says the business should read as one thing in a single breath. This contradicts the build the rewrite claims.

judge.verdict: This is essentially the writer's email with trivial edits and no real Twain voice. The notes and lesson describe moves, such as a narrator and a cumulative breath, that are not in the text, so the teaching value is very low.

Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: Clean't the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, and she talked a solid hour about her neighbor's cat. Come evening I was tired out, but I was proud of myself, too, which was a curious thing.

rows.text: Clean't the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, and she talked a solid hour about her neighbor's cat. Come evening I was tired out, but I was proud of myself, too, which was a curious thing.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: I was proud of myself, too, which was a curious thing
notes.cite: Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, ch. 32, ¶ 2

lessons: The writer's page reads like a diary list; Twain's narrator talks it, so I ran the three chores on one plain "and... and..." line and let the grandmother's hour on the cat finish the sentence deadpan. Where the writer said "weirdly proud," I kept the pride but dropped the writer's phrase, and turned it with an aside ("which was a curious thing") so the oddness sits without being explained.

outline.gist: cleaned gutters, fixed sink, called grandmother who talked an hour about her neighbor's cat
exhausted but weirdly proud

plan.gist: cleaned gutters, fixed the sink, called grandmother
plan.why: the news first, plain, in the order it happened

plan.gist: an hour on her neighbor's cat
plan.why: the longest thing of the day gets the longest clause, and the joke lands deadpan at the end

plan.gist: tired but proud
plan.why: the short turn that closes it, the pride let alone so it sits

faults.quote: Clean't the gutters
faults.why: The writer's 'Saturday' is gone. The framing 'Things I did on Saturday' is dropped and nothing in the rewrite replaces the day.

faults.quote: Clean't the gutters
faults.why: 'Clean't' is not a word or a real Twain dialect form. It reads as a typo or garble, and it opens the piece badly.

faults.quote: I was tired out, but I was proud of myself, too
faults.why: 'Exhausted' is softened to 'tired out'. The 'but' contrast is also flattened by the added 'too', which shifts the degree of the feeling.

faults.quote: which was a curious thing
faults.why: This is a generic aside. Twain would give it a comic extension, an exaggeration or a mock-solemn comparison. The passage as a whole is thin modern prose with a few colloquial touches ('Come evening', 'a solid hour') and little Twain wit.

faults.quote: cites Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, ch. 32, ¶ 2
faults.why: Joan of Arc is a poor and probably fabricated source for a deadpan comic aside. The chapter and paragraph citation looks unverifiable, and Huck Finn or Life on the Mississippi would suit better.

faults.quote: [structure] Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The notes are sparse. They do not mention the dropped 'Saturday', the dropped first-person framing, the deadpan placement of the cat, or the weakened 'exhausted'.

faults.quote: I ran the three chores on one plain "and... and..." line
faults.why: The lesson is concrete but narrow, and the stated reasons are thin. It gives no reusable technique for building Twain's humor, such as understatement or exaggeration.

judge.verdict: Fidelity is mostly preserved, but the rewrite drops 'Saturday' and softens 'exhausted'. The garbled 'Clean't' and a generic aside leave the voice thin, and the Joan of Arc citation and sparse notes weaken the teaching value.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town ought to shut Main Street against the teams and wagons on a Saturday and a Sunday, and let the people have it.

Because as it is, the putting of a rig downtown is a thing to make a body lose heart, and the sidewalks are so narrow that a person with a baby-carriage can't turn around in them, and I do believe if they were any narrower the people would die.

Other towns have done the same, and their shops are doing better than ever they did before.

Now there be some owners of shops that will stand up and complain that the customers can't get at them. But they'll get used to it. And the honest truth is, the most of the people walk from the stable anyway.

We ought to try it out this coming summer, and that's the end of it.

rows.text: Our town ought to shut Main Street against the teams and wagons on a Saturday and a Sunday, and let the people have it.

notes.text: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
the voice names the days in his own way, since he has no word for weekend; keeps the matter, plain
notes.after: on a Saturday and a Sunday

rows.text: Because as it is, the putting of a rig downtown is a thing to make a body lose heart, and the sidewalks are so narrow that a person with a baby-carriage can't turn around in them, and I do believe if they were any narrower the people would die.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 1, given a paragraph of its own.

rows.text: Other towns have done the same, and their shops are doing better than ever they did before.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 1, given a paragraph of its own.

rows.text: Now there be some owners of shops that will stand up and complain that the customers can't get at them. But they'll get used to it. And the honest truth is, the most of the people walk from the stable anyway.
We ought to try it out this coming summer, and that's the end of it.

lessons: The writer's page states an argument in short, flat, modern sentences; Twain would let the town talk it, piling the complaint high in one long "and ... and" run that turns at the end ("if they were any narrower the people would die") and never explains the joke. The objection gets its puncture last and shortest ("they'll get used to it"), and the whole closes on a short verdict. To practise: say the absurd thing deadpan and put the turn at the end of a long cumulative sentence.

outline.gist: close Main Street to cars on weekends
parking is a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow
other towns did it, shops better than ever
business owners will complain customers can't reach them
they'll get used to it; most walk from the garage anyway
try it this summer

plan.gist: put the plain proposal first, town talking
plan.why: the voice states the business flat, then lets the jest out slow

plan.gist: the downtown's trouble, piled up
plan.why: a long complaint gathers weight, then turns

plan.gist: other towns and their shops
plan.why: the proof comes before the objection, so the objection answers to something solid

plan.gist: some owners will complain
plan.why: the voice gets the objection out in the owners' own form, to be punctured

plan.gist: they'll get used to it; most walk anyway
plan.why: the turn lands short and deadpan, the punch last

plan.gist: try it this summer
plan.why: close on the verdict, short, the matter settled

faults.quote: and I do believe if they were any narrower the people would die
faults.why: Invents a new claim (hyperbolic death from narrow sidewalks) and a first-person aside not in the draft. This is added content, not commentary on what is there, and it overstates the feeling.

faults.quote: against the teams and wagons
faults.why: The draft says cars. Replacing cars with teams and wagons changes the proposal's content. Closing a street to horse traffic is a different matter, and the era swap is not flagged as a substitution of fact.

faults.quote: from the stable anyway
faults.why: The draft says garage. A stable is not a parking garage, and this changes the concrete fact, which also muddles the argument that people already walk from where they park.

faults.quote: and that's the end of it.
faults.why: Adds a note of finality and bossiness not in the writer's mild 'We should try it this summer.' The point of a trial is that it is provisional, so this contradicts the sense of 'try'.

faults.quote: the putting of a rig downtown is a thing to make a body lose heart
faults.why: Muddled. 'Parking is a nightmare' means finding a space. 'Putting a rig downtown' reads as bringing a rig there at all. The period-voice patching leaves the point of the complaint unclear.

faults.quote: Now there be some owners of shops
faults.why: 'there be' is stage-rustic dialect, not Twain's narrator voice. It is costume rather than his syntax.

faults.quote: Because as it is,
faults.why: A sentence fragment opened with 'Because' cut off from the previous paragraph. This is not how Twain builds a cumulative run, and it breaks the single-sentence pile-up the lesson claims.

faults.quote: their shops are doing better than ever they did before
faults.why: Redundant and clumsy. It is not a Twain wit move, just archaic filler.

faults.quote: a person with a baby-carriage can't turn around in them
faults.why: Modern 'person' beside the period 'body' is inconsistent, and the strollers detail is awkwardly reworded.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the voice names the days in his own way, since he has no word for weekend; keeps the matter, plain
faults.why: Inaccurate and incoherent. Twain did have 'weekend' available in sense, and the note ignores the bigger liberties: cars to teams and wagons, garage to stable, the added death joke. It is also garbled.

faults.quote: Structure: The rest of your paragraph 1, given a paragraph of its own.
faults.why: Notes are mechanical and repetitive. They name no Twain moves with sources, and do not report the added hyperbole or anachronism swaps.

faults.quote: piling the complaint high in one long "and ... and" run that turns at the end
faults.why: The lesson describes a long cumulative sentence, but the rewrite splits it into separate paragraphs with a fragment, so it does not show the move it teaches. It also praises the invented joke as the model, which the draft never contained.

faults.quote: Other towns have done the same, and their shops are doing better than ever they did before.
faults.why: Splitting the draft's first paragraph into three short paragraphs breaks the unit and the build the outline describes (one long run). The call at the end is also weakened by the added finality.

judge.verdict: The rewrite swaps in period props (teams, wagons, stable) that change the facts, adds an invented death joke and a bossy ending, and its voice is a rustic costume rather than Twain's. The notes miss these liberties and the lesson praises a move the rewrite does not actually perform.

yours:
I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite:
I've never rightly seen Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy, and he allows it was the best one he ever had.

rows.text: I've never rightly seen Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

notes.text: Your first sentence says you have never been to Paris; your second says the last time you were there it rained all week and you spent the trip at the embassy. Those two cannot both be true of one visit. I changed the denial so it denies having properly seen Paris, not having gone there: the claim softens to 'never rightly seen Paris,' which every later sentence allows, since a week of rain inside an embassy is hardly seeing the place.
notes.after: I've never rightly seen Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week

rows.text: We spent most of the trip at the embassy, and he allows it was the best one he ever had.

notes.text: 'allows' is the narrator's deadpan verb for a claim it would be trouble to dispute, softening the brother's verdict without adding any new fact.
notes.after: and he allows it was the best one he ever had

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage states the facts and lets the reader add the joke; his manner deadpans the facts so the joke lands on the last line without being explained. You lean on "still says it was the best vacation"; I rendered it as "he allows it was the best one he ever had," letting the narrator's flat "allows" carry the absurdity, and put it last so it turns the whole story. Practise ending a sentence on the punch and never explaining it, and running the proof together in one long "and" before the turn.

outline.gist: never been to Paris
last time rained all week, brother lost passport
spent the trip at the embassy
brother calls it his best vacation

plan.gist: never properly seen Paris
plan.why: the denial opens flat and his manner loves a flat claim the rest will quietly undo

plan.gist: rained the whole week, passport gone on the second day
plan.why: the proof piles up in one long and-and that ends on the joke of the passport

plan.gist: the trip spent at the embassy
plan.why: the news lands here, plain, after the build-up

plan.gist: brother calls it the best vacation
plan.why: the punchline goes last, deadpan, and never explains itself

sense.problem: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris; your second says he was there the last time, for a week, at the embassy.
sense.quote: I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week
sense.resolution: Either drop the denial or change it to a denial of the place's charm, not of the visit: “I've never been to the Paris of the postcards” / “I've never really seen Paris.” That keeps the opening claim and every following sentence true of one trip. If the intent is a flat contradiction, that intent cannot be told from the words as written, and the passage reads as an error rather than a joke; the least change that makes all four sentences agree is to deny having seen Paris properly, not having gone.

sense.problem: Echo of a Twain scene: tourists solemnly admiring famous sights and being let down (The Innocents Abroad).
sense.quote: We spent most of the trip at the embassy.
sense.resolution: A faint echo only — the trip that never reaches the thing it was for — and not a true echo of that book's scene by tourists at a shrine. A rewrite may borrow only the comic habit of measuring the trip in what actually happened (hours at an embassy) rather than in what was supposed to happen; nothing of the sights themselves is here to echo.

faults.quote: I've never rightly seen Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.
faults.why: Barely changed from the draft. It keeps the modern contraction and flat syntax, and has no Twain-style elaboration, simile, or digression, so it reads as the original with a few folksy words swapped in.

faults.quote: he allows it was the best one he ever had
faults.why: One dialect verb is the only real Twain touch in the whole piece. The rest is plain modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: the best one he ever had
faults.why: 'Vacation' is dropped for 'one', whose antecedent is unclear because the sentence's nearest noun is 'trip'. 'Still says' is also lost, so the brother's lasting, repeated insistence turns into a one-time allowance and the comic persistence vanishes.

faults.quote: I've never rightly seen Paris.
faults.why: The mending is weak. 'Last time I was there' still implies several visits, so 'never rightly seen' only half resolves the contradiction. The fix also asserts that the embassy prevented seeing the city, which the text never states.

faults.quote: 'allows' is the narrator's deadpan verb for a claim it would be trouble to dispute
faults.why: This is a muddled justification. It also contradicts the lesson's claim that 'allows' makes the verdict absurd and softens it, since softening the brother's verdict is not what the draft's 'still says' does.

faults.quote: the proof piles up in one long and-and that ends on the joke of the passport
faults.why: The rewrite has no long and-and construction. The first paragraph is unchanged, so this describes a move that was not made. The lesson's 'running the proof together in one long "and"' is likewise unsupported.

faults.quote: Practise ending a sentence on the punch and never explaining it, and running the proof together in one long "and" before the turn.
faults.why: The advice isn't grounded in the rewrite, which changed almost nothing. The writer can't see how Twain would actually build the passage, and no sources are cited for the moves.

faults.quote: We spent most of the trip at the embassy, and he allows it was the best one he ever had.
faults.why: Merging the two sentences removes the beat before the punchline, so the deadpan drop is weaker. The notes also claim the paragraph order was rebuilt when it was kept.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the contradiction and mends it, but only lightly, and it is almost unchanged from the draft, with one dialect verb standing in for Twain. The notes and lesson claim moves, such as the long and-chain, that are not in the text.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we ought to work but four days to the week, and let it go at that. The people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has quit, and that settles a good deal of it. There's studies, too, that show a man does as much work in four days as he does in six, and sometimes more. And it would help us get men, besides.

I know it's risky, and the customers might not stand for it. But we could try it for three months and see how it comes out.

rows.text: I think we ought to work but four days to the week, and let it go at that. The people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has quit, and that settles a good deal of it. There's studies, too, that show a man does as much work in four days as he does in six, and sometimes more. And it would help us get men, besides.

notes.text: the narrator's deadpan verdict on the engineer quitting, framing the matter the voice's own way; it is the teller summing up what the writer's two facts already imply
notes.after: and that settles a good deal of it

rows.text: I know it's risky, and the customers might not stand for it. But we could try it for three months and see how it comes out.

lessons: Your six short, bare statements become one man telling a proposition aloud, and the difference is the run of it. Where you wrote "People are burned out and our best engineer just quit," I piled the clauses on "and" so the trouble mounts and lands on the quit man ("the people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has quit, and that settles a good deal of it"); that is the cumulative move, and the teller's verdict makes one sentence do the work of three of yours. And I stated the joke flat instead of pointing at it: "a man does as much work in four days as he does in six, and sometimes more" — the deadpan lets the absurdity sit, the "and sometimes more" saved for the last word where it can land. Practise ending your sentences on the strongest word, and joining reasons with "and" rather than listing them, so the reader is carried along to the point.

outline.gist: switch to a four-day week
people are burned out, best engineer quit
studies show productivity holds or rises
helps hiring
risky, clients may dislike
try it three months and see

plan.gist: work only four days to the week
plan.why: the voice states the scheme plainly up front, as a man making a proposition aloud

plan.gist: people wore out, best engineer quit, in one long 'and' run
plan.why: the teller piles the trouble before the remedy, letting the run build and land on the quit man

plan.gist: a man does as much in four days as six, sometimes more
plan.why: the absurd result stated flatly, the 'and sometimes more' saved for the end as the joke

plan.gist: helps get men besides
plan.why: a short sentence after the long one, as a turn

plan.gist: risky, customers might not stand it
plan.why: the honest objection before the answer, so the trial lands hardest

plan.gist: try it three months and see how it comes out
plan.why: the modest close, the voice not over-pressing his own scheme

faults.quote: a man does as much work in four days as he does in six, and sometimes more
faults.why: The writer said productivity 'stays the same or goes up' under a four-day week. The rewrite invents a six-day baseline and a different claim, since the company presumably works five days. It also restates the studies' finding falsely.

faults.quote: and let it go at that
faults.why: Adds a rhetorical flourish that changes the force of the claim into a take-it-or-leave-it stance. It sits oddly with the tentative, collegial proposal and is not reported.

faults.quote: and that settles a good deal of it
faults.why: This is an added judgment: the writer never said the burnout and the resignation settle the matter. The note admits the addition but calls it a liberty. It also shifts the writer's reasoning toward a stronger, more certain claim.

faults.quote: the best engineer we had has quit
faults.why: Drops 'just' (recency), which was part of why the writer raised it. The 'we had' also hints at a finality the writer didn't state.

faults.quote: And it would help us get men, besides.
faults.why: Reads as plain modern prose with a few period words. It lacks Twain's characteristic hyperbole, mock-gravity, or concrete comic image, so the voice is only lightly costumed.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the narrator's deadpan verdict on the engineer quitting
faults.why: Only one note is given. It does not flag the 'six days' change, 'let it go at that', the 'and' clause-piling, or the dialect choices ('There's studies', 'wore out'), and gives no sources for the moves. The notes under-report real changes.

faults.quote: the deadpan lets the absurdity sit, the "and sometimes more" saved for the last word
faults.why: The lesson praises as a joke the very phrase that distorts the writer's claim. The writer is taught to treat an invented figure as a craft success. The 'one sentence do the work of three' claim is also muddled.

faults.quote: a short sentence after the long one, as a turn
faults.why: The outline describes the hiring sentence as short, but it is nearly as long as the preceding ones. The description is inaccurate.

judge.verdict: The structure is kept and the diction is lightly period-flavoured, but the rewrite invents a 'six days' comparison that misstates the writer's evidence and adds an editorial verdict. The notes and lesson fail to report these changes and even praise them, and the Twain voice stays thin.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana put off our dinner I wasn't the least bit put out. Honest, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I am not proud of that, either.

I told her it was all right, and we would do it another time. I don't reckon we will.

rows.text: When Dana put off our dinner I wasn't the least bit put out. Honest, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I am not proud of that, either.
I told her it was all right, and we would do it another time. I don't reckon we will.

notes.text: the voice lets the narrator's polite answer show itself for a fib, since the past week's dread is on record; it frames, it adds nothing new
notes.after: I told her it was all right

lessons: Your chief difference from Twain is compression: you say the whole matter in five clipped lines, where he would let it run in the voice of a man talking, and put the joke last. I made the narrator talk as Huck does — \"put off,\" \"the least bit put out,\" \"I don't reckon we will\" — and kept each feeling plain, then closed on the honest doubt so the turn lands on \"we will.\" Practise the cumulative sentence: let the clauses string on \"and\" and save the short verdict for the end where it can strike.

outline.gist: Dana cancels dinner, narrator feels no upset
relief
dreaded it all week, not proud
tells her it is fine, another time
doesn't think they will

plan.gist: the cancellation arrives
plan.why: the voice opens with the plain fact before any feeling, so the relief lands against it

plan.gist: relief confessed flat
plan.why: the deadpan verdict, short, after the long fact

plan.gist: dreaded it all week, not proud
plan.why: the narrator turns the joke on himself, as Huck does

plan.gist: told her it was fine, another time
plan.why: the lie to be civil comes after the true feeling, so the reader knows it

plan.gist: doesn't think they will
plan.why: the honest doubt last, where the joke lands

faults.quote: and I am not proud of that, either.
faults.why: "either" is added and implies a prior thing the narrator is not proud of; the original has no such earlier item, so it adds a slight meaning.

faults.quote: I wasn't the least bit put out.
faults.why: Changes "upset" to "put out" and "at all" to "the least bit"; roughly the same meaning but slightly milder, and "put off" followed by "put out" is a clumsy echo.

faults.quote: When Dana put off our dinner I wasn't the least bit put out. Honest, I was relieved.
faults.why: The rewrite is nearly the original with a few word swaps. It lacks Twain's cumulative sentences, deadpan hyperbole, concrete comic detail, and ironic framing. It reads as modern prose in light costume.

faults.quote: Honest, I was relieved.
faults.why: "Honest" as an adverb is a dialect gesture, but it is thin; there is no extended humorous self-indictment or simile as Twain would supply.

faults.quote: put off our dinner I wasn't the least bit put out
faults.why: Repeated "put" creates an unintended pun or jingle that feels clumsy rather than humorous.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 1 had several changes (put off, put out, Honest, the whole week, either) and none are named, so the writer cannot see the moves.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the voice lets the narrator's polite answer show itself for a fib, since the past week's dread is on record; it frames, it adds nothing new
faults.why: Describes a liberty that the rewrite does not actually make. Paragraph 2 only swaps "fine" for "all right" and "I don't think" for "I don't reckon", and nothing frames the answer as a fib. The note is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Practise the cumulative sentence: let the clauses string on "and" and save the short verdict for the end
faults.why: The rewrite does not do this (it keeps the original's short sentences), so the advice is not demonstrated in the text. The claim that the rewrite is longer or talkier than the original is also false. The lesson is therefore largely ungrounded.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: setting (the cancellation arrives...
faults.why: The outline claims a restructuring (plain fact first, etc.) but the rewrite keeps the writer's exact order and sentence plan, so the stated structure is not what was done.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and feelings but is mostly a light word swap that barely sounds like Twain, and it adds an unwarranted "either". The notes and lesson describe moves (cumulative sentences, framing the fib) that the text does not make, so the teaching value is low.
